The Sensational Alex Harvey Band THE ROXY, L A — As a small child I was notably frightened by a band with an ad- jective in its name and consequently in these later years have shied away from such modest outgrowths of rock ego. The Sensational Alex Harvey Band has cured me for life much to the dismay of my rockiatrist Alex Harvey, vocals, was backed by four musicians (keyboards, drums, guitar, and bass) each of which played such an intrical part of the sound that it is impossible to single one out for special merit They reflected and complemented each other with the spontaneity of music just being mass written No one un- derstands this relationship better than Harvey who knows when to stand back and let the band have at it Most memora- ble of these times was when he ascend- ed to the mid-audience table tops for his salute of pride, "That's my band!" It was the light-hearted presence and pure goodwill nature of Harvey that stabilized the momentum as the show in- tertwined serious music spiced with a comedic approach and custom made theatrics The Roxy fit the band of Scot- tish origin like a stateside womb continued on pg. 50 Willie Nelson Sweethearts Of The Rodeo TROUBADOUR. LA — And the contin- uing saga of America pushes out about a country mile further A year ago Willie Nelson played this club to the virtual blind spot of his peers and public, but for what might be best described as a "small, vocal minority." One year later (now), backed by the weight of a number one single, Blue Eyes Cryin' In The Rain," and a brilliant (and hot) conceptual album, "Red Headed Stranger," he has returned in a triumph of sorts With full label (Colum- bia) support and a live broadcast over KWST-FM at his disposal, he blew 'em away On the basis of commercial sales, this story is nothing out of the ordinary So, what's the haps? It's called change While his artistic performance is necessarily the bottom line, pure auditory appeal is only half of what Willie Nelson represents to country music And because country music com- mands the attention of a major portion of the American public, it is significant that any change within that form is born of and has bearing upon a much wider social spectrum than is perceptable to the naked ear Since the steamrolling influence the four Beatles commanded over our culture, the natural pastime has been standing watch for the next aggressor(s). It is doubtful that Willie Nelson could or ever would be willing to try and put over such a force on the people — it isn't his nature to dress up for the occasion And that, in itself, defines the difference of style that separates him from the mainstream of country Compared with Willie, nearly everybody else in that end of the business is just trying too ns. d to be the star It is therefore both obvious and perti- nent that Willie Nelson has been re- garded by some within that mainstream as a misfit, a troublemaker and probably an object of no small amount of jealousy A misfit because he performs in tennis shoes and a scarf/sweatband instead of diamond rings and "suits" designed by Nudie A troublemaker because he makes no continued on pg 51 cashbox Bob Dylan And The Rolling Thunder Revue PALACE THEATER, WATERBURY, CONN — The traveling troupe of troubadors arrived relatively unan- nounced to present their new concept of living room entertainment. The stage was set in a semi-circle of amps and acoustic guitars on a huge persian rug. The standing room only crowd held that sizzling edge of excitement that is only to be expected prior to a Bob Dylan performance, something entirely dif- ferent, an historical event. The players walked on stage and that sizzling edge immediately transformed to rolling thunder, deafening in apprecia- tion The first segment consisted of what was to be the backup band throughout the show. Each member stepping up and doing one of their own numbers Bobby Neuwirth acted as MC and leader with Rockin' Rob Stoner on bass and Mick Ronson (of David bowie fame) on guitar. Ronee Blakely was then called out to join in. Ramblin' Jack Elliot, the Brooklyn Cowboy, arrived picking and yodeling through "Mule Skinner Blues" and "Pret- ty Boy Floyd” and finally Roger McGuinn joined in on banjo. Neuwirth then stepped up and said "I want you to meet another friend " The rolling thunder became an explosion as Dylan entered Right out of "Pat Garrett And Billy The Kid" brown hat with flowers, vest, ever present scarf Dylan and Neuwirth: "When I Paint My Masterpiece,” sensational in its lack of polish . "It Ain't Me Babe," Dylan spin- ning toward the audience at the end singing through his harmonica, frantic ovation . "Hard Rain's A Gonna Fall," rockin' rollin' Dylan, dancing, laughing, at ease . seems to perform songs dif- ferently from original conceptions Scarlet Rivera on fiddle for the last number, Isis, before intermission Curtains still down . "Blowin' In The Wind," Dylan and Baez together, acoustic The band re-enters, curtains up, "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine," "I Shall Be Released" Dylan and Baez complementing harmony Baez, now alone, with "Diamonds And Rust," her song to Dylan, standing ovation "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot," "Joe Hill," "The Night They Drove Old Dixie Down" interlaced with Lily Tomlin imitations Loosest, most buoyant Joan Baez to date McGuinn reappears, jolly (those were the vibes), “Chestnut Mare," “Eight Miles High" . . well rehearsed, reminiscent of the Byrds The stage clears, the master re-enters, acoustic guitar, harmonica brace, black leather jacket with the always ap- propriate "Simple Twist Of Fate” again in a new style When the Rolling Thunder, the whole package, comes back it's "Hurricane" time Utterly powerful, Dylan’s clarity and emotion move the crowd, Rivera's timely fiddle infiltrations add dimension Some new tunes from the upcoming LP then "Knockin' On Heaven's Door," the whole band joining on harmonies, Neuwirth alternating verses with Dylan coup de grace, as the whole of the Rolling Thunder Revue (Allen Ginsberg and David Blue included) joined together for Woody Guthrie "This Land Is My Land" . inspirational! The show was a success, no less. His creative talents have paved the way for many musicians to follow, as in his influence in helping to create the "Bay Area funk" sound Hancock has also been in- strumental in the "new directions music” of Miles Davis a few years back. In his performance here, Hancock successfully joined these two influences, with a sound that kept the packed house mov- ing while never losing coherency The show opened with the familiar tune "Watermelon Man' 1 from the "Headhunter" album The show moved right along with Hancock doubling on electric piano and synthesizer, exchang- ing riffs with the very talented Bennie Maupin on saxes and Blackbyrd McKnight on lead guitar. Also included in the evening's itinerary were pieces off Hancock's latest Columbia LP, "Manchild." Coming back for his much demanded encore, Hancock did his old single "Chameleon " Herbie Hancock is always a treat for the creative ear The opening act was Casablanca re- cording artist Hugh Masekela Masekela, as well as his band, is of direct African decent, thus an inevitable African beat was present throughout the show. The set began and ended with the conga player alone on stage pounding his primal beat in unison with his poetry and African chants. Much of the material performed was from Masakela's latest LP, "The Boy's Doin' It.” Masekela plays a masterful trumpet, and also sings along with the rest of his band With lots of percussion and chanting the music en- ters your adrenalin glands, and whether voluntarily or not, you find yourself in a rhythmic twitch b.s. Break- ing up with your old man or lady. Realiz- ing a relationship is making it or falling apart. We’ve all been through it so, in a personal musical sense, it is the easiest to relate to. Maxine Seller's Troubadour outing worked on a whole lot of levels but her forays into the streets where the heart lives proved the most endearing, Maxine (a Capitol gut-level) derives her performing posture from the classic belter's stance. The mind's eye forms re- ality on a literal range and, in Maxine's case, memories segue to vocals for an overall feel that is beyond a doubt. But the course of Maxine's set was not totally rooted in hardness Her songs often relfected a sense of spirit; laughing at the cold facts of life as well as dealing with them. continued on pg. 50 Charley Pride Gary Stewart Dave And Sugar FELT FORUM, NYC — This show marked Pride's Manhattan debut, strange considering his sturdy reputa- tion in the country music field It was an all RCA show, part of the Al Aronowitz helmed "Country In New York" series and both shows were nearly clean Pride himself sang for one hour, repris- ing most of his early material and keep- ing well in the field of country love songs, that is, love lost, unrequited, and guilty. Around 75 percent of his material was confined to this genre of country music — "Does my ring hurt your finger when you go out at night?" and "The likes of me don’t fit with you" he sings. It is a wise decision because such songs are the bedrock of country music, im- pervious to fad and fashions, resistant to now country, outlaw country or whatever. z&shbox/news kBC Claims ADI Measurement Shows Audience Increase NEW YORK — Area of Dominant Influ- ence (ADI) measurement techniques, currently being used by the ABC Radio Network research department which sponsored network radio's first national ADI measurement, showed that radio network tabulated audiences are up from 42 to 77 percent, according to Al Pariser, director of research for the network. He said: "Total radio listenership, average quarter hour, Monday through Sunday. 6 a m. to midnight, was 27 million by the ADI count and 18 million when measured by Metropolitan Survey Area (MSA). "It is not a hy- poing technique but a better way of counting heads,” he said. “We have had a data explosion from our findings and are having trouble handling our data. There just is not enough staff yet and we are having an on line computer built to handle our needs.” Pariser claims that other measurement techniques show a bias against the small station in favor of the metro areas and in one survey out of 2,500 network af- filiates some 1,600 were never mea- sured Pariser added: "ADI market design dif- fers from radio's traditional MSA and the Total Survey Area (TSA) by defining each market exclusive of any others. There is no overlap.” Pariser also claimed that ADI research made it a valuable advertising tool, not so much that it turned up more listeners than previously estimated but that it would be compatible with other media, TV and print for example. The company would start "a national sweep” in April and May next year ABC pioneered local ADI radio research in Chicago with station WLS in 1971 and it was expanded to seven other ABC owned stations in 1973 "Everyone else has compatibility with other media." stated Pariser, "Only radio has lagged behind ” President of the ABC radio network, Hal Neil stated network dollars from ad- vertising had "been rather static for ten years and we have got to get a bigger pie " He stressed that ADI would be of service to all radio "We are not trying to juggle dollars but to advance We gain nothing juggling." Alice Welcomes Tahoe To His $450,000 Nightmare’ First Theatrical Rock Show Booked into Saraha Showroom i HOLLYWOOD — Alice Cooper has an- nounced his engagement for a one-week stand at the Sahara Tahoe Main Room, commencing December 12. His produc- tion of "Welcome To My Nightmare," featuring a $450,000 set and a cast and crew of thirty, marks the first time a rock and roll theatrical stage show has been tried as a headlining act within a Nevada gambling house. The two-hour show will be seen once nightly at 10 p.m , except Friday and Sat- urday when the performance will begin at midnight Neither food nor drink will be served during the show. In making the announcement, Cooper admitted he doesn't know what kind of audiences are likely to greet him, but in- asmuch as he considers himself an en- tertainer above all, he looks forward to the proposition of being the first from the rock medium to tackle that arena. Earlier this year Alice began a calculat- ed assault on the mass media with his "Welcome To My Nightmare” campaign, including an album soundtrack from his TV special ("The Nightmare,” April 26), a 70-city tour of the United States followed closely by 1 2 dates in seven cities. Final- ly, a feature-length film of the stage show, directed by David Winters, will be released through Key Pictures this com- ing week. A large-scale promotional campaign has begun in preparation for the engage- ment, aiming to reach the world market on a variety of levels. Highlighting the ef- fort will be a 35-foot helium balloon replica of Alice which will appear in the Gimbels Thanksgiving Day Parade (to be televised nationally), and a video presen- tation of portions of the stage show, to be supplied for hotel lobby viewing. These and others endeavors to alert the public to Cooper's Nevada gig are being coor- dinated by promoter Gary Naseef; Atlan- tic Records president Jerry Greenberg; Lenny Martin, vice president in charge of entertainment for the Del Webb chain of hotels; and Alive Enterprises, Alice Cooper's personal management com- pany. Carly Simon Re-Signs With Elektra HOLLYWOOD — Carly Simon has re- signed with Elektra Records for a period of five years, it was announced by David Geffen, chairman of Elektra/Asylum- /Nonesuch Records With the release this week of "The Best Of Carly Simon,” a retrospective collection of Ms. Simon's hits since her emergence as a major female contem- porary artist in 1971 , Carly's involvement with Elektra/Asylum begins a new chapter in a career that brought her into national prominence. Her initial single “That's The Way I’ve Always Heard It Should Be” (the first cut on her new LP) set a standard for her vocal and compositional achievements which have brought her wide popularity in FM progressive and top 40 circles; although her live appearances have diminished somewhat since her mar- riage to James Taylor several years ago, her accomplishments in the studio, often under the aegis of producer Richard Perry, have brought the intent of her lyrics and piano artistry into perspective. Ms. Simon's "Anticipation," “You're So Vain” (which earned her a first gold record award) and "Mockingbird" (with James Taylor — also gold) have been de- finitive of her style and contribution in the 1970 music market. box/news Stop Launches Promo For Silver Convention \ NEW YORK — The success of Midland international's Silver Convention is not ! of the instant variety. BIG 3 — "Record execs are aware that something's breaking in the print busi- ness, but they often don't know where or how." says Herman Steiger, executive vice president of Big 3 Publications. In the last five years the company has climbed from $800,000 to $5,000,000 in gross sales annually, and has just moved into a 86,000 square foot warehouse facility. Steiger feels the strength of Big 3 lies largely in diversification. “Psychological- ly, a small publisher cannot function as a successful print marketer. A large publication company functions well by forming a combination controlling a large amount of catalog." Big 3 holds print rights for a varied selection of publishers, including Unart (due to their affiliation with United Artists). Robbins. Miller Music and numerous others, in- cluding a hefty selection of country publishers. At this point, Big 3 controls rights approximately one-third of the average weekly Cash Box country chart. "Aside from the catalogs you control, the most important thing is knowing how to utilize them, which is a matter of put- ting the creative talents of the organiza- tion to work." Big 3 has branched into countless facets of print, covering all possible tastes and needs. Personality books put out by Big 3 in- clude artists such as Jim Croce. Frank Zappa, Deep Purple. Phil Ochs. Janis Ian and, in the near future, a folio of Bruce Springsteen's "Born To Run.” The Springsteen book exemplifies the highest degree of management and artist involvement in the production of a personality book, which included Bruce and Mike Appell supervising nearly every note written down.” Every song on the album had to be truly interpreted as recorded, which of course required call- ing in a top recording arranger for the correct interpretation. The folio will run about 76 pages, which is quite long for an album of eight songs. The score of "Jungleland" alone runs 16 pages, re- ducing the instrumental progress of the entire band's recorded rendition includ- ing the saxophone solo, to piano-vocal form. Other utilizations of catalog include the educational, where stage and marching band arrangements for all types of music, from Duke Ellington charts revised for the college and high school levels, to arrangements for the latest Electric Light Orchestra LP With control of the Blue Note catalog. Big 3 is launching an extensive jazz series for the schools. Since the book will cover public domain and material from the '20s and '30s for which the company owns rights, Feldman anticipates a successful volume, SCREEN GEMS-COLUMBIA— Pack- aging and marketing are the keys to this business." states Frank Hackinson, vice president of Screen Gems-Columbia Publications. In five years, the company has expanded to fit a 50,000 square foot facility in Miami which includes all phases of the operation beneath one roof. Hackinson describes the success of Screen Gems. "We're now number one in the area of popular sheet music, con- trolling 30 to 40 percent of the weekly Cash Box top 100 singles, and we've established ourselves as a leader in the field of personal ity books. Screen Gems' most popular personali- ty book artists include Chicago. Olivia Newton-John. B ach ma n-T u r n er Overdrive and Carole King. Covering a wide variety of musical styles is where solid production and attention to detail are essential. “In Chicago we have a group whose music lends itself to the two major divisions of interpretation in print: there are singles: there are melodic singles like Color My World,' which are the ideal raw material for piano-vocal arrangements, yet the group is instrumental ly oriented to the point that their music is perfect for concert and marching band charts for the schools.” "With Screen Gems an artist can be critical and demanding that the arrange- ments be superb and exactly as re- corded We consult with the artist on the leadsheets and recorded versions, to de- termine the differences that develop in the final recording. The arranger takes no liberty: our arrangers are up with today's music, youth- and trend- oriented.” Hackinson explained that Chicago had always proofread the final editions of their music books until "Chicago 8." where their confidence in Screen Gems was such that they didn't feel the need to check up. Carole King in the often difficult to sing original keys, so the edition was printed in side-by-side versions with easier keys included. "Leon Russell's cumulative folio was pro- duced by Screen Gems-Columbia because his manager personally visited the plant, and was convinced our facilities could best serve the artists's needs. " Continuing in the subject of packag- ing. Hackinson pointed out that the burgeoning market in personality books should not overshadow “the tremendous mixed folio market which is often over- looked The artist is far from the only means of selling printed music — there are approximately 15 million Americans who play an instrument, and a demand for hits and standards arranged for all in- struments on all levels of competence.” Screen Gems employs its catalog in grouping together favorite tunes in books for every instrument from "easy” organ to flute to harmonica. Production is facilitated by Screen Gems' patented photo-engraving pro- cess. which they claim is more economical than the older hand and plate engraving methods, and yields more attractive results than the musical typewriter. According to Hackinson, publishers from Italy and France have visited Miami to observe the process, since plate engraving in Europe is a master art which is disappearing with modern times. Terrific blend of drums, brass and Scottish pipes for a Christmas (or anytime) party flavor. Pop and MQR programmers should ail consider the answer to the question "what will warm our hearts this winter?" — “Scotch On The Rocks. ” Flip: No info, available. Here it’s all goodtime with "boogie on down” cooling off the refrain, as sung by the rest of the group. R&b. The melody, above all, makes ’Struggle In Darkness’ a prime contender for AM pop stations. Flip: No info, available. CAMEO (Chocolate City CC 001 ) Find My Way (3:30) (Charles K. Harris — ASCAP) ( J. Johnnie picks up a beauty at the disco, takes her home and moves with her only to find that she doesn’t really respond until she can dance. (And you have to be on your feet for that). Chugging, sweeping background. Flip: No info available. JIM CAPALDI (Island IS045-A) Love Hurts (3:30) (Acuff-Rose — BMI) (Boudleaux Bryant) Softly quilted bells open into a jumping MORocker with a beat along the lines of a subdued "Get Back.” (Love) “takes a lot of pain/love is like a flower/it takes a lot of rain/love hurts." JONATHAN CAIN (October OCT 1001 -AS) Til It’s Time To Say Goodbye (3:33) (Blue Lick— BMI ( J. Cain) First outing for October label is an extremely impressive one. Simple words, melody and an ar- rangement familiar enough to the collective consciousness to retain the voice as the focal point, which it definitely should be in this case. Flip: No info available MARTHA VELEZ (Sire SAA-722) Aggravation (3:04) (Jonali — BMI) (Moore) Boiling conga rhythm sets the mood for a chanting opening: “I don’t want no aggre- vation/l don’t need no aggrevation/l can’t handle no aggrevation/don’t give me, don’t you give me no aggravation.” Martha Velez, at various times, chirps like Maria Muldaur and belts like Tina Turner. O Neill’s voice is cool and cutting, with a personality all its own. Bill has a good time with this and it comes across. Flip: No info, available. MOONLIGHT (Pickwick International Productions PDJ-651 3) The Little Drummer Boy (5:00) (Mills/Korwin — ASCAP) (Davis, Simeone, Ororati) Drummers of all sorts — from your conventional traps through your jungle congas and bongos — get a workout carrying on the basic rhythm with only a smattering minimum of the necessary bass to disco-ize this Christmas standard. It's also the kind of record that keeps artists in business. Ripe soul vocal. Flip: No info, availa- ble. EAST COASTINGS — That Is An Error Dept.: In the continuing saga of “find the Sensational Alex Harvey Band in New York," a Harvey rep, brings us the following up- to-date info. At the moment, Alex Harvey and co. are suing Little Feat for the latter's refusal to have the band on the bill with them at the Beacon Theatre, though con- tracts seem to have been fully executed. Also, despite advertising to the contrary, contracts were never signed (so the rep. says) for the group's alleged dates with Procol Harum at the Felt Forum nor with Peter Frampton and Dave Mason at Madison Square Garden. It seems there's a lack of communication between agency and group. Patience, patience. NEW VINYL — David Bowie’s new single is due out any minute, going by the title “Golden Years.” (See singles review.) It is part of an upcoming LP which features the RCA artist with Roy Bittan (Springsteen's keyboardsman). guitarist Earl Slick, plus as- sistance from Alice Cooper, Peter Frampton, Bobby Womack and Ronnie Wood Supertramp’s follow-up to “Crime Of The Century” is called “Crisis, What Crisis?” (See album review.) . . . Eno’s new one entitled “Another Green World” . . . Jefferson Starship begin work on their new album shortly, with recording set to begin after Jan. 1 ... THE RIGHT MIXTURE — Cuba Gooding, lead vocalist, and Luther Simmons, vocalist and arranger for the Main Ingredient, were in New York last week solidifying plans for a number of future projects. These include developing their own company, Supergroup Productions, which is now recording albums by a group named Family Affair, vocalist Johnny Brown (you may remember the heavy-set fellow from "Laugh- In") and a band on Buddah called Charisma. They're also working with filmmaker John Henry on a short subject examining a small part of their lives as a touring group, with more shorts and a feature length work in the planning stages. The third annual awards luncheon honoring consistently outstanding performances in various classifications, was held at the Roxy Theater. Honorees were selected by ballot vote of their peer members in the chapter, such as musicians, vocalists, producers, arrangers, composers, conductors and engineers Participating in the awards presentation were Artie Butler, who emceed, Don Burkhimer, Don Ellis, Snuff Garrett, Mike Post and Bones Howe who announced the winners. cashhoxK&Bnews report r&b ingredients A warm and lovely lady dropped by the office last week. She records for RCA and has a new LP out entitled "RSVP.” Her name is Zulema of just plain Miss Z, Born and raised in Florida, Zulema has been into music for many years. Can't tell you the number of years because that would give away her age, and with ladies it's always a secret. She is a young talented lady and a Capricorn. Some of the fine selections off her current LP include 'Coins In The Bottle,” "You Had To Know, " “You're So Empty” and her current single "Just Look What You've Done.’ Zulema has always been a musician; however, her singing career began in the chorus room in high school. Some of the groups she was in previously before going solo include the Blakettes, The Chordettes, the Four Crystals and Lovells which later became Faith Hope & Chari- ty. They had a semi-hit back in 1969 on Sussex entitled “So Much Love.” Currently Miss Z lives in New York where she enjoys a quiet life when she is not working. She hates to go outside when she is in New York, but loves to entertain her friends in her home, take care of her plants and her dogs. Someday Zulema would like to move to California but she has a fear of earthquakes: "I'm from Florida and I know what hur- ricanes are like, but earthquakes scare me because you can't see ’em coming.” South Shore Commission continue to be on the right track as their single on Scepter "We re On The Right Track" keeps steaming along. The South Shore Com- mission are Scheryl Henri, Sidney Pinchback, Lantz Arnell, Eugene Rogers, David Henderson, Warren “Hamm” Haygood, and Frank McCurry The Main Ingredient celebrated their fifth anniversary in show business at the Roxy last week in a special one night appearance. Cuba, Luther and Carl were in fine form in their black velvet tuxes and red velvet bow ties. The guys crooned and swooned the audience with "Everybody Plays The Fool," "Happiness Is Just Around The Bend,” "Rolling Down The Mountainside,” and selections off their latest RCA release "Shame On The World.” Windy O'Grady, my Chicago disco spy called in to say that the one making everybody bump and fump is "Tonight's The Night” by S.S.O. Johnnie Taylor and Don Davis are putting on the finishing touches on his first Columbia Records release. No title or release date as yet. . Even when they don't work clubs, concerts or films, Bloodstone is involved in the community. The group along with Don Mac of KDAY recently did a benefit for Fremont High School in L A to help raise money for the school. The group is currently waiting for the release of their film "Train Ride To Hollywood,” nationally. Currently it is being shown in key markets. Their latest single “Give Me Your Heart" is still proving to be a winner Jeff Lane is currently producing Garnett (“Cry Baby”) Mimms and after that will get right into the third B.T. Express LP Bob Crewe is finishing up the Eleventh Hour LP, whose single "Hollywood Hot” is hot. 20th plans to deliver the LP sometime in Dec . . The Originals new single looks to be a winner. “Everybody's Got To Do Something,” is their latest on Motown . The Dimples Disco chain held disco awards this year and the Crown Heights Affair were voted the #1 disco group. Also their label DeLite Records was voted the #1 disco label. Crown Heights Affair are continuing the momentum they created with "Dreamin' A Dream” with "Every Beat Of My Heart." Pops Staples is out of the hospital and just got back from a trip in the Bahamas. Their single "Let's Do it Again" has been declared gold after only six weeks of release . . . Papa John Creach’s next single on Buddah will be Joyce " They're coming out with a special disco version, but the one for pop airplay will be 2:45 Currently Papa John hasgot a monster on his hands with “I'm a Fiddlin' Man." . . Impressions have finished up their next LP and it is due sometime in Feb. Their new single "Loving Power," should keep the guys in the spot they like — #1 ... Bobby Womack is moving about the U S. on a promotional tour for his latest LP on UA "Safety Zone Commodores are doing some dates with Earth, Wind & Fire and K.C. and the Sunshine Band. Their LP "Movin' On" on Motown is a smash with "Sweet Love," and "Time" being just a couple of the great cuts Two new groups to watch out for the first part of the year are the Brass Construction and Hidden Strength. Both groups will record for U.A. and are from New York. From reliable sources these groups are super-funky Atlantic/Atco has released a special disco version of "Baby Face,” by the Wing & A Prayer Fife & Drum Corps. The disco record is part of the special disco series the label has and it is a 6:48 minute version. It’s a gas . . . Sometimes you receive weird things in the mail, but last week something came which was fantastic. It was the acetate of the new Dennis Coffey LP entitled "Finger Lickin' Good" on Westbound Records. It is sensational. Dennis' guitar work is un- believably super-fine. Wait for this one to steamroller up the charts . . . The new Ron Banks and Dramatics single is off their latest LP "Drama V." The whole LP is great, but their choice is excellent. "You're Fooling You." is the single which should be gold quickly Disco fans will enjoy the Reflections’ LP on Capitol Love On Delivery " If you love to dance, dance with Reflections . . "Pressure Sensitive" is the largest selling debut LP in the history of Blue Note soul waves Are The Ratings Overrated? Chris Hall, pd KATZ-St Louis - I don't know exactly, however I think more or less that ratings have more value to top 40 radio than they do in black radio Maybe in some markets, but in my opinion ad agencies in general markets don't buy black and save the least dollars for the black market, so ratings really don't entail the same benefits I have to say that I do think of ratings. I have to be sales conscious with my staff, however I don't worry or get uptight about them With my staff I try to maintain a good level of standards, whether we re in a rating period or not I try to downplay the ratings to the staff I think sometimes you can pressure yourself too much What I try to do is prepare for quality and be consistent. Chuck Smith, pd, KKDA-Dallas — No, they're not. However radio finds itself in- volved in the rules of the game Radio stations are run to generate response and revenue, so rules are needed I don't think the ratings are terribly accurate regarding programming but they exist and you have to acknowledge them or I don't know how you can be in the business Ratings are just something people in radio have to live with. I don't think people ever show up as well as they ought to in ratings. I think there is a built-in bias to begin with It's very hard to deal with something on paper that con- cerns the ears Bob Moore, pd, KDKO-Denver — Yes definitely Especially in black radio In most cases it doesn't matter what we do because the ad agencies are not that concerned with our ratings when the rating periods come up. All I do is hope the audience is up during the rating period I cannot say I do not think of ratings, because you can t help but think about ratings, however one thing ratings do is stop good radio program- ming In a lot of cases other bigger and richer stations start giving away the moon dur- ing rating periods Once the rating period is over the contests stop and some of the records that were being played are no longer played. Everyone is against this prac- tice but no one does anything about it No one trusts anyone else when the records are no longer played I do not feel ratings are true indicators of the numbers. I think there is a need for improvement in ratings and some sort of new rating device or technique integrated into the system Rob Singleton, pd. KRE-FM-Berkeley — We don't subscribe to any of the ratings, however I feel certain stations manipulate their ratings and know about them so well that they have it down to a science I don't think ratings can be totally fair I don't believe they give a complete overall picture of radio or of the listeners. Ernest James, pd, WBMX-Chicago —- I think ratings are the necessary evil in radio They may not be perfect but they are a pretty good barometer for people who buy commercials on stations. The advertisers want to make the best buy just like anybody else. I do feel however that the ratings could use a little revitalizing regarding black markets I don't think black people are properly counted as to what radio they listen to Many black stations don’t get credit for their listeners. I don't think ratings are overrated, however they need to be improved upon. Jim Maddox, pd. KDAY-Los Angeles — I suppose ratings are overrated if you don't have any, Jim chuckled. However I think if you are into ratings which most stations are. that you have to take them with a grain of salt, because there are many different ratings and they show different things. Ratings become a necessary evil because they are important and not important in many cases. I believe in doing the good quali- ty job day in and day out. week to week and am not that interested in the one rating period week. There are always ups and downs in radio, however there are certain things that can be done to remove some of the risks I just try to make a go of it and as- semble professionals who do the job well Bernie McCain, WHAT, Philadelphia — "I think so in that one is never assured of get- ting a completely accurate account of the make-up of one's audience If a survey were taken in a borderline community in terms of racial balance, there could be a chance of not contacting a proportional number of black families, for instance All I ’m saying is that no system is infallible.'' "The question is almost a moot one — at this time we need to work within the rating system Ad agencies base their buying on them, so we have to deal with the same guidelines. With money as tight as it is, ratings represent the easiest way to choose a station on which to advertise. Advertisers in these times often can't afford saturation advertising "I try not to let ratings affect the way the station runs to any undue degree. Ratings or not, I still have to work to make the station appealing in any way I can." Harry Jeffery, WOOK, Washington. D C — "I would say the ratings are as accurate as they can be, and any problems with them lies in the extent to which they're used They are after all based on small samplings of a market, yet many advertising agen- cies use them as a bible for buying airtime. "Our whole financial status now rests on the ratings. They often determine whether people hold onto their jobs, and are important in determining revenues for the sta- ations, "I think that rating services can be a good medium for finding out what's happening out there, but I can t see relying on them entirely Advertisers should develop other means of research to balance off the point of view the ratings give They could look to the response to advertising, or see how effectively a station promotes with its listeners. The band is in the midst of a short U S. tour to coincide with the release of their new LP, “Siren” (Atco) and single. “Love Is The Drug.” Plans now call for the group to return to the states after the holidays for a more extended stay Roxy are in the headlining slot this time over, with the exception of a date with Frank Zappa and a double bill with Dave Mason, due at least in part to the fact that their stage apparatus, especially lights, makes it difficult for them to be in the second slot and still do the kind of show they desire. Asa matter of fact, it's even difficult to be in the second slot with Roxy Music, as the Hello People learned in Philly last week, where the latter amicably bowed out of their opening spot when it became clear that Roxy's staging would not accommodate (on the smallish stage) the Hellos equipment Undaunted, the group went on under a quickly-devised pseudonym for some acap- pella vocalization Meanwhile, future Roxy Music plans include new solo efforts from Brian Ferry, guitarists Manzanera and reedsman Mackay. Manzanera noted that the increased sales the band has experienced with each successive album makes them "feel that we’re at least making progress. . The new album is more of a rock album, and that may also be helping it along.” NUGENT IN THE RAW — Ted Nugent, rock and roll's answer to raw meat, is pictured in his back to the woods pasttime, which is killing and eating his own food. Nugent, soon to hit Los Angeles, is the one on the right THE WAY TO RUN AN AIRLINE DEPT. — Dave Mason and his band made an un- scheduled stop on their tour about a week ago, when the private Convair in which they were traveling caught on fire 200 miles away from Cincinnati. The entourage heard the pilot calling "mayday” as the engine flared up , forcing them to make a crash landing in Parkersburg, W, Virginia. Shaken, but apparently uninjured, the band pushed on to their gig by chartering three small planes, and miraculously, made it on- to the stage only about a half hour late. Ironically, Mason had just had a new will at- tested the day before; and, in addition, his manager, generally afraid to fly, had chosen this occasion to exercise his fear and was not on the plane, for the first time since the tour began in October. Bill Wyman finishing solo effort in L.A. FOLKROCKFOLKROCK David Bromberg took some time off last week from a very busy touring schedule which included 26 dates last month, an average for his band He admits it's a grueling pace but "we don't get paid an astronomical fee and so we have to keep working like this. It's a rough way but right now it's the only way." Bromberg also noted that he is not particularly happy with his label, Columbia, and is considering a change. "I suspect my album sales would be greater with another label." he commented, adding that he feels that Columbia does not know exactly where to pigeonhole his kind of music. "I’m a folkie to the rock'n’rollers and to the folkies I'm a rocker. But why eat one kind of cheese? I like a lot of music — blues, bluegrass, rock. I started out backing up people like Chubby Checker and I love tradi- tional music, although I think that traditional musicians are always messing with the music, so in that sense I'm a traditional musician. I love being a bandleader and sometimes I just miss being a back-up musician, a studio man. There’s no doubt I could probably earn more money in the studios. That’s the reason why my music is so crazy.” Bromberg has seen his audience grow around the country and in Europe and believes there is an untapped market for his records. "We headlined the Troubadour in L.A. when we were just supposed to be a supporting act. They couldn't get a headliner and we had little or no publicity, but the club did more business than they'd had in the last three months.” PIECES — Renaissance are blitzing the New York area these days, with successive dates at the Felt Forum (two nights), Hempstead. Pace College. Westchester and Madison, N. J. . . Tom T. Hall is stopping concertizing for four months to concentrate on a book project and his new album. . . cashbox/international news Italy MILAN — At the recent Dischi Ricordi convention in Santa Margherita, Dischi a&r and promotion manager Lucio Salvini addressed the issue of the return of the single and the loss of interest in foreign music, particularly pop music. Salvini also spoke of the universal pro- pensity to take into consideration product instead of the artist Dischi has intensified its artistic research activity, looking for new producers and collecting a cast of young performers (Corrado Castellari, Napoli Centrale, etc.). Dischi also has its ear to "revival" and "folk” streams (folk of the Romagna area, in- strumental, etc). Renzo Benim, sales manager, talked through the economic situation Total in- come (1974) was up 23% over 1973, with unit sales showing an increase of 34% for single records, 4 9% for LPs and 5 6% for pre-recorded tapes. Luigi Mantovani, international reper- tory coordinator, speculated that the crash in foreign music has caused a rise in prices, breaking out groups and re- duced tours. Mantovani also announced the acquisition of some new labels: Black Lion, Mainstream (jazz) and Capricorn (country-rock) Several foreign guests were present at the convention, including Leo Missir, vice president, Barclay; Michael de May, European manager, A&M Records; Des Brown and Teddy Meir. Chrysalis in- ternational manager and Responsible European promotion; Tome Hayes, in- ternational manager, Island; Simon Draper, general manager. Despite a semi-riot opening night, due to confusion over ticket availability, a relatively peaceful atmosphere pre- vailed as American jazz-rock band, Chicago drew 45,000 spectators to the National Auditorium over a three-date performance schedule According to Gustavo Robles, at- torney for the Delegacion Miguel Hidalgo, the official agency overseeing all shows at the auditorium, "investiga- tions" are being conducted in order to determine the feasibility of future con- certs to include such parties as James Brown and The Osmonds who have performed here in the past The possibility is also being reviewed of stag- ing a future Chicago concert at Azteca Stadium which has a capacity of nearly 110.000 Eduardo Tonella, head of the Hidalgo agency commented that the first night of the current stand may have at- tracted as many as 50,000 more than the 15.000 that the auditorium could accom- modate In order to quell the crowd, loudspeakers were installed outside the concert for the last two appearances Speculation abounds that upcoming rock concert schedules may include such cities as Guadalajara and Monter- rey Sixty to seventy percent ot the Mex- ican population is estimated to be below the age of 25 Cat Stevens To Island Worldwide NEW YORK — Island Records Inc. has signed a new, long-term agreement with Cat Stevens to distribute his records worldwide, with the exception of the U S., Canada and Japan where his product will continue to be released on A&M Records. Te-'-as music, as southern ! ,; c did several years ago with the >Vk:K!ns. wii! break out of Texas with the corning year. While the .-''Stic eco remains centered for the part around Austin, the fact that I quality studios are already present in I Dallas will continue to draw the technical ! and business ends. The spectrum between MOR country music and rock and roll ie>'clusive of those extremes) will continue to develop with a great deal of help from radio, KOKE-FM in Austin and KFM-FM in Dallas in particular. KOKE was the first to program a consis- tent diet of progressive-minded country oriented music and KFM is the first major market/major wattage (100,000) station to do so. Judging from what the local listeners told me, KFM's programming provides a needed alternative to rock and roll and traditional country as those forms exist today It is that middle- ground hybridization of forms that draws upon pre-1955 country and rockabilly as the base, with contemporary ex- periences and instrumentation overlaid. The energy behind the movement is vast and the Lone Star state, as big as it is physically, will not be able to contain that energy much longer. An indication of this will be the fall ARB results for the Dallas TSA, which will be released in January It will be an important book; people will be interested in the outcome Shortly before my visit to the Big 'D, " KFM threw a birthday party for Ray Wylie Hubbard on the same day his first Warner Bros album was released The celebration was held in the station's 4-track recording studio and David Allan Coe joined Ray Wylie and the Cowboy Twinkle Band for the live broadcast Before cutting the 50- pound cake, which is not a mass of frosted Twinkie as you may suspect. Warner’s Murray Nagel, Ray Wylie, Capricorn's Danny Nowack, David Allan Coe, and KFM pro- gram director Chuck Dunaway lined "up against the wall, redneck mothers " for a photo And speaking of rednecks, David Allan Coe performed “Long Hair Doesn’t Hide A Red Neck” for the first time in public at the party; the tune's lyrics are. in the literal senses of both words, truly out- rageous, and will be released as David's next single very shortly, KFM is already programming the live party version while waiting for the single, Steve Fromholz, one of the artists who will break out of Texas next year, kicked off his new weekly hour-long KFM broadcast with Rusty Wier, another artist bound to bust out this year; Fromholz" show provides interviews and songs with fellow artists involved in progressive country with an artist's viewpoint, and the first show was very well-received by listeners. KFM additionally is co- sponsoring Willie Nelson and his band in concert at Dallas' Sportatorium on Dec. 7; Dunaway, the man who was very suc- cessful in top 40 and hung it up to go back to Texas, is behind KFM's involve- ment with the music and its artists, said that the station will tape the concert for broadcast New Year's Eve If you would like a copy of his playlist or have any other questions. Chuck will be more than happy to answer them. Give him a call. The King Biscuit Flower Hour for Dec 14 will present Labelle in concert; that set features an extended version of “Lady Marmalade” that reportedly has the power to curl toes The same evening Roxy Music will be presented live and that set includes R M.'s big I British single “Love Is A Drug.” Future dates will be set for concerts by Dave Mason, Janis Ian, Sparks, Queen, and in- dividual concerts by three bands who represent the tastiest in Southern fried rock and roll — the Allman Brothers, the Marshall Tucker Band, and the Charlie Daniels Band. New Riders of the Purple Sage, Armadillo World Headquarters (Austin) adoptees, are also upcoming; future dates to come as they are set. D.I.R. Broadcasting enters into its fourth year after the first of January with a few changes; the number of stations on the syndication roster has grown from 175 to 186 Mary Travers is working other phases of her career and will no longer be hosting “With Mary.” Conversations with WNEW’s Dave Herman will be broad- cast on the fifth Sunday of each month in 1976 containing the extra Sunday; D I.R.'s Pat Cox told me that interviews with the individual Beatles are on Dave's 1976 agenda Herman interviewed Roger Daltrey last week on his show In addition to producing the DIR syn- dicated shows, D.I.R. president Bob Meyrowitz and vice president Peter Kauff are working on the production of a documentary that will consist of 14 hour- long segments designed for broadcast over a 12-month period. “The Way It Went Down” offers a socio-cultural view of the sixties' music and the events that made that decade one of insight and turmoil, peace and war The loose his- tory features authentic newscasts from the period, includes segments of the 1963 Newport Folk Festival, and seg- ments of speeches given at the Washington Memorial at the culmination of the Poor People's March on Washington DC, Because of the social commentary present in many songs of the sixties, the events and music are in- tertwined, the documentary's structure ties the events and music together dur- ing the course of the broadcast. D I R, is negotiating with WNEW’s Scott Muni currently for his narrative services. The Earth News segments for the week beginning Dec. 15 will feature George Harrison in an interview with Earth News’ Lew Irwin. Harrison's discussion ranges over the phases the Beatles travelled in their years together as well as current and future Harrison projects Earth News is widely distributed; check your local listings forairtime. The late Ralph J. Gleason was in- terviewed by Studs Terkel for Berkeley's Pacifica station KPFA in 1970; a 30- minute edit of the original 3-hour inter- view is available from Fantasy Records (where Gleason was a vice president) on reel to-reel for a $3 tape-dubbing charge Gleason comments on many of the artists he wrote about in his posthumously published book "Celebrat- ing The Duke & Louis, Bessie, Billie, Bird, Carmen, Miles, Dizzy, and Other Heroes,” published by Atlantic Monthly Press/- Little Brown Contact Terri Hinte at Fan- tasy Records, 10th and Parker, Berkeley, Ca 94710 WHCN in Hartford, in conjunction with Warner Bros . asked listeners to name Little Feat’s “Last Record Album” in ex- change for a trip to Washington D C and a date at the Watergate with Feat's Lowell George. WHCN's winner was Janet Booth of Hartford; her entry was "Barbi and Ken Sing Songs For Young Lovers.” WHCN program director Mike Shallet and Warner Connecticut promo- tion manager Pat Rustici accompanied Ken and Barbi on their Watergate date. Wanda Ramos has been promoted to the music directorship at WLIB and WBLS-FM in New York by station owners Inner City Broadcasting: Wanda has been at WLBS-FM for the last three years. Over 600 college students and radio and record industry people attended the 6th Annual Loyola National College Radio Conference in Chicago Nov. 21-23. The attendees participated in several college radio panels, exchanged information, and scrutinized new broad- cast equipment on display. The Loyola University conferences were sponsored by Loyola stations WLT (Lewis Towers campus, Chris Kusiac, coordinator) and WLUC (Lake Shore campus. Jann Lawson, coordinator) and was the largest conference so far, ac- cording to Loyola sources. Among the subjects discussed at the symposium were public affairs program- ming. the duties of radio station general managers, remote broadcasting poin- ters, progressive programming, black programming and the FCC. Representatives from Earth News, the FCC, and record company executives joined the staffers of college radio sta- tions nationwide to discuss college radio and how to move from college radio to commercial radio. Among the speakers at the "careers in broadcasting” session held Sun, Nov. 23 were WBBM general manager John Catlett, Arista's Mike Klefner, WXRT-FM disk jockey Mitch Michaels and WLS disk jockey Bob Sirott, who discussed the various ins and outs of gaining access to and developing careers in broadcasting. The vast majority of the students attend- ing the symposiums held album-oriented progressive radio as their main interest. The dates for next year's conference have been set for Nov. 12-14 Allison Steele and Bobby Womack igreeted each other warmly as Bobby stopped at WNEW-FM in New York on part of his promotional tour in support of “Safety Zone,” his most recent album on United Artists While he was in New York to promote Bobby's album, a Thanksgiv- ing party was given for UA album promo- tion director Billy Bass and Starship/Hot Tuna manager Bill Thompson, who was in New York for a date with some Hot T una UA's Stu Sank held the bash at his house and Jodie Tausag from UA publici- ty co-hosted. Attending were UA's Walter Paas, Arista s Aaron Sixx, Bearsville president Paul Fishken, Buddah vice president Tom Cossie, Patrina Wells and Mark Shulman from Atlantic, GRT/Janus' Dick Wingate, Sire Records' Lenny Schaffadi, MCA publicist Kathy Schenker, RCA s Karen Williams, producer Jerry Love, WNEW-FM's Dennis Elsas, Country Music’s Patrick Carr among many other friends and as- sociates. Pacifica’s listener sponsored outlet KPFK in Los Angeles will present its International Merrie Christmas Fair at the Santa Monica Civic Dec. 19-23 from noon to 11 pm. KPFK functions are usually a lot of fun and the admission $3 for adults, 50<t for kids under 12 — helps keep the non-commercial station going. Tickets are less expensive by ad- vance mail order; send $2.25 per ticket to KPFK Fair Tix — Box 8639, Universal City, Ca. 91 608 before Dec 1 Last week a postcard arrived for me at Cash Box from Pete Moore of the Miracles; the postamark was Osaka, Japan The Miracles are having a very successful tour in Japan and Pete re- ports that their “Love Machine” single "is going great guns on JOQR in Tokyo and also on the Armed Forces Network with C.J. McMurray.” Many thanks for the card. Mr Moore, Stephen peeples STATION BREAKS FROM NEW YORK Ron Thompson, program director of WWVA AM/FM, has opted a new policy concerning records with profanity or dis- tasteful. Thompson; "If possible we will edit and play a hit record. Should the title not pass our code of ethics, or an edit be impossible, the record will not be aired." Gil Scott-Heron called in from Windy City and said if you come to Chicago be sure to bring an igloo Gil has been super busy of late as he and Brian Jackson have been working on the musical score to the film "Baron Wolfgang Von T ripp, " Gil said the film should be released sometime this Easter By the way Gil was recently placed among the top five male vocalists in the 40th Annual Downbeat Readers Poll His latest LP and single "From South Africa To South Carolina, " and "Johannesburg, " are continu- ing to move up the charts. Gil told me that the interesting background rhythm on "Johannesburg" single was done on an instrument called a Chinese drum. Gil said the rhythm used on the single is called gamboot. "It is a rhythm the miners in South Africa use when they work. HOORAY FOR THE DELLS - Mercury Records recently held a party honoring the Dells on their 23rd anniversary. Currently the guys have a hot single and LP out en- titled "We Got To Get Our Thing Together." Shown above helping the guys celebrate from left to right are LaDonna Tittle of WBMX and Chili Childs WGCI. WOL, Washington, D C. comes out of the "Count 'em for Cash " contest having dis- tributed $5,000 in cash and a grand prize of 1 .000, Cortez Thompson, pd reported the station cutting back in total news programming slightly, while moving to a more “easy- going” news format, with feature stories and bylines. In the meantime, WOL will con- tinue giveaways of LPs and tickets, while programming new and old Christmas music. Cortez also made official a shift switch: Chuck McCool is now on from 7 to 12 p.m ; Nat Washington is on the air 1 0 a m. to 3 p.m, Frankie Stewart, The Soul Ranger returns to WRAP, Norfolk after being away nearly three years. He mans the afternoon drive. WOOK radio was involved in a few important public services in the Washington, D C, area for the Thanksgiving holiday "Project Harvest" was a drive for food to be distributed among needy families. Chuck Long came over the air with remote broad- casts from the drive center, keeping the population informed of progress and spur- ring many people and organizations to greater contributions of food and money. WOOK also sponsored a 100 turkey giveaway of its own running into several indig- nant reactions from listeners who weren’t lucky enough to win. Harry Jeffery, pd, was a little surprised at the reaction, saying he'd never encountered the like in any giveaway of cash or loot. He went on to say the experience brought home the re- alities of poverty in the Washington area. jess levitt/phil dimauro 20 December 13. 1975

i WAR IN PHILLY — Shown above are UA recording artists War with friends after a re- j cent gig in Philly. Standing from left are: Carl Helm of WDAS, War's B,B Dickerson, War's Harold Brown. Keri (Mrs. Lee Oskar), War's Lee Oskar, and War’s Charles I Miller. Seated from left are: Carmene Bonano and Steve Epstein of W.M.O.T, Produc- tions, Wars’ Lonnie Jordan, Bruce Garfield of Far Out Productions, Georgie Woods of WDAS, War's Papa Dee Allan, Al Edmondson, Universal Distributors and Tony Brown ofWDAS-FM. Burke Johnson, former pd of WAOK, Atlanta, will be honored at a testimonial dinner on Dec 1 9, 1 975 at the Royal Coach Inn in Atlanta. Senator Julian Bond is scheduled as keynote speaker. Atlanta Mayor Maynard Jackson will be on hand for the event, along with other elected officials and community leaders. Chuck Jackson and the Soulful Brass Band will head the entertainment lineup. Burke Johnson served as program director and worked at WAOK for more than 18 years During his tenure he developed and initiated many community affairs projects, bringing the station closer to the city. The dinner is being sponsored by the Fair Play Committee, a New York based or- ganization that deals with minority problems in the radio and entertainment industries on the national level, and the Burke Johnson Testimonial Committee. cashbox, news 3 LP Releases For HOLLYWOOD — MCA Records will re- lease three albums this month, accord- ing to vice president Rick Frio. Kenny Starr leads the list with the LP “The Blind Man In The Bleachers.” This is Kenny Starr's debut MCA LP featuring the title song, his single, “The Blind Man In The Bleachers” by Sterling Whipple. Singer/songwriter/guitarist Starr began performing with Loretta Lynn and Con- way Twitty after winning a talent contest; he now travels as part of Loretta's show. Included in Starr's first album are “Where Love Begins” by Ray Griff, "To- night I'll Face The Man Who Made It Happen” by Bob Morrison and Bill An- thony, “You, Me And Her” by Walter Haynes and “Put Another Notch In Your Belt" by Mac Davis. Kenny Starr's LP was produced by Snuffy Miller Conway Twitty also has an album, “Twitty,” set for Dec. release. This album features the single releases “This Time I've Hurt Her More Than She Loves Me” by Earl Conley and Mary Larkin and “Jason's Farm” by John Adrian. Bluesman Jimmy Witherspoon makes his LP debut on Blue Note with "Spoonful,” while John Lee and Gerry Brown have teamed for “Mango Sunrise,” the first outing for the two. members of Larry Coryell's Eleventh House, produced by Skip Drinkwater. The third album to be released by MCA this month is “Music From The Original Motion Picture Soundtrack The Hindenburg.' ” The Universal motion pic- ture, “The Hindenburg," is the story of the disaster of the giant German Zep- pelin Hindenburg that met its fiery death thirty-seven years ago in New Jersey. The music for the film was composed and conducted by David Shire, a man whose credits include such films as “The Conversation.” “The Taking Of Pelham One Two Three" and “Farewell, My Lov- ely.” The album includes a newsreel pro- logue with Herb Morrison (news com- mentator from radio station WLS in Chicago) actually reporting the ex- plosion itself. The new LP. “Home Cookin'." will not only be the first musical collaboration for the group and Garrett, but is the first one for the newly re-formed 5th Dimension. GRT Releases New Classical Quad LPs HOLLYWOOD — GRT Corporation has announced the release of a second group of classical albums in a quadra- phonic/compatibie 8-track configura- tion. The releases were announced last week by GRT vice president of market- ing Herb Hershfield. Joe Schneider, GRT product manager, told Cash Box that the new releases constitute an addi- tional 1 7 titles, added to the 50 originally released in mid-1974. “The decision to offer these 17 new titles was made as a result of our watching the stable development of the first project," Hershfield remarked. "Our research has always indicated that classics buyers tend to be very loyal to the retailer who stocks classics. These buyers tend to visit a retailer week after week and provide a steady source of new revenues." Hershfield said. The GRT classic package was de- signed to aid retailers who demanded a mid-priced classical line to attract marginal classic buyers. The quadra- phonic compatible LPs offer the listener the advantage of only one program inter- ruption. and offers the retailer the op- portunity to stock a much smaller inven- tory Listeners can purchase the GRT re- cordings, which retail at $4.95 each, knowing that they can later convert to quad without having to purchase new tapes to replace their existing library. The GRT releases include works by such composers as Vaughn Williams, Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, Tchaikovsky, Mahler. Wagner. Ravel. Brahms and Saint-Saens, and features the enclosure of liner notes from the original albums, providing vital information for both the beginning and mature classical listener. Performing the works selected from Vanguard and Westminster catalogs are the Utah Symphony Orchestra under the direction of Maurice Abravanel, organist Anton Heiller, Hanover Recorder En- semble, American Symphony Orchestra under the baton of Leopold Stokowski, William Steinberg conducting the Pit- tsburgh Symphony Orchestra, Herman Scherchen conducting the Vienna State Opera Orchestra and David Blum con- ducting the English Chamber Orchestra. Musicor-Springboard In Distribution Deal NEW YORK — Springboard Interna- tional, the budget label, has acquired the rights to the Musicor Records catalog, the result of a deal between Art Talmadge, Musicor president and Dan Pugliese, Springboard president. Agreement will be officially signed next week when more details will be an- nounced Talmadge stated that Musicor will con- tinue to produce new product on both the Musicor and Dynamo labels. Included in the Musicor catalog is product from Gene Pitney. George Jones, Melba Montgomery, the Platters and others. cashbox/insight&sound HOLLYWOOD-CASH BOX’S GREATEST HITS:THE EDITORS DISCUSS THEIR 75 FAVES PHIL ALEXANDER Bruce Springsteen JESS LEVITT Van McCoy Perhaps no other figure in our busi- ness emerged with such tremendous trade and consumer exposure as did Columbia’s Bruce Springsteen this year. Not only did Bruce occupy the front cov- ers of both major news weeklies, and garner top singles and LP chart posi- tions, but his resurgence into the spotlight spurred renewed interest in his past catalog Columbia's expertise in all areas, promotion, art. publicity, market- ing — must be commended, and looked upon as an example of the potential of how important they feel Bruce is both to their label roster, and to the consuming public as well. On the California coast, during his openings at L A 's Roxy and on the University of California campus in Santa Barbara, even the most hard-core skep- tics agreed that an "east coast phenomenon" was in fact a brilliant new composer-performer. Jon Landau was prophetic when he said several years ago "the rock and roll future" was Spr- ingsteen. That future has now become present. Promised Land The last half of 1975 is showing the strong emergence of happy-time get down dance music. This music is hot. funky and tight. Disco music for no better label is sweeping the world. People around the world are doing the bump, and doing the hustle. The dance music phenomenon that looked like a fad six months ago is now building to a frantic peak. It is the happening sound. Van McCoy, writer, producer, arranger and singer is a man responsible for many super hits this year His sound is smooth, it flows and cools everything out. Many other fine new artists are emerging from the disco world Crown Heights Affair, Gary Toms Empire, Commodores, Ohio Players, Buddy Miles, Donna Summer, K.C. and the Sunshine Band, Leon Haywood, Silver Convention, Armada Orchestra, B.T. Express and People’s Choice are just a few of the groups changing the looks of the pop charts. Special disco singles and long versions are popping up continually to give the people more of what they want — and "that's the way they like it." "Uh-huh." These "white punks on dope” know what they want from life. BEST NEW MALE VOCALIST “ Have you seen Toots and the Maytals? Those who haven't will get a chance to see Toots Hibbert on the current Who tour, and will be treated to the most accessi- ble, dynamic reggae vocalist currently doing it! Toots has an amazing facility for enchanting his audiences consistently. Simply terrific! BEST NEW FEMALE VOCALIST — In a year in which record companies seemed hard-pressed to sign significant new female artists, Arista's Melissa Manchester emerged as this writer’s most logical choice. 116 BEST OF THE NEW-IES BEST NEW GROUP — There were many fine new groups this year but one looks to have the most staying power for years to come Hot Chocolate on Big T ree Rec- ords is a six piece band from England that expresses just about every musical taste available. Two big LPs this year "Cicero Park" and "Hot Chocolate" and singles "Emma" and "You Sexy Thing," should help establish this act for a long time to come A monster group now for the future. BEST NEW MALE ARTIST — It took awhile for this guy to get started but from all indications Ronnie Laws on Blue Note Records is going to be a man hard to beat from now on. His latest single “Always There,” blends the best of pop, jazz and r&b. BEST NEW FEMALE ARTIST — This one was easy as Natalie Cole on Capitol Rec- ords looks to have all the magic needed to establish her as a major star. “This Will Be" is more than a motto with Natalie. An upcoming Beach Boys date will include New York’s Jeffrey Ballet. QUOTE OF THE WEEK: From the lips of Thee Image guitarist Mike Pinera comes this bit on songwriting under stress. "I wrote Ride Captain Ride’ in a bathroom in about fifteen minutes.” marc shapiro EAST COASTINGS - From Past Experience: They really aren't the good old days to Noel Redding, former bass player with the Jimi Hendrix Experience, now comfortably living in Ireland, with a new band and a new RCA album, “Klonakilty Cowboys.” Redding was in New York last week working on an upcoming tour and promotion of the LP He reckons that his legal actions over his time with Hendrix (ending in 1970), should be over next spring, one way or the other. Redding thinks that he deserves more from that period than he actually got, that the three platinum albums and eight gold LPs should have brought in more than he actually ended up with — in fact, he considers he should be a pounds sterling millionaire with his Hendrix trio earnings. "They were good times then," he admits. “All that rushing around, alcohol and the young ladies. But now is better. I live in a house in Ireland, and am very settled. Just Guinness and darts . For the past six months we have been getting the band together . . With Hendrix, Redding was one of the pioneers of the working-and- living-in-the-studio school of recording artists. No more. For the new album, Redding rehearsed the band before, went and booked the studio (Basing Street, owned by Island Records) and did the whole album in one week straight. “It’s rather boring — after 36 takes you lose all the feeling. I don't even try if we don't get it down after five takes.” Redding has not heard the new Hendrix tapes but has no desire, even if asked, to do any posthumous dubbing. "I was pretty messed up when we split with Jimi I just want to get the lawsuit settled, get what I think I deserve, and concentrate on the new band. On my new life.” WHO’S THE BEST - The Who wound up Part 1 of their projected 3-part U.S. tour at Philadelphia Spectrum last week. If the music of the Who represents a concern with aging, the performance of the Who belies no evidence of this in the members of the band The Who in Philly were as tight, as strong, as powerful as at any time in their 1 years plus career. The 1 hr, 40 min. set was economical to just the right degree to convey the essence of what is, at this point, the greatest rock and roll band. Opening with ”1 Can’t Explain” and “Substitute” from the days of the birth of the English in- vasion, the band burned its unbelievably energetic way through a capsule history of the band (with an avoidance of “Quadrophenia ”). They played 30 minutes of “Tommy” as it was meant to be, showing the inherent fallacy in all attempts to make it an MOR work. Throughout, Pete Townshend created the tension that is the basis of The Who by balancing at a point of being just angry enough to play well without completely los- ing any sense of order. The best use yet of lasers in a rock setting enhanced the fine lighting. By the time of the closing “Won't Get Fooled Again,” it was clear that when the Who are on, no one can touch them. cashboxR&Bnewsreport r&b ingredients With the holiday season drawing closer every day we at Cash Box would like to wish everybody out there a joyous holiday season and hope 1976 will be an excellent year for everybody connected with black music. The latter half of the year has been quite hectic — not strictly busy-busy, but hectic in the sense that so many great records have been released by many fine artists out there doing their thing. With such a good last quarter 76 looks to be a monster year in the world of black music. The Ramsey Lewis/Ronnie Laws show at the Roxy last week was a killer. It was pro- bably the best package the club has presented in a while as both groups really cooked. Ronnie Laws and Pressure came out smokin' as the Pressure Band which is composed of Roland Bautista, lead guitar, Bobby Lyle, keyboards, Steve Guiterrez, drums, Kent Brinkley, bass, and Chip Steen, percussion really laid on the funk. Ronnie and Pressure worked out on " Delusion,” "Tell Me Something Good," and his hit : ingle “Always There.” The only disappointment was that the set was not longer. Ron- nie Laws is one talented man. Ramsey Lewis then came on and blew everybody out as he opened his show with "What's The Name Of This Funk (Spiderman)." This tune knocked everybody out. Ramsey, a favorite with everybody for years, has changed with the times as his trio has grown into a quintet of super talented people. Brenda Mitchell, vocalist, Oerf Reklawra Raheem on congas, flute and sax, Bernard Reid on bass, Bryon Gregory on lead guitar and Morris Jennings on drums are superslick and super bad. Other hot selections included in Ramsey’s set were "Don't It Feel Good,” which is also the title of his latest LP on Columbia, "That’s The Way Of The World,’ "Livin’ In The City,” and “Sun Goddess.” Would have been a treat for the crowd if Ramsey had done a medley of his golden oldies such as "Wade In The Water,” and "In Crowd," etc. LAW BREAKERS — Shown above celebrating after Blue Note recording artists Ron- nie Laws engagement at the Roxy recently are left to right: Ray Anderson, UA vp pro- motion; Frankie Crocker. WBLS-FM program director; Al Teller, UA president; Ron- nie; Nancy Sain, UA promotion and Bobby Womack. Gene Russell has signed an exclusive world-wide distribution deal with Sutton/Mil- ler for his Quarican Record company. Two of Gene's upcoming projects include former Miss Indiana singer/actress Kellee Patterson. Kellee is scheduled to go into the studios immediately and product should be available in the very near future Also Gene is set to produce another one of his groups, Cheyenne. Look for a release from this group sometime in January. Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff and Jimmy Bishop of Philadelphia International are in town this week for confabs Al Green is scheduled for upcoming appearances on Dinah Shore and Men# Griffin. “Full Of Fire" is still burning up the charts The Sylvers did a benefit concert last week for St. Mary’s Academy in Westchester The high school donated the most toys in a contest sponsored by Capitol Records and KDAY The contest helped raise over 8,000 toys for underpriviledged youngsters. The Sylvers are turning on the U S. with their latest single, "Boogie Fever.” Their latest LP was released last week entitled "Showcase” Speaking of good times, Ralph Carter, one of the stars of the show “Good Times," made an appearance on Dick Clark’s American Bandstand over the weekend, where he performed his latest single on Mercury "(Extra, Extra) Read All About It." Chelsea/Roxbury/Hot Licks are resting during the holidays but come the first of the year look for new singles by Jim Gilstrap, Stuff & Ram Jet, Defasco, Ujima, Monti Rock as Disco Tex and the Sex-Q-Lettes and Robert Brookins . Ohio Players are taking some time off this holiday season but the guys did release a Christmas single entitled "Happy Holidays (Part One and Two)." The guys are going to being doing something a bit unusual come New Year's Eve. First they are appearing at a New Year’s Eve gig in Phil ly and lateron the same night at 3 a.m. they will be appearing in New York City. Lenny Williams is in town huddling with Leon Ware about his upcoming LP. A new reggae group on Asylum called the Shakers will be coming with a single in January and an LP in February . . David Ruffin, hotter than a pistol with his single and LP on Motown, "Walk Away From Love,” and "Who I Am,” is planning to gig around the country with Eddie Kendricks after the first of the year. The event is going to be called "A Tempting Evening" . Label le have finished touring for the year and are now in New York recording their next LP which will be entitled "Chameleon." It is expected the middle of January . . . Willie Hutch doesn’t look to have an easy holiday season as more dates are being added to his current tour. No title as yet and it is not expected to be released until sometime next spring. . . Bo Kirkland and Ruth Davis are in the studios recording "Easy Lovin' ” for Claridge Records. Bo's brother Bob will be producing . . . A little satire never hurt anybody and the National Lampoon gang are up to it again with the release of a special Christmas single “Kung-Fu Christmas." As usual it is the typical insane humor from the Lampoon crew. The Total Experience club in L A held a Christmas party over the weekend for its many friends. The real surprise of the evening came when ‘Big’ Harry Williams of Bloodstone came out as Santa Claus. He looked very chtc in his fire engine red Santa Claus suit designed especially for him by Omar of Oxnard . . . The Temptations continue to be one of the hottest groups in the country. Their LP, "House Party,” is a monster and the guys recently completed three one-night engagements in the south where they grossed over $200,000 for the three days. Mercury Records is into the world of reggae with two very fine LP releases. The two new releases are: "Disco Reggae," by Bryon Lee and the Dragonaires and "Leave The Reggae To Us," by Greyhound. One cut in particular that is very fine on the Greyhound LP is a reggae version of the Bobby Darin classic “Dream Lover". . . Carl Carlton has a new LP on ABC which should help re-establish this talented young man. It is entitled “I Wanna Be With You" ... My disco spys from all across the nation all called in excitedly last week to talk about the tremendous response "Inside America (Part One & Two)” is getting. The tune by Juggy Murray Jones is a bicenten- nial disco dilly . . . Fantasy recording artist Patrice Rushen has been in town doing a gig at Concerts by the Sea. This is her first L A appearance and coincides with her second Fantasy release, “Before The Dawn." The Spinners have been having some good luck and bad luck lately. First the good news. The guys look to have another #1 record with "Love Or Leave." Next the guys, all football nuts, got to perform the national anthem at Miami Dolphin/Denver Bronco game at the Orange Bowl in Miami. The bad news is that fifteen of the Spinners' cos- tumes were taken during a robbery at their cleaners in Detroit. The Spinners are of- fering a reward for the return of the costumes and if that isn’t satisfactory Billy Hen- derson of the Spinners said they would make an offer to the robber to join the group. 20th is still putting out records even as the holidays draw to a close. Hot off the presses are Barry White’s latest single “Let The Music Play," and an LP from the Love Unlimited Orchestra, “Music Maestro Please.” Should be a lot of dancing going on during the holidays and 20th has some new ones for all the dancers out there. Their latest single on Roadshow/Scepter is entitled "Close To You.” It’s the old Carpenters hit done beautifully. It will freak everybody out, . . Look for a new group on Capitol to shake up the record business come this January. The group is call Sun and a single should be out in January with an LP in February. Westbound Records is looking to juice up everybody's holiday season with some fine LPs. "Finger Lickin' Good" by Dennis Coffey is a killer. Also released are "Freeze" by Junie, "Here I Am Again" by Denise LaSalle and "Get Out’a My Way” by Houston Person featuring his hit single "Disco Sax” . . . Happy Holidays . . . In the way of fund-raising, NATRA will be marketing products, including games, puzzles and calendars, some dealing with the music industry, or directly with the association's logo, a stylized picture of a broadcast microphone A catalog for the products is now in the final stages of design. Plans for next year's convention are now being finalized. Kitty emphasized that the entire year should not be devoted to the convention; rather, energy should be devot- ed to raising money and increasing the organization’s activities ail year round. The new office, for those who might need to contact Ms. Broady, is located at 3705 Liber- ty Heights Ave , Suite C. Baltimore. Md. 21215 Telephone (301) 542-1370. cashbox/insightAsound PHIL DIMAURO The impact of reggae, best represent- ed by Bob Marley & The Waiters, began primarily with artists and this year has spread to the popular audience, demon- strating the power a fresh yet deceptive- ly simple form can have on musical think- ing Peter Frampton has continued to make important contributions to "mainstream'' rock, transcending the category by many opinions. As rock con- tinues a simultaneous multidirectional expansion, the call for simplification and recognition of the form's true identity persists Melody Maker's referral to Roxy Music’s return to “the nitty gritty" from "the visual contrived scene" denies the sophistication progressive experimenta- tion can lend to any musical form Wit- ness lOcc’s live performance, which in- corporated visual and program elements into music that is often exotic yet de- cidedly popular rock. Bob Marley Back to the Roots?
