Maceo Woods. the Highway QC's. the Pilgrim Travelers. Alex !'adford' ant! Pmdràe Crouch and the Disciples. Branches fr the consolidation at Capitol was done several years ago. Approximately three years ago, the Boston branch was changed from a depot to a sales office Capitol at one time had as many as 25 sales offices; they recently consolidated five into existing offices and now have thirteen. The company now has three pressing plants. Several years ago, the Scranton plant was sold when a new plant was opened in Winchester, Virginia. Product has always been returned to Capitol pressing plants. In the last 60 days, however, returns from the east coast started going to the Virginia plant instead of to the Bethlehem, Penn- sylvania depot. The label has no further consolidation plans. Much of the consolidation currently going on in the industry is due in great part to the increasing efficiency of the trucking and shipping firms, according to Walter Lee, national sales manager for Capitol. "If it is less expensive to truck product into an area than to have a depot there, I say truck it in." said Lee. CBS The CBS operation, which began in the early sixties and stabilized to more or less its present form in the late sixties, has changed little since then. .The com- pany currently has two depots plus three pressing plants which also serve that purpose. The depots are in Elmhurst. New York and Dallas. Texas. Two years ago the Chicago -Skokie depot was changed to a sales office. The recent addition of a Seattle sales office brings the total number to 20. All returns have gone back to the pressing plants for the last five years, explained Paul Smith, vice president of sales and distribution. Before that time they went back to the individual branches. The CBS plants are in Pitman, New Jersey. Terre Haute, Indiana and Santa Maria, California. Smith said that CBS has no further plans to consolidate its distribu- tion setup. RCA RCA's branch operation began in late 1972 and was completed in 1973. They have three deposts, and one pressing plant which also serves that purpose, in addition to 17 sales offices. The Rockaway, New Jersey and Hollywood, California pressing plants were closed recently, leaving only the Indianapolis, Indiana operation. All returns go back to the depots, and Jack Kiernan, vice president of market- ing for the company, said that RCA has no further plans to consolidate. "Our system is very efficient," Kiernan declared. "Each of our depots covers one-third of the country." MCA Much of the current trend towards consolidation in the record industry is "a page out of our book, from five years ago," according to Rick Frio, vice presi- dent of marketing for MCA Records. Frio was referring to the setup which MCA ac- quired from Decca and the changes which they made in it. According to Frio. "Every town with over 100,000 people in it had a sales office with inventory." MCA now has five depots; one each in Atlanta. Dallas and Los Angeles, plus two press- ing plants which also serve as depots and sales offices. The Chicago and Cleveland depots were closed approx- imately a year and a half ago. The company has 22 sales offices, in- cluding the two pressing plants, which are located in Pinkneyville, Illinois and Gloversville, New York. All MCA product is returned to these plants. Phonodisc In 1974, Phonodisc had six depots. In the last months of that year, they cut back two depots, and in 1975 they cut back another two, leaving them with two. At the same time they opened a new de- pot, giving them their present setup of three. The Cleveland, Chicago, Dallas and Atlanta depots were closed in that order. The new depot was opened in In- dianapolis. Indiana the remaining original depots are in Union, New Jersey and Sun Valley, California. Indianapolis handles the midwest, Union, the east coast and Sun Valley, the west coast. The Phonodisc returns used to go back to each of the six local depots; they now go back to three points. Returns in the midwest region go to the CBS plant in Terre Haute, Indiana, where Phono - disc has a warehousing arrangement. (Cutouts for the midwest are also handled through this operation). The Sun Valley depot handles returns for the west coast and Union handles the east coast. The pressing for Phonodisc is done at almost a dozen different plants through- out the country. The company also has eleven sales offices. Phonodisc does have plans for further consolidation, according to Dave O'Con- nell, president of Phonodisc. However, O'Connell noted that the company is not big enough to lead the way. "We are stu- dying the question of whether the in- dustry is ready to accept the higher freight costs involved in consolidation," said O'Connell. "But I think it is going to come on an industry -wide basis." WEA WEA has closed one depot in its five year history, leaving them with their present lineup of seven. They have eleven sales offices, plus the depots which also serve that purpose, for a total of 19 sales offices. WEA recently made news in the in- dustry by centralizing all returns into one location at PRC's warehouse in Rich- mond, Indiana. Formerly, returns went back to all seven WEA branch depots and tapes went back to Elk Grove, Il- linois. The Warners label is pressed by Capitol. Atlantic uses various plants and Elektra/Asylum uses Columbia. The company has no further plans for con- solidation at this point. All WEA tape is handled now by Capitol. The new returns system is "more effi- cient, and that's important," said Henry Droz, executive vice president of WEA. He added that while there has been some negative response to the move, that "some of the response we have had is positive." 12 May 15. 1976 www.americanradiohistory.com

TALENT ON STAGE Bob Marley & the Wailers/The Bluesbusters BEACON THEATER, NYC - Critics seem anxious to categorize reggae as an unspoiled, unrefined type of music, unaf- fected by commercialism, and therefore something new and fresh. Bob Marley & the Wailers' reggae is the most exciting to hit the U.K. or America thus far, and a large part of its effectiveness comes of its being a sophisticated fusion of soul, calypso and rock, played with modern in- struments and executed with precision. The bass and drums of Aston and Carlton Barrett maintain the painstaking tempo within which the musicians create tension, as opposed to most rock, where "hotter" and "faster" are synonymous. The keyboards of Tyrone Downie fill the hypnotic riff of "Want More" with rich colors, while the I Threes backing vocals provide solid patterns over which Marley can weave his unique vocal inflections and intonations on "Them Belly Full," or "Positive Vibration," the cut that leads off the Wailers' latest LP on Island Records, "Rastaman Vibration." The evening's re- pertoire, running about one hour and 40 minutes, concentrated on that album and the flawless "Natty Dread," although all Marley's American releases were represented. By the Wailers' closing performance, any apparent psychological distance between musicians and audience had disappeared. The crowd sang and swayed to Marley's every motion, while the dreadlocked rastafarian gyrated as one spiritually possessed. If the rights Marley was singing about in "Get Up, Stand Up" were not identical to the rights the audiences was standing up about, it didn't seem to matter. Although the pop music field has never encoun- tered any practical problems with the paradox of selling political subversion at several dollars a seat, it's uncanny that Bob Marley's cultural and religious in- spiration are foreign to anything the average American under 25 has ever ex- perienced or believed. His message breaks the boundaries. Aside from the announcer's amazing Jamaican radio voice, the show began with Scepter recording artists the Bluesbusters. Philip and Lloyd. Their set combined original numbers with reggae - influenced versions of soul hits like the Temptations' "My Girl." p.d. Genesis STARLIGHT BOWL, L.A. - The current U.S. tour by Atlantic recording group Genesis has been their most important, if not crucial one to date. The absence of former lead singer/fellow composer Peter Gabriel and its effect on the musical chemistry of the band, no doubt left a number of anxious questions in the hearts and minds of Genesis' loyal following. The outdoor Starlight Bowl, was filled to the brim with what can only be described as zealous Genesis fanatics who turned out in carloads to support and relish the musical fantasies of one of rock's finest exponents of the surreal, spacey music in the Pink Floyd. ELO genre. Limited parking facilities and not -to - easy access to the Bowl itself caused a slight delay, but no one seemed to mind. Thunderous applause greeted the band's entrance and those first anxious moments regarding the group's durabili- ty and musical direction were immediate- ly answered on a most positive level. Kicking off with "Dance On A Volcano." an infectious tune from their current "A Trick Of The Tail" LP, Genesis displayed keen awareness for the audiences' every desire and whim with a highly polished set that allowed the band to control and guide their dis- parate yet cohesive themes throughout a non-stop, high energy, two hour performance. Phil Collins has now assumed all of the vocal chores and his transition from drummer to lead vocalist was not only smooth and satisfying, but actually in- spiring. The man is quite an entertainer and his up -front stage presence was re- markable considering that he had always been behind the scenes supplying the muscle on drums and adding occasional harmonies. With Bill Bruford (ex - drummer for Yes and King Crimson) car- rying the weight with his impeccable percussion talents on this tour, Collins had plenty of room to show off his dis- tinctive showmanship qualities. He was literally all over the stage; singing, danc- ing, and carrying on with playful antics and a charm that will certainly endear him to many, many fans. Having seen the old Genesis twice before, I feel there is another positive aspect to the present group's overall ap- peal. While Collins commands the prime focus of attention, the remaining mem- bers have also become less inhibited and therefore more accessible to the au- dience. Michael Rutherford, likened to a human rhythm machine by one fan, sup- plied punchy bass lines and tasty 12 string guitar work while adding some vocal harmonies. Dowd says Stewart's new effort "contains more rock 'n' roll than 'Atlantic Crossing,' although we employed the same mixed bag of musicians, cross-pollinating everybody." Dowd also said to watch for two singles on a new label from a new singer - composer named Allan O'Day, which will be distributed by Atlantic Records. COSH BOX RI R&B INGREDIENTS The new B.T. Express single for Columbia is out. Entitled "Can't Stop Groovin'," this one looks to be one of the hot records this spring, along.with the Isleys' latest, "Who Loves You Better." The Tavares brothers have released a new single on Capitol that is going to burn up the charts. It is entitled "Heaven Must Be Missing An Angel." More mellow harmonies from the fellows from Boston ... Aretha Franklin also has a new single out. It's called "Something He Can Feel" from the movie "Sparkle." Curtis Mayfield produced this one for Aretha. Also watch for the latest from Margie Joseph on Cotillion. "Hear The Words, Feel The Feeling," is the title and it's hot. Gary Gotham called in from Gotham City to say that "Swing" by Hokis Pokis on the Shield label is happening in a big way in the discos of New York ... Bobby Bland, the main man when it comes to the blues, has just released his latest single for ABC entitled "It Ain't The Real Thing. " This is a killer ... Jimmy Briscoe & The Little Beavers have finally released their new single for Pi Kappa distributed by Buddah. "Ain't No Way" is the title and it's a smash. BACKSTAGE VEGAS - Natalie Cole recently made her Las Vegas debut at the Hilton along with Bill Cosby. Shown above from left to right celebrating backstage are Chuck Jackson and Marvin Yancy, Natalie's songwriters and producers; Natalie: Kevin Hunter. Natalie's manager; Larkin Arnold, Capitol's vice president and general manager, soul division; and Bob Schwaid. Jackson and Yancy's manager. Marilyn McCoo and Billy Davis, Jr. will be making their Las Vegas showroom debut August 5 at the Riviera along with Don Rickles ... Rufus, featuring Chaka Khan will ap- pear on NBC -TV's Mac Davis Show June 3 ... Richard Gersh Associates are now repre- senting KC and the Sunshine Band for public relations ... Keisa Brown, an up and coming vocalist, is burning turntables around the country with two cuts off her "Live" LP. "L.A. Catcher" and "Midnight Train To Georgia" are lighting up the phone request lines ... A May 20 concert at UCLA will establish the Julian Adderley Memorial Scholarship Fund at the university. Appearing at the benefit will be the Cannonball Adderley Quintet featuring Nat Adderley, Walter Booker and Ron McCurdy. Also ap- pearing will be Flora Purim, Airto, Freddie Hubbard, George Duke and David Axelrod. Other friends appearing on the bill will be Louis Hayes, Jimmy Smith, Sam Jones, Ernie Andrews, Jimmy Cleveland, Ernie Watts and Victor Feldman. The concert is being pre- sented by the Center for Afro-American Studies at UCLA, in cooperation with the Committee on Fine Arts and Special Productions. The Miracles are back from their four week tour of England. The guys will have no vacation however as they are set for a heavy summer schedule including five engage- ments at Disneyland during May and June, plus an engagement July 25 at the Universal Amphitheatre with Al Green. Quincy Jones is off to New York to record a "salsa" LP. Ray Barretto will be on con- gas along with a solid line-up of other Latin musicians. Ray is lining up the Latin players for the sessions ... Buddah is bringing more pleasure to the airwaves with their two latest single releases; "Mama Mia." by the Leer Brothers and "Dance And Free Your Mind." by the Sins of Satin. These are going to jump up on the charts .. . The Temptations have released a single from their smokin' "Wings Of Love," LP. The single is "Up The Creek (Without A Paddle)." Their new LP is fabulous ... Kessler - Grass Management have signed Garland Green to an exclusive management contract. Green has a new single out on Casino Records called "1.0.U." Chelsea Records has added a gospel line to their catalog. Bee -Gee and Vee-Jay Records are the new labels to Chelsea. Gentry McCreary is heading the operation in Los Angeles, along with Chelsea's R&B coordinator Lygia P. Brown. The first LP re- lease for Bee -Gee is "Another Direction," by the Five Blind Boys. A hot selection off the LP is "I Love The Lord." Also watch for Rodena Preston's latest single "Where Peaceful Waters Flow." Other artists on the Bee -Gee label who will be coming with releases very shortly include The Edwin Hawkins Singers, Geary Faggett and the Patterson Trio. If you're into gospel music Bee -Gee, and Vee-Jay have got the hits .. Speaking of gospel Columbia Records has also just released an LP by the queen of gospel music Mahalia Jackson. The LP is entitled "How I Got Over," and should be a hot item for those who remember one of America's all-time great singers. The Pablo Festival came to L.A. last week at the Shubert Theatre. The show was sensational. Ella Fitzgerald, Count Basie and his orchestra, Oscar Peterson and Joe Pass put on quite a show. The ensemble will be traveling all around the country this summer and if it comes to your area don't miss it ... Ann Peebles has another monster on her hands with the release of her latest single on Hi entitled "I Don't Lend My Man."... Natalie Cole's new LP is out and it's hot. It's entitled "Natalie," and already "Sophisticated Lady," her single, is smokin' up the charts. This is another monster LP for Natalie and her songwriters and producers Chuck Jackson and Marvin Yancy. Believe it or not the Sons of Champlin have come up with a very soulful LP for Ariola. The whole LP grooves. Check out the Sons' version of "Slippery When It's Wet." It's hot, hot, hot... Bill Cosby's LP is out and programmers better make plenty of room for this one. Bill's sense of humor is, as always, "rat own, rat own."... The 200th anniversary of the U.S. is coming shortly. UA records has done a very tasteful LP to commemorate the event with the release of "Ballad For Americans." All the listeners have to do is identify the artist and song title over the air and they will then win the LP or 45 that they correctly identified. KYAC in Seattle is having a contest in conjunction with London Records called "Train Ride To Hollywood." The winner will receive a train ride to Hollywood to at- tend the premiere of the new Bloodstone film, "Train Ride To Hollywood." The trip will also include a tour of Universal Studios, dinner with the Bloodstone, a visit to a Bloodstone recording session and other goodies. Also KYAC is having another pro- motion in conjunction with Casablanca Records called "Evening Of Magic." KCOH in Houston had a radio telethon over the weekend for the United Negro College Fund. Worth is saluting artists in its weekend programming, according to Bernard Miller, Mr. B. at that station. In past weeks the station has salutec Johnnie Taylor, Al Green and Brothers Johnson by playing old and new hits by the artists twice an hour. The Originals are back into the thick of things with their latest release on Motown entitled "Touch." ... Timmy Thomas has a new single release for Glades entitled "Love Shine. " It's hot ... Wade Marcus and Mayuto have signed recording deals with Impulse Records. Kessler -Grass Management have just completed negotiating a re- cording deal for their client Otis Clay with Henry Stone's T.K. Records. Clay is currently in Chicago recording his first single for the label. Gil Scott -Heron was in town last week at the Roxy. Gil, Brian Jackson and the Midnight Band were hot as they presented a tremendous 90 minute set. Gil and the band have been touring extensively of late but Gil hopes to get back into the studios shortly to record a new LP for Arista. Gil wants to go in and record a tune entitled "Possum Slim, Don't Mess With Him." The tune is dedicated to Ed Meyers, a 105 year old man known as Possum Slim. Gil said the reason for the song was that Possum Slim was invited to a birthday party for some friends and when he arrived he was robbed. He went home, got his gun and shot the two people that robbed him. Now he is in jail ... Also forthcoming on Arista will be the General Johnson LP at the end of this month ... "Long And Winding Road" will be the new single on Warner Bros. for New Birth. The title of the LP will be "Love Potion." Jimmy Bee dropped by the Cash Box offices last week with his single "Breaking Up Is Hard To Do" on Calla Records. Jimmy, has been a singer most of his life. His last big record was for Kent in 1970 entitled "I Only Have Eyes For You." Jimmy is also one of the hottest promotion men in the country and said the key to good promotion is not just going into a radio station with a record. Besides that, he must also cover the music shops in the area, the one -stops, the distributors and the discos to be totally ef- fective in promoting a record. The reason why Jimmy recorded Neil Sedaka's tune was that he felt the single should have been an across the board smash. "I recorded the record so black audiences could hear it. "... RCA has released two more fine jazz LPs on the Flying Dutchman label. "I'm In The Mood For Love" by Groove Holmes and "A Dream Deferred" by the late great Oliver Nelson should zing up all the charts. Gospel music is having a resurgence and Nashboro Records have some fine new releases worth looking into. They include: "Guilty Of Loving God," by The Twenty - First Century Singers, "Through It All" by Delois Barrett Campbell, "I Want To Be Loved," by Tommy Ellison and the Five Singing Stars, "Dry Bones," by Reverend Will- ingham, "Don't Close In On Me," by The Pilgrim Jubilee Singers, and "Holding On," by Sister Lucille Pope ... Tower of Power are back on the scene with an exciting new LP release for Warners entitled "Live And In Living Color"... Get on it. Polydor Records has come up with some super exciting new jazz releases. They are on the Verve label and -they are deluxe yo -record re -issue sets that include Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, Jazz at the Philharincñnic, Dizzy Gillespie, Lester Young, and Billie Holiday. These are beautiful records and a must for jazz buffs ... Prestige Records distributed by Fantasy also has some exciting new jazz releases ... The new releases include: "Central Avenue," by Wardell Gray, "Images," by Oliver Nelson featuring Eric Dolphy, "Zootcase," by Zoot Sims, Kenny Burrell and John Coltrane and "The Gene Ammons Story," by Gene Ammons ... ITON STAGE Diana Ross CEASARS PALACE, L.V. — Only the most glamorous and talented show busi- ness people perform in Las Vegas. At ex- pensive dinner shows people want to fantasize, relax and be totally enter- tained Diana Ross, a superstar already in records and movies, conquered this medium in her most recent Vegas showroom appearance. The opening night tension and excite- ment could be felt immediately entering the theatre amongst the gaming crowd and celebrities at hand. The show began with the orchestra playing softly under the directorship of Gil Askey on a darkened stage. A butterfly appeared and then a shimmer- ing white spotlight hit Diana's face. The stage lights were turned on Diana's white smock as it unraveled into a long out- streched screen. As Diana sang "Here I Am." a projector zoomed a photo mon- tage of shots of Diana onto the screen from the Berry Gordy film. '"Mahogany."' in which she starred. After this Diana pulled off the smock and displayed a stunning lemon-yellow sequined bodysuit. Most singers use dancers in the back- ground. Instead three mimes. Stewart Fischer, Don McDleod and Heywood Coleman, took turns and created il- lusions and dramatic overtones for Diana's repertoire. The highlight of these features included Miss Ross and the mimes doing an act together on “The Point." " Love Hangover” has been one of the hottest records in the country for the last few weeks. This song was cleverly performed. Diana and the orchestra began doing it live. Then suddenly she told the orchestra to take a break while she changed costumes. A tape had been playing simultaneously and when she walked off the song didn't miss a beat. The mimes then brought out a lifesize cardboard statuette of Diana and placed it on the stage. Diana was then shortly carried on and continued performing live. Another medley Diana performed was of impressions of four great black vocalists of the past, Josephine Baker. Ethel Waters, Bessie Smith and Billie Holiday This portion of the show was ex- cellent and the costumes were magnifi- cent. No Diana Ross show would be com- plete without a medley of her hits when she was with the Supremes. "Keep Me Hangin" On," "Stop In The Name Of Love" "I Hear A Symphony," and “Baby Love." were a few performed. In the closing portion of the show Diana performed the "Theme From Mahogany,” " Ain't No Mountain High Enough.” and “Reach Out And Touch.” On the latter everyone in the audience rose to their feet, joined hands and swayed back and forth in a touching finale. Everything in the show was pro- fessional, tasteful and beautiful. Las Vegas and Detroit are miles apart, however Diana Ross has finally arrived and should be around for some time. j.l. Doobie Brothers/Memphis Homs Pablo Cruise FORUM. LA. — The Doobies are one of America's supergroups and last week the fellows further emphasized the fact. Lit- tle doubt was left in anyone's mind that they still are one of the hottest bands on the rock scene today. The fellows — Tiran Porter. Jeff "Skunk" Baxter. Patrick Simmons, Mike McDonald. John Hart- man. Tom Johnston and Keith Knudsen. came out smokin' for the capacity Forum crowd. The Doobies turned everybody loose time and time again through their high energy rhythmic rock "Jesus Is Alright With Me" started things off nice- ly. It set the pace for a rollicking time for all on hand. Tom Johnston's return to the band after a recent illness was most welcome as his hearty throaty voice wailed all evening. The Doobies' latest LP “Takin' It To The Streets" has exploded onto both the pop and R&B charts. This evening most of the material performed was from the new LP. Overall, the LP contains many tunes in keeping with the Doobies spirit. The Doobies engineered high energy and power along with a highly rhythmic background and earthy lyric. However, there are some new sounds added to the group with the addition of two ex-Steely Dan players. Mike McDonald and Jeff "Skunk" Baxter. Now faint tinges of the Steely Dan influence combined with jazz are heard in such tunes as "Rio.” They have the jazz feel but display the power- ful and soothing Doobie harmonies Another dimension that added to the continued on pg. 48 Pablo Jazz Festival Robin Trower/ Steve Marriott j LONG BEACH ARENA — Some of the best rock n" blues guitar work and the world s largest p.a. system are two things that Robin Trower brought with him as he recently blew out the Long Beach Arena. The Chrysalis recording artist loved the crowd and the more he gave, the more they wanted. The vibrating rhythms of James Dewar. Bill Lordan and Trower are the hard rock blues, with even some heavy disco influence that caused people to move. That hysterical caught-up feeling of being totally enter- tained was evident with people up and down out of their chairs, off the arena risers, just to get closer and get as much of a dose of what was going on musically as possible. And the largest p.a. in the world helped to generate that excite- ment. With 114 speakers and 36 amplifiers surrounding the stage, the force behind all the group's tunes was rich and loud. T rower's desire to get in front of a live audience and make his music is something he goes at almost spiritually moving and playing with the intensity of really communicating the powerful rock force he has created in his career thus far. In his first Southern California ap- pearance as a solo artist Steve Marriott displayed all the guts and tenacity that made him surface as the primary force behind the devastating Humble Pie. one of the seventies' premier arse-kickin' rock ’n’ roll bands. "I said I'd be back and I am. ain't I?" grinned the energetic cockney songbird as he ripped into a new arrangement of a familiar Humble Pie favorite "I'm Ready " Ably backed by his strong tour- ing unit, which features Pie veterans Greg Ridley on bass and Dave “Ciem" Clempson on guitar. Marriott additionally drew on the vocal talents of his old friends, the Blackberries. After loosen- ing up a bit. Marriott began to ply his irascible punk-wit with telling effective- ness in a calculated effort to induce the audience to join in with his good-natured ribaldry by taunting. “I didn't come here to bull you. so don't bull me. You can sing louderthan that!" Marriott’s four octaves plus were in prime working order as the Kid pro- ceeded to prove his mettle via blockbusters like "East Side Struttin' " and the dynamically melancholy strains of Randy Newman's "Louisiana." In his inimitable avalanche-cum-Tina Turner vocal style. Marriott also covered several tunes which bore an unmistakable funk feel, most notably the Ray Charles classic. "You Don't Know Me In an all-out effort to involve the au- dience in the energy of his show. Mar- riott delivered a scathing tongue-lashing to the stage-side security guards as has not previously been witnessed in these parts. Though some reviewers will un- doubtedly find his outbursts to be in poor taste and highly unprofessional, it would serve them well to remember that Mar- riott's persona of the ultimate cockney punk-rocker is not merely a glitter and make-up facade; on the contrary, this kid's for real! I n these days of super-hype with little real substance, that's a refresh- ing change of pace. Closing his show with an explosive rendition of the Humble Pie hit “Thirty Days in The Hole.” Marriott exited the stage and then returned momentarily to deliver a parting apology for the restric- tive actions of the stage guards, vowing to “find out who the big boss is and work this thing out.” It sure is consoling to know that if God saw fit to take Eddy Cochran away from us. it was only so he could improve on the old model and give us back a Marriott. Rock On! j.b.c./n.n. SCHUBERT THEATRE. LA — It had all the glamor of an Old Hollywood pre- miere. Not your typical rock 'n' roll show, people of all ages filled the classy venue to hear Ella Fitzgerald. Joe Pass, Oscar Peterson, and Count Basie and his or- chestra. any one of whom would have been a major attraction on his own. Divided into three parts, the show kicked off with Oscar Peterson running through some solo acoustic piano pieces. Peterson, long considered a legendary keyboard player, performed with great sensitivity The crowd was par- ticularly enthusiastic, shouting encour- agement. when Peterson flashed his hot left and right hand unison riffs. These were complicated lines that he made seem easy; plus, they really swung. Joe Pass, probably the best jazz guitarist we’ve ever heard, came out for a couple of dynamic, interesting duets. His chord- ing was marvelous, keeping a walking bass line, but never sacrificing melody. His technical proficiency was such that the musical thoughts seemed to be piped directly into his fingers. Count Basie then joined the duo. The double pianos were by no means overwhelming; curiously, the pieces seemed to be even more subtle and delicate. Pass accom- panied the two with fast and interesting chords — he was a one-man rhythm sec- tion. The three played some blues- ragtime arrangements that pleased the crowd immensely. After a short intermission Count Basie returned with his orchestra, and ran through a number of classic jazz pieces. His orchestra was outstanding and the Count is liberal with solos. His drummer was particularly impressive — he and Basie held down the rhythm of a big band with no problems. The third section of the show was de- voted to Ella Fitzgerald. The singer, backed by the Basie orchestra, debuted a couple of new songs (new for her): "Feelings” and the title song from the Broadway show "The Wiz." Fitzgerald’s voice is still strong, and she did this new material well, but the highlight of the show had to be when Joe Pass came out and accompanied her on some smooth improvised blues. Fitzgerald was excit- ing when she soared up and down the scale, responding to Pass's ultra-fluid runs. Definitely live, not on tape. j.m. Bill Wray ROXY, LA — Legend's Bill Wray brought his Louisiana “country boy" dream to the Roxy last week showcasing his dynamic style of rock and roll; sharing that dream with the crowd. Wray sings with intense excitement, constant- ly parading among his backup group, but never losing touch with the audience. He totally controls the show and the mechanics are down pat. His strong vocals on "Sailin'." and "Dancin' Shoes." coupled with the full depth background vocals and instrumentals, are a straight- ahead honest reflection of one seeming- ly built-in purpose: to entertain to the maximum After a brief instrumental overture. Wray comes on strong doing a short tap dance to a couple of drum rolls. He swings the mike in the air. over his head, behind his back, and recovers it in time to emphatically vocalize the next line of his song. Wray's band is at full strength, working with him on ending a song in whatever mood he feels. Some tunes start super strong, ending with Wray's very soft, almost whisper-like in- terpretation with the instruments accom- panying in the same mellow tone and then disappearing altogether in perfect harmony on his last word. If Bill Wray takes the same strong rock and roll presentation he exhibited at his Roxy de- but to other dubs, he should be suc- cessfully received. j.b.c. Mel Tiliis/Donna Fargo Don Williams MAGIC MOUNTAIN. VALENCIA. CALIF. — One of Southern California’s top amusement parks recently featured three of country music's top performers under the stars. Perky Donna Fargo opened in the Showcase Theater with a Vegas-slick set highlighted by her latest Warner Bros, single, “Mr. Doodles." The petite Ms. Fargo had the audience sing- ing along to her hits "Funny Face,” "It Do Feel Good," "You Can't Be A Beacon" and "The Happiest Girl In The Whole USA.” and received a standing ovation for her bicentennially timely "U S. of A." She has acquired much more stage pre- sence and polish over the last couple of years, and like the title of her Warner Bros, debut LP. Donna is definitely “On The Move." Mel Tillis may have his problems talk- ing. but when it comes to singing the MCA artist has no problems at all — ex- cept maybe keeping track of all his many hits. Backed by his band the Statesiders. Tillis never faltered on his self-penned hits "Mental Revenge" and “Ruby. Don’t Take Your Love To Town," and even almost made it through the talking part of “Detroit City." Mei was also in top com- edic form with stories that kept the au- dience in the Showcase Theater laughing between songs. Receiving the greatest audience response was Tillis’ new MCA single, “Love Revival.” They may laugh when he talks, but nobody laughs when the man sings. With his faded denims, cowboy hat and boots, Don Williams looks like he just moseyed in off the range to Magic Moun- tain's Contempo Pavilion. The manner in which he sings looks just as casual, mak- ing each number seem more effortless than it really is. Rather sparse backing (only two guitars, plus Williams' own) al- lows his smooth vocals to shine through on such mellow ballads as "Love Me Tonight,” "These Are The Times That Bind" and his latest hit, "Till The Rivers All Run Dry,” from his ABC/Dot LP, “Har- mony.” I.f.c. 30 May 22, 1976

41 Polydor EV 6905; 39 Black Retailers Need Help LOS ANGELES — If the level of aware- ness isn't dramatically heightened on the part of the small record retailer, he may soon become an extinct species, accord- ing to independent R&B promotion specialist Jimmy Bee. "When ! go into a store, the first thing I do is try to establish a relationship with the owner. I tell him. 'You're in a black area, you get a lot of traffic. Your display space and turntable are worth money. You've got to realize that manufacturers pay for this expo- sure.' So many of these cats aren't aware of the advantages they can have." Bee told Cash Box. Bee works R&B records for Arista. Buddah and Casablanca, to name three of many and contends that he has ded- icated his life not merely to thorough professionalism, but also to helping the black businessmen he comes in contact with during the course of his work. He has devised his own formula for promot- ing records. His first step upon entering a given market is to canvas the local R&B radio stations. He has a respectable suc- cess ratio which he attributes to his "knowing my product.” Most promotion men consider airplay to be the end of a day's work. Bee feels airplay is the beginning of his job Elaborate Routine "Once I know a radio station is going to play my record. I then go visit the local distributor." Bee elaborated. "I make him aware of the record and tell him when it'll be getting play in the area. ! tell him what I feel he should initially order I never hype him If it's a work record, I'll make him aware of that fact. I tell him it's a good record, but it's gonna take time to happen and he's going to have to keep on it. If I feel it's an out-and-out smash that will sell big as soon as it gets played. I'll suggest he buy heavier.” continued on pg 45 44 May 22,1976

===== PAGE 45 =====
Black Retail „ After Bee leaves the distributor, he visits the local one-stops repeating his information as well as his gut feeling. He leaves product samples with one stops and lets them know the local distributor when the record will be on the air If the one-stop in question does not buy from the local distributor Bee will pro- vide him with a list of distributors in nearby markets who also handle the re- cord. Key Phase The last phase of Bee's game plan highlights why he is one of a rare breed of promotion people. Bee actually visits retail stores in a given market promoting his records by dropping off samples and apprising owners of imminent airplay. It is in this key area of retail relations that Bee feels a need for improved com- munication with the manufacturing com- munity Bee summarized: "I try to get to know the owners of each store. I ask them if they ever get complimentary tickets to local shows. In almost every case, no is the answer. I ask them if they are visited by salesmen Again the answer in almost every case is no." When asked by CB how store owners found out about new product, available deals involving radio print or display ad- vertising Bee responded. "They're not aware of what's due them — they don't get their fair share I try to get them to understand their own individual impor- tance. They have strong buying power There are stores that do $ 1 0.000 a week in business and have to pay cash on de- livery. Most of them are not even aware of how to get credit They are not offered deals and in some cases have to pay more for product than competitive stores in white neighborhoods. Because of this they are forced to work on a smaller pro- fit margin "When a store is forced to pay C O D he's limited in the amount of product he can stock and he becomes unable to take chances on new product. This not only cuts his volume down but it definitely hurts manufacturers in exposing new product and new artists. Solution? Is there a solution? "I've been working on various solutions." Bee stated. "I go into different areas and try to get dealers to form co-ops. to combine and open up a central warehouse that would be able to buy for all stores. This type of opera- tion would give them buying power and would enable them to get the best deals available. According to figures I've seen R&B product accounts for about 30% of the income of the record industry If every major market could open a co-op. and let's say there are 30 co-ops. and R&B represents 30% of a $2 2 billion in- dustry. anybody can see how important these people can become At that point 30 central warehouses could control over $600 million of volume. These co- ops could go to banks and establish credit as well as doing the same thing with distributors. Even if it's small to begin with, it could be built up in time." Ethics The subject of business ethics is not something that has escaped Bee I know the limitations of this and that's why I’m also trying to teach individual store owners how to do the most effec- tive business within our present system I try to make them aware of the im- portance of a credit line and what it takes to qualify. I tell each owner that he's im- portant to the industry because of the im- portance of R&B product and his role in selling and exposing it. I'm trying to teach them that they can get paid by manufacturers for window displays, billboard displays and in-store play They continued on og 48 ADDITIONSTO R&B PlAYLISTS KYAC - SEATTLE Heaven Must Be Missing — Tavares — Capitol Move Me — James Gilstrap — Chelsea Can't Stop Groovin — B T Express — Columbia This Masquerade — George Benson — W B New LPs — Isleys. "I feel like a mother to every one of them." he said "It's only natural, you know, because I've been liv- ing with the deals for months " While this is Bramson's first full season of booking, he has worked over the last couple of years, in virtually every capa- city for the hall He's been on the stage crew, in the box office, and hall manage- ment Now he is responsible for co- ordinating all these different jobs and making the place run smoothly. "We've got nine guys on salary for the stage crew." Bramson explained "We add another fifteen for each show Other expenses? Well, there's the box office sound and lighting rentals, advertising, and operations, which takes in the ushers and the parking lot people A Prestige Hall The Amphitheatre is an interesting hall. It’s outside, in L A , and only seats five thousand people Obviously, if a band wants to make some fast big money, it will play the Forum, with eigh- teen thousand plus seating capacity. "That's just it." Bramson said "Playing the Amphitheatre is not like playing a one-shot gig. You've got to like the place to do it. and to make money you have to play a few nights But this is a prestigious hall — MCA owns it. the dressing rooms are like homes ' "It's too small a hall for some people." Bramson admitted But groups can hang around L A for a few days, do some PR, maybe some recording, and play at a nice place Los Angeles is home base for a lot of artists.” he added, "so it doesn't really cost them anything to go out Marketing and Analysis How does Bramson decide what acts he will hire? In such a fast season, everything must be calculated with ex- treme care, for the Amphitheatre only has a chance to be used during the sum- mer months "Radio's really what it's all about in terms of marketing." Bramson asserted For The Record * ,» "You've got to be aware of what's hot. and what the kids like." Along this line, many of Bramson's evenings are taken up by concerts at other places. "You've got to be constant- ly aware of the market, throughout the year " he said Analysis follows right along with that awareness When he first took the job Danny Bramson spent two months going over the figures from the previous season, "Your calculator's really your best friend." he laughed. Going through last year's concerts was an incredible learn- ing experience." Bramson said on a more serious note. "I got into all the rec- ords and numbers, and really figured out how to cut expenses; I analyzed ever- ything " Along with its heavy mail-order busi- ness. the Amphitheatre deals with Ticketron outlets, and Bramson must make sure that everything’s working smoothly. Broken ticket machines, co- ordinating the budget along with the out- going checks, people calling up for free tickets — these are some of the many things Bramson has to deal with in addi- tion to making all the deals. The Universal Amphitheatre started out as a place where you could see mov- ies for a buck and get all the popcorn and beer you wanted for free Bramson got the idea to incorporate a rock and roll act (Flash Cadillac and The Continental Kids) into the movies, and helped run. for the summer of seventy-four, a rather suc- cessful season. He chose all the movies for the program Now, in his new position, he does more than just choose movies, and it's a more than full time job After this season is over, he will take the month of October "to get the bright lights out of his head" and then start all over in November with those phone calls. "I’m very proud of the place. " Bramson concluded. "If the Amphitheatre is the one gig a group remembers from a tour, well, everything’s worthwhile." Current rules applied only to the city where the FM station of license was located If an FM station were based in the suburb of a big city with a co-owned AM station, that station was exempt from the non-dupli- cation rules The determining factor will now be the city with the most population. Miami's country music station staged six hours of uninterrupted comedy last April 30 from midnight Friday until 6 a.m Saturday. The program, whose only interruptions came from the announcement of comedy artists and call letters, was the culmination of a month’s promotion on WWOK and in local newspapers. Bob Cole hosted the show and comedians featured included Jerry Clower. Wendy Bagwell , Justis Wilson, Jerry Jordan. Andy Griffith, Charlie Douglas, Jim Nesbett, Oscar Ray and Bob Murphey. Also featured were Hudson & Landry, Bill Cosby, W.C. Fields, The Bickersons, The Watergate Comedy Hour and others . Roy Clark is set to tape an Oral Roberts special in June at Grandfather's Mountain. Entitled "Jerry Clower— Ambassador Of Goodwill." this year's annual album effort was recorded before a live audience at Mississippi State University. Clower's alma mater. In Starkville. Mississippi. Title of the album reflects a recent honor given Clower by MCA label president Mike Maitland. The Country Music Foundation of Colorado recently held a cancer fund benefit for Gary Courtney and Blackie Minor, well-known country music entertainers that have been stricken with cancer. Gary is well-known as a member of the team Patty Gallagher, Gary Courtney & The Showdowners. He has been a member of the Country Music Foundation of Colorado since '69. Blackie has been in country music for over 34 years and is well-known for playing the steel guitar. Blackie and Gary are both members of the Colorado Country Music Hall of Fame. New York's leading country music nightclub will celebrate its third anniversary on the waters around Manhattan in a musical expedition called "O'Lunney's Bicentennial Boat Ride. Barn Dance and Birthday Party. " The event, which is scheduled for Wed- nesday. June 23. from 7:00-1 1:00 p m., will be held aboard the Circle Line's largest boat, with a capacity of 575 persons. Four bands and a variety of single acts will enter- tain, representing “country music" styles that range from 200-year-old English and Irish folk tunes to modern and progressive country music. O'Lunney's instituted a strictly country music policy in May 1973 and celebrates its anniversary with a big party each year . . . Joe D. TALENTON STAGE O’Jays Melba Moore WESTCHESTER PREMIER THEATRE, TARRYTOWN. NY — The O' Jays, one of the foremost exponents of the "Philadelphia sound." brought their stick stage show to the Westchester Premier Theatre Supported by the Backstabbers Band, they offered polished renditions of songs that have permanently secured their position as one of the maior forces in contemporary music. "Survival" and "Give The People What They Want as well as "Unity" and "Family Reunion." their latest Philadelphia International album re- layed the lyric importance to a receptive crowd. Successfully warming up the au- dience. the O Jays performed a short ex- citing medley including such hits as "Backstabbers." "Love Train" and "Put Your Hands Together, abruptly slowing down the pace for a stirring version of Morris Albert's "Feelings." Never a gap to be filled they broke into "For The Love Of Money" complete with manual vocal phasing and an uptempo version of "Livin' For The Weekend, their latest hit. After encoring with “I Love Music. Eddie Levert. Walter Williams and the temporary member Sammy Strain were presented with gold record awards for their latest album and single, a deserved encore for a superb musical evening Buddah recording artist Melba Moore opened the show with songs from her latest album "This Is It." Faring well on ballads like "I'm His Lady" and Gershwin's "Summertime Ms Moore seemed to enthrall the audience with her high-pitched falsetto on "Make Me Believe In You" and "I Got Love." The Santana group's latest incarnation includes old and new personnel, playing a similarly mixed bag of pieces from the group's Columbia repertoire At the center of a darkened stage adorned with tall and quite alive oalm trees straw-hatted San- tana emerged in the spotlight strumming an acoustic introduction to "Gitano. from the new album, "Amigos." From there the show attained increasing levels of intensity each piece reaching its own peak of excitement The single "Let It Shine." was danceably rhythmic, while "Eurooa" was the most dramatically ar- resting new song. The sometimes confusing echo quality of the overall sound, usually a problem Byron Berline & Sundance /Steven Fromholz TROUBADOUR L A - Lately it seems that every new country artist comes out of Texas, and Steven Fromholz is no ex- ception. Fromholz has been a fixture on the Austin scene for several years and was a member of Stephen Stills' "Manassas." but has only this year begun to receive national attention. Now he has a brand new debut LP on Capitol Rec- ords and Willie Nelson's version of his "I'd Have To Be Crazy" is soaring to the top of the country charts. Fromholz shouldn't have to wait too long for a chart record of his own. because he has not one but two new singles — "She's A Lady" (a John Sebastian hit a few seasons ago! aimed at the pop market, and "Late Nite Neon Shadows." which was composed by Fromholz and is geared for country play. Eric Andersen SCHOENBURG HALL UCLA — The young woman repeated the three words to herself over and over "Violets Of Dawn " Eric Anderen didn t play that one much to the woman's disappoint- ment. but he did run through a number of his older songs as well as songs from his recent Arista LP "Sweet Surprise." Andersen is one mid-sixties trouba- dour who has been able to stay in touch with the times His writing has changed, matured in both style and content One song from his new album " How It Goes has a lyrical depth and melody strong enough to compare it favorably to some of Dylan's latest work. Particularly moving was Andersen's performance of his song that has become a folk standard "Thirsty Boots “ Dedicated to the memory of Phil Ochs the tune has been musically reworked through the years and is now an entity in itself. The guitar arrangement was supremely tasteful and always interest- ing. and Andersen's gritty, emotion- packed voice became a collage of dif- ferent meanings. Another pleasing number was the successful single from the "Blue River LP "Is It Really Love At All." Andersen has remained in the in- dustry mainsteam for so long, in part because of his innovative ways with melody That tune was a prime example of his talent in that direction More re- cent songs indicated that his abilities have matured even further. With these new. tightly crafted tunes Eric Andersen's performance cries out for a backing band While his guitar play- ing is more than proficient, he really needs a drummer, piano player and backing guitars in order to put across the full power of his songs. i-m. Al Wilson/D.J. Rogers/ Streetcorner Symphony INTERNATIONAL ROOM. BEVERLY HILTON. BEVERLY HILLS — "I've Got A Feeling" that Al Wilson is going to be a lot bigger, was the feeling everyone had at the culmination of a strong set by this Playboy recording artist recently at the Beverly Hills Hilton. Wilson's dynamic soul voice provided a constant get-down beat that, complemented by the backup instruments, saw an evening of some of the best strict R&B stuff unfold right in front of your ears Wilson s success so far has been mostly from hits that haven't taken the nation by storm, but his versatility on his own and others' material certainly allude to a big future for this artist. Dressed in an all-white suit. D.J. Rogers strutted on stage ready to put on a really funk show And that he did Rogers' intimacy with the audience (he had 'em all clappin' on the second tune) is phenomenal When he works a song lyrically, the group behind him work the same song in movement. It's that total commitment by the headline star and the group that give the audience their money's worth. From the pulsating rhythms of songs non-so- familiar to Rogers' fans, to the lilting vocal on "Say You Love Me " a smash for D J . the show's aliveness and ex- uberance were something that caught on with all. Streetcorner Symphony, a group that does their thing a cappella, do it well, but they take too long They do a '50s and '60s medley of hits like "I Can t Help Myself " and "Have You Seen Her?" that is pleasant and well received But if this group wants to achieve success wherever they go. they must find a way to bottle up the energy that both enchants but soon begins to annoy the crowd And they should bottle up the time taken to distribute that energy for sometimes an opening act should be short and sweet, so the audience can call it back if they like. j.b.c. Dr. Feelgood The Ramones Dr Feelgood on version of Lieber and Stollers “Riot In BOTTOM LINE NYC Columbia and the Ramones on Sire are two recently signed groups that stand out with individually styled caricatures of rock 'n' roll. Although some sense of humor seems necessary in the apprecia- tion of either, they do not parody or make any all out attempt at humor. Rather, they emphasize or exaggerate some feature or period of rock music, turning out sounds that seem bizarre against the mainstream of contemporary popular styles. Dr Feelgood derives some of its re- pertoire from the fifties, and even its original numbers effect the rhythm and blues that must have been heard in English pubs over a decade ago. Feelgood members are outspoken critics of the slickening techniques of the modern studio, and their live performance proves their actions are true to their word Their sound is crisp, their renditions tight, and the musi- cianship. especially in the case of lead guitarist Wilko Johnson, is sophisticated to a point belied by the simple forms in which they work Lead vocalist Lee Brilleaux joins Johnson in some out- rageous onstage antics, while he con- tributes with harmonica and slide guitar. Dr. Feelgood presented selections from their album "Malpractice." from shuffles like “Going Back Home" to rockers such as "Another Man " Traditional numbers included Muddy Waters' "Rollin’ And Tumblin' " and a pull-out-the-stops Cell Block #9." where John B. Sparks' bass and Big Figure's drumming pro- vided more than enough bump and grind Although their desire for dance- ability can lead to a steadiness in rhythm that becomes tiresome by the set's end. Dr Feelgood are exciting on stage. As an encore. “Great Balls of Fire" left ever- yone with a good taste. Occupying a musical slot somewhere in the dark netherworld between Herman's Hermit's and ZZ Top. the Ramones are presently in the position to expose their brand of New York Bowery rock to a national audience. This “open- ing” coincided with the release of "Ramones’’ on Sire, although the leather-jacketed crew still play at their old hangout. CBGB’s. No instrumental expertise is involved in their music's ex- ecution, yet the concept is esoteric. When looked upon as the extreme of rock at its most basic, the Ramones music seems to appeal to critics who would normally have no use for middle ground hard rock groups. The entire set. over 15 tunes in all. was executed in un- der 30 minutes, including "Beat On The Brat" and the single. "Blitzkrieg Bob." Truthfully, unless one tries really hard to believe, the various permutations of three chords that make up the Ramones' repertoire might easily all sound the same. As musical extremists, the Ramones seem to inspire love and hate and those reactions promise to continue. p.d. May 29 1976 37

4SHB0KR&B : R&B INGREDIENTS The tall pine trees and crystal blue waters of Lake Tahoe were the perfect back- ground for AI Green's debut at the Sahara Tahoe Hotel. Al's great voice was clear and sweet throughout his show. Al's band and Quiet Elegance made the evening memora- ble. Later backstage Al said that the 7.000 foot altitude did affect his voice at first dur- ing rehearsals prior to the show, but after a few days he said he had it together. Jimmie Walker, one of the stars of “Good Times,” opened for Al. Jimmie was red-hot opening night. Jimmie, who records comedy LPs for Buddah said he is currently working on material fora new LP plus working out details for his next motion picture. Ben Vereen was also in Tahoe at Harrah s along with Don Rickies. Ben is loaded with talent, and he won the crowds' hearts with a dazzling display of singing and dancing. One of the highlights being a tribute to Bert Williams, a vaudeville star back in the days of the Ziegfeld Follies. Don Rickies', everybody's favorite Mr Nice Guy. as usual had the crowd rolling in the aisles with his rapid-fire humor . For The Record * 29 Another event to watch for potential talent is the upcoming Garden Theatre Festival which will touch down on Barnsdail Park, 4800 Hollywood Blvd. for 21 days, July 2-25. One of a series of such happenings up and down California, this year’s festival organized by Warren Christensen will feature much more than mimes, magicians, plays, movies, crafts, dancers and jugglers. There will also be a variety of musical of- ferings including folk, country, blues, chamber, dixieland, flute quartets, brass quin- j refs and a number of "singer!songwriters. " Festival will also feature special concerts I bv Stephen Michael Schwartz and Sandy Ross (who handles talent at the Bla Bla). Chaka Khan and company are presently in the studio getting their next album together Having sat on the NARAS screening committee last winter, this re- porter was a bit surprised to find the experts saying Rufus is as much a pop group as it is R&B. But it's true. Tom Sullivan is one of those guys that guys like me resent. It's not just that his book. “ if You Could See What I Hear,” is in its fifth printing or that he used to skydive. It's not that he qualified for the '68 Olympics team in wrestling or that he’s singing the na- tional anthem at this year's Indy 500. I don't even mind that he won the Outstanding Performance Award at the Yamaha Music Festival in Tokyo or the fact that he golfs in the high 80s. What burns me up is that this ABC recording artist has the nerve — on top of all that — to be blind. His latest LP . “Yes, I'm Ready." Broadcast Graduates *• 24 gram, but more than that, we send out letters to stations informing them of our graduates as well as providing informa- tion to graduates from alumni who report job openings." The head of broadcasting at the University of Southern California. Joe Saltzman. had a word too "I would tell students who are graduating to get out of the big markets and look in the small markets." This is a statement that parallels the typical radio career, since many jocks in major markets have worked their way up through smaller markets and stations. Saltzman said that some students graduated and enjoyed going to a smaller market station "They like the lifestyle there, they upgrade the station with their professional back- ground. and then they can work their way uptothe bigger markets if they want.” Rosy Picture? The job situation for broadcast graduates from universities is certainly not the most rosy picture one could paint But the expertise of these depart- ment heads who have seen their graduates leave and get something or nothing is important. The fight is just beginning for job seeking graduates, but it's how professional they are in both their approach and background training that should determine if they will land jobs and the future they want. Record Company Report One record company that does pro- vide some help for the graduate is Atlan- tic Records Judy Libow in the New York office told us of a report that's mailed to all radio stations on the Atlantic mailing list The report is a compilation of graduates' mini-resumes, their phones and addresses, and the areas they would prefer to work in Atlantic issues a letter yearly to college broadcasting depart- ments. soliciting graduating students to send this information to the company. "We call it the Job Hunting Service and it's our fourth year Libow commented. It is a start and although some people do get jobs from the listings, we don't always get feedback from either the ap- plicant or radio station. That's what we would like to have more of." This year's issue is 18 pages long and although it is too late for a graduate to have his re- sume listed now. it would be an early start for next year's graduates. It's a sim- ple step and could possibly save a lot of looking Soul Waves * 39 WSOK is having a local fund raiser for two families who recently lost their homes in the Savannah area, according to Don Wilson, music director at the station Bill Moon, program director at WCKO in Columbus said that his station is starting a public affairs program called ‘‘Fuss Behind The Bus,” which is a documentary educa- tional feature on busing. Copyright Collection 21st Full Control Since 1911 Copyright Act Moon Award To Somers At 8th BMI Canada Dinner For Outstanding International Contributions LONDON — The Music Publishers As- sociation has taken over full control of the Mechanical Copyright Protection Society at a total purchase cost of about 350.000 pounds sterling. The new managing director is Bob Montgomery (previously with Chappell Ind.) and former MCPS directors Bill Abbott and Bert Pratt have been retained as consul- tants. Commenting on the new MPA president Dick James said. 1 For the first time since the Copyright Act of 1911 U K. copyright owners will have full con- trol of their collection of mechanical royalties. The importance of this was reflected by the large turnout at the meeting.'' DJM Records has signed two deals with CBS in Holland. The first gives the CBS plant in Holland complete rights to the manufacture of DJM Records for the whole of Europe including tapes The deal was negotiated by Stephen James and Nick Hampton, managing director and group business coordinator for DJM respectively and Peter Bowwens for CBS in Holland. The second agreement is for distribution of DJM product in Holland, whereby DJM will select re- leases for the Holland territory Market- ing, promotion, sales and distribution will be undertaken by CBS in Holland This deal was negotiated by Stephen James and Nick Hampton for DJM and John Vis, Chas Chandler: Barn Records LONDON — Chas Chandler has set up his own label, to be known as Barn Rec- cords Chandler's current publishing company is known as Barn Music, and acts appearing on the new set up will be Slade Brian Parrish and Medicine Head Last week Chandler flew to Hamburg and signed a world-wide (excluding the USA; distributing and manufacturing deal with J. Dieter Bliersbach. senior vice presi- dent of Polydor International. This new deal replaces the existing agreement for Slade which was due to expire at the end of the year and covers all product on the new label Chandler started life in the music business as bass player with the Animals, and then went on to manage the legendary Jimi Hendrix, and after his death Slade First release on the label will be an album from the reunited Animals. Co-founder of London Records and Disney and Buena Vista veteran jazz musician Tutti Camarata was guest of honor at a lunch hosted by Sir Edward Lewis of Decca Records to celebrate Tutti’s 30 years as an artist with the com- pany and to re-sign his contract. While at Disney he produced over 300 children's LPs before leaving to start his own studios in Los Angeles known as Sunset Sound. He then went on to co-found London Records with Sir Edward. T utti is currently recording a new album in Kingsway Hall titled ‘Opera For Orchestra — La Boheme. Com- menting on the new GTO managing director Leahey said. "This is an ex- tension of a highly successful working relationship which has been built up over many years. Now that GTO Records is highly structured world-wide. I see this marriage as the perfect opportunity to develop our publishing strength.' ‘Price Cutting’ Common, Says The Agency’s Cottini TORONTO — The Agency is the latest entry into the Canadian booking agency field, formed in March of this year by Dave Bluestein and Tim Cottini. both formerly with Concept 376 in this city. With about five years' professional ex- perience between them in the agency field and additional experience in con- cert promotions and band management, the two severed dealings with Concept and set about building up a personal hard-hitting national booking agency that attempts to work with a few select artists and build them up step by step There is always a certain amount of backfighting among agencies,' Blue- stein says, "but we don't really get too in- volved since we have our hands full tak- ing careof ourown operation.” Cottini claims that "price cutting" on acts that haven't signed exclusively to one agency is a fairly common practice and asserts that “when an agency is sup- plying regular entertainment to clubs, then the agent's interest is with the club ' more than with the band. Both Cottini and Bluestein are in agreement with Music Shoppe International's Ron Scrib- ner, also based in Toronto, on the fact that foreign acts are better off signing TORONTO — Toronto composer Harry Somers was this year's recipient of the Harold Moon Award for his outstanding contributions to Canadian music on an international level at the eighth annual BMI Canada awards dinner. The award, named after BMI Canada's founder and first managing director, car- ries with it a cash prize of $500. Moon has been active in the Canadian music industry for the last 27 years and remains a consultant and member of the board of BMI Canada Limited. The citation to Somers was based on his participation in World Music Week celebrations in Canada last fall, attended by representatives from 44 countries. Delegates at that time had the opportuni- ty to hear no fewer than four major works by the composer, including "Sonata for Violin” commissioned for and performed with a Canadian agency for representa- tion at the booking level in this country. "The fact is that the two countries are stuck together at the border but a Cana- dian agent can save a foreign act a great deal of money because of his own specific knowledge of this market." Blue- stein says. Staffed by four full time agents and a secretary. The Agency has been suc- cessful in placing a number of domestic acts on top-line concert shows as openers across the country, largely through co-operation with major concert promoters such as Donald Tarlton in Montreal and Concert Productions In- ternational's Mike Cohl in Toronto. In ad- dition, The Agency has ties with Studio City and Bruce Allen Talent Promotions in western Canada. Frank Wiener in northern Ontario and Entertainment Contacts in the Maritimes. Bluestein considers club bookings to be a major revenue earner for his com- pany at this time but feels that there are not enough across the country to handle the amount of business that is available. Among the acts that have signed for exclusive representation with The Agen- cy in this country are Gino Vannelli, Brutus. Downchild. Charity Brown. Fludd. the Stampeders. Good Brothers. Ken Tobias. A Foot In Coldwater, and Harry Chapin. Both Cottini and Bluestein are looking into national package tours with acts for the fall by Yehudi Menuhin, and the opera "Louis Riel." Subsequent to World Music Week several foreign countries asked for tapes for rebroadcast. Bicentennial Effort The Canadian Opera Company's pro- duction of "Louis Riel” was also staged in Washington as part of Canada's contribu- tion to the U S. bicentennial. This perfor- mance was recorded as a joint effort of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC! and the U S Public Broadcasting System. "Louis Riel" was broadcast across Canada especially for the official opening of the CBC-FM stereo coast-to- coast network, the longest of its kind in the world. The recording was distributed to the more than 120 stations of the Public Broadcasting System. Somers' “Gloria" was also performed at Kennedy Center last year as part of the bicenten- nial celebrations. "It is interesting to note." continued the citation, "that the index of recordings produced and distributed by Radio Canada International around the world contains 18 of Somers' works, more works than by any other Canadian." ("Loves Me Like A Brother" and "Dancin' Fool"); Ken Tobias ("Run Away With Me" and "Lady Luck"); and Randy Bachman of BTO, the group that walked away with three Junos this year ("Hey You" and "You Ain't Seen Nothing Yet"). Bowie, Kinks LPs Released By RCA NEW YORK — RCA Records is releasing two greatest hits packages and one previously unreleased album from its vaults. “Changes One Bowie" is a compila- tion of Bowie hits being released simul- taneously with his first motion picture, “The Man Who Fell To Earth,” containing "Fame,” Space Oddity,” “Changes," “Dia- mond Dogs." “Young Americans” and others. “Celluloid Fleroes” is a collection of the Kinks' best works on RCA, including heretofore unreleased live versions of album cuts including “Here Comes Another Day” and “Skin And Bone,” along with studio versions of “Musweil Hillbilly,” "Everybody’s A Star,” “20th Century Man” and the title cut. The previously unre- leased album is the Guess Who’s “The Way We Were,” recorded in 1 970, featuring Bur- ton Cummings, Jim Kale, Gary Peterson, and a pre-GTO Randy Bachman. Brotherhood Of Man Leads Pye LP Release NEW YORK — The Brotherhood of Man leads off Pye Records' four album June release schedule. In addition to “Save Your Kisses For Me,” The Brotherhood of Man's first American album release, are Nikki Giovanni's “Truth Is On The Way,” on Right On Records distributed by Calla Records; “I'll Go Where Your Music Takes Me,” by British artist Jimmy James; and "Falling In Love," by The Ninth Creation, newly signed ten piece R&B band from California. Capricorn Releases 2 MACON, GA. — Capricorn Records, has announced the release of two albums for June: The Marshall Tucker Band’s “Long Hard Ride” and the Capricorn premiere of Billy Joe Shaver, “When I Get My Wings." LOS ANGELES — This week marks an ex- citing milestone in the brief history of Mer- cury Records’ compact west coast branch office. The event — a chart-entry LP by the label’s brand-new female rock band. The Runaways, only one week after its initial issue — illustrates in practical terms how a relatively small group of individuals can represent a rather large firm, even though the operation is divided by 2,200 geo- and a more well-defined role,” says Denny. “We all know exactly what we're doing. We have to; because there's no one else to shove it off to. I don’t think anybody here feels the need for having anybody else, though. We'd love to have an assistant or a helper for those times when it just turns banana city, but we can handle the lion’s share." This view may be somewhat cavalier. From his vantage point in Chicago, Irwin Steinberg oversees a combined Mercury force of 130 employees — not very many compared to some companies which may have 130 individuals in Los Angeles alone. To place the west coast office in perspec- tive, over the past three years Denny Rosencrantz has exercised the label’s reach here presiding over a staff of four — west coast publicity director Susanella Rogers; west coast regional marketing director George Steiner; southern Califor- nia promotion manager Lindy Gaetz; and Rosencrantz himself, general manager and west coast A&R. David Vs. Goliath Inasmuch as the west coast must now be defined as the center of record industry ac- tivity, this David and Goliath mismatch would seem humanly impossible tograpple with. Rid Of Dead Weight "We're down to more business with 50 acts than we used to do with 100," Denny emphasizes. “Irwin got rid of a lot of dead weight and got the company to where everybody’s really cooking. And that means more money available for every act on the roster; nobody gets lost in the record company shuffle for priorities. The princi- ple, still, is to find acts that are entities — that are going to be stars and cover a wide spectrum." A group like the Runaways, perhaps? Rosencrantz is really enthused in answer to this question which was posed even before the release of the band’s first album: Same Old Feeling “I have the same sociological feeling for the Runaways as I had for other acts at their beginnings before they came to this label,” Rosencrantz offers. "Acts like Bowie, Rod Stewart, even the New York Dolls. Here's the Runaways, five young teenage girls playing rock and roll. Real teenage girls (every member of the group is under 17) writing and playing their own stuff. "First time I saw them they were a power trio and I didn't quite like them. Whatever they were trying to do, they couldn’t quite pull it off. But when they added the lead singer and the bass player and made it into a regular band, I fell in love with them.” Cash Box asked Rosencratz about the signing process: is it a joint decision? continued on og 23 New Jazz Product Through MMO Labels NEW YORK — Music Minus One, best known for its self-teaching music methods and participation records, has ventured into a full scale release of some European and American jazz catalogs including product by such artists as Jean-Luc Ponty, Archie Shepp, Phil Woods and Zoot Sims. Irv Kratka. president of Music Minus One, Inc., has reactivated Classic Jazz Records, a label designed to market swing and traditional jazz, and has formed Inner City Records, a label which will specialize in progressive jazz, blues and gospel music. Inner City’s initial releases are Archie Shepp’s “Doodlin' " and “Phil Woods and his European Rhythm Machine." Other albums soon to be released on Inner City are by such artists as Jean-Luc Ponty, Art Ensemble of Chicago. Memphis Slim and the Free Jazz Crusaders; Ornette Coleman, Don Cherry and Paul Bley. Inner City Records will retail for $6.98 with nationwide distribution. Classic Jazz Records initial releases are Jane Harvey’s “You Fats, Me Jane." a tribute to Fats Waller and "Zoot Sims and Friend” with guitarist Bucky Pizzarelli. Classic Jazz Records will retail for $6.98 as well. Until the debut of the new product. Kratka had been licensing material from abroad and releasing it in the U.S. as well as negotiating the rights for major jazz catalogs from two major European firms. Arrogance, Elvin Jones Lead Vanguard LP Set NEW YORK — "Rumors," the debut album of rock group Arrogance, headlines Vanguard Records’ latest album release, with Elvin Jones' second for the label, "The Main Force.” leading off in the jazz category. Arrogance is produced by John Anthony, while drummer Jones’ session in- cludes Dave Liebman, Steve Grossman, Pat LaBarbera and Ryo Kawasiki. “The Essential Louis Armstrong” isajazz twofer with selections recorded live in Paris in 1965, while "The Essential Ramblin’ Jack Elliot” is a double-record set featuring material not recently available. For classical listeners, the budget Everyman label offers a five disk set of Richard Strauss tone poems, with Strauss himself conducting the Vienna Philharmonic in 1944, while Mozart's Requiem K. 626 is per- formed by vocalists led by Johannes Somary, and the English Chamber Or- chestra.
