Jack Craigo Broaden The Base LOS ANGELES — Jack Craigo, vice presi- dent and general manager, marketing, for CBS Records, noted a number of points that from a marketing standpoint were necessary ingredients for continuous growth at CBS. “First of all, we need to in- crease our understanding of the demo- graphics and premeditated buying power levels of our targeted consumers. Secon- dly, we need to broaden the base of the music buying consumer. And following that, increase the effectiveness of advertis- ing in both consumer advertising and national label media advertising invest- ments. We need to develop and increase the sales for eight-track and cassettes. And finally, increase the unit sales for disk and tape per square foot of available retail marketing space.” Craigo added that CBS must improve its market share, even at the expense of com- petitors, noting that, “We want every share point you can capture.” He declared that the “bottom line for promotion is to get the record played, and the measurement for sales is to get the order.” He cautioned that he or CBS were not arrogant, but “we’re into new creative thinking, imaginative techniques, creative planning and into focusing our attention upon broad projects which will produce growth for both the company and your own personal develop- ment.” Zeroing in on the success of CBS, Craigo declared that “we’re working with three groups of partners in our business: our ar- tists/their managers and agencies, radio programmers and our customers." He called the label “proud and experienced, prudent and innovative, aggressive and competitive and persistent. A company connected with the artists, with radio, and its customers to form a music business community within an industry. We’re CBS Records.” Paul Smith Sales Up 39% LOS ANGELES — “There is nothing that we at headquarters demand of you that we don’t demand of ourselves,” declared Paul Smith, vice president of marketing, dis- tribution. “Play to win as an individual and asateam. Know the position and getthejob done." Smith congratulated the sales force on “the best six-month period in our history, with sales up 39% over the same period last year. In each month since our last conven- tion, July 1975 through June 1976, you’ve outbilled the corresponding month in any prior year." He attributed their success to “consistent, outstanding one-on-one performers.” Bruce Lundvall in 4 • A balanced product flow: “A commit- ment we made to you and a commitment that we’ve kept. Closer communication and understanding between A&R activities and marketing needs has resulted in a far more even and intelligent balancing of releases throughout the year.” • Country music: “A hot spot today.” • “At the same time, we’ve built the largest, most professional and totally staf- fed special markets team in the country.” • Single records: “We’re a hot singles company and we’re going to stay that way.” Lundvall also spoke of the growth of the Epic and associated labels, the company’s west coast expansion and the company’s moves to sign artists in every area. In con- clusion, he noted the text of an ad that CBS ran in Cash Box last week: “We’re music lovers in the music business." And he ad- ded that he was “honored to serve as your president” of the “#1 record company.” CBS Associated Labels Premiere New LPs LOS ANGELES — At the CBS Records 1976 Convention, CBS associated labels announced the release of twelve new albums, including LPs on Richard Bran- sen’s Virgin Records, Gamble and Huff’s Philadelphia-International and TSOP Records, Steve Paul’s Blue Sky Records, Don Kirshner’s Kirshner Records, James Guercio’s Caribou label and Fred Foster’s Soundstage labels. On the Philadelphia-International schedule are new albums by the O’Jays and by Bunny Sigler “My Music." Archie Bell and the Drells will release their second album on TSOP. “Supercharge” is the title of the first Virgin album by the English group of the same name, and Dan Hartman, will make his Blue Sky debut as a solo artist. Kansas’ newest album will appear on Kirshner Records, Caibou will release the initial LP effort by James Vincent and an album by Eddie Russ will mark the re- emergence of Monument’s affiliated label Soundstage 7. LOS ANGELES — New albums on Colum- bia Records by a wide range of artists were previewed at the CBS Records 1976 con- vention. In all, more than 40 albums to be shipped within ninety days of the event were introduced to the CBS Records per- sonnel and invited guests attending the convention. A combination of live ap- pearances, filmed presentations and slide shows was used to showcase the new product. Among the releases premiered were the new album by Earth, Wind and Fire, “Spirit”; the label debut of the Miracles, and two-LP live packages by Herbie Hancock and Laura Nyro. Also on the Columbia schedule are “Delicate & Jumpy" by the Fania All-Stars, and “Inside Star Trek,” a spoken-word album featuring the producer, Gene Roddenberry, and stars, William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, of the television show. Progressive music will be represented by albums by Freddie Hubbard (“Windjam- mer"), The New Tony Williams Lifetime (“Million Dollar Legs”) and the first Colum- bia album by poll-winning flautist Hubert Laws. Established Columbia artists with new albums in the offing include popular singers Jon Lucien, Mac Davis, Bill Withers and Andy Williams, as well as veteran music-maker Ray Coniff. Contemporary artists with LPs due include Journey, Tom Jans and Cecilio & Kapono, and second Columbia albums by Flo & Eddie (“Moving Targets") and Artful Dodger (“Honor Among Thieves”) will also be issued in the post-convention period. TALENTON STAGE fortherecord ZZ Top TULANE STADIUM. NEW ORLEANS — Many bands have named themselves for their place of origin, but probably no other has done as much public relations for their home as ZZ Top. The “little ol' band from Texas" is currently touring afull production including flora and fauna of the big state, along with a Texas-shaped stage and lights and backdrops simulating the shifting pastel hues of the desert plains. The show’s opening leans heavily on visual elements, with a curtain drawn back to reveal the bur- ning sun as a lone wolf howls. For a few seconds a black bison and stately longhorn steer fade into view, tended by tall peaceful figures in ten-gallon hats. A windmill spins gently in the quiet breeze, and a vulture fans its graceful wings. While this motion picture scenario might suggest the soundtrack arrangement of program rock, ZZ Top's music is the sim- plest and most straightforward of hard rock blues and boogie. This evening they opened as they do on the live side of “Fan- dango" with “Thunderbird.” The three-man group displays an equality of parts where the three instruments blend into one sound, and although guitarist Billy Gibbons and bassist Dusty Hill carry this further by standing unusually close to one another on stage, they do alternate the front-man's duties. Gibbons shows the influences of many varieties of blues. On “Chevrolet” he is a strutting, plunking image of Chuck Berry, or he can lean to the deep growling boogie of a John Lee Hooker, as well as coming close to the riffing, rapping style of B.B. King as he advfses on the treatment of a lover during "Blue Jean Blues." All in his own kindly manner, appealing to the audience’s ego and feeling them respond as one. Dusty Hill's raunchier voice is featured on the single, “T ush,” part of a long encore that included “La Grange” and covers of “Jailhouse Rock" and "Folsom Prison Blues." The band saluted the serpent at the tip of the stage with a novel version of Peter Greene's “Rattlesnake Shake," while a song from their upcoming London album, “Love Is The Only Thing That Drives Me Crazy," was carried along/by a steady ac- centuation of the upbeat by drummer Frank Beard. Another bit of Texas culture was in- troduced in thesecond encore's "Backdoor Medley," with Gibbons and Hill one-upping each other in the frantic chant of the auc- tioneer. ZZ Top’s unrefined brand of guitar boogie is not the type that finds airplay on all stations and they certainly have made no musical compromises simply for the sake of appeasing their unfavorable critics. Their audience is young by nature, and this eve- ning in this city about 50,000 strong (with J. Geils on the bill). Whether they crack their toughest market, the northeast, this time around, no doubt they will always remain the same. p.d. Sylvers Dorothy Moore Johnnie Taylor Brass Construction FORUM, L.A. — Even though the house wasn't full those who attended probably saw one of the best R&B packages assem- bled this past year. The show got better and better with the entrance of each act. Opening the show was the lovely Dorothy Moore. Wearing a flowing black chiffon gown this girl from Jackson, Mississippi added thousands of new fans to her already growing legions. Dorothy Moore is a won- derful performer. Even though her reper- toire is not loaded with greatest hits yet, it will be. Everything she sang was filled with emotion, warmth and beauty. Dorothy Moore has star quality. Brass Construction then came on stage and blew everyone out. Randy Muller and company were wearing some very hot space costumes to go along with some very tight, crisp instrumentation. Several times during their show they had the audience up and on their feet to boogie and sing along. “Movin’,” was the #1 crowd pleaser. The Sylvers have greatly improved their show to sheer perfection. The group has really got things organized and all that can be said about them is watch out for future developments. The choreography was im- peccable and their stage presence was flawless. Exceptional numbers performed were their new single "Cotton Candy,” "Storybook Girl,” and their version of Wings "Silly Love Songs,” and Morris Albert’s "Feelings.” The finale, "Boogie Fever," was just icing on the cake. The fantastic Johnnie Taylor came on last and it was worth the wait. The man cooks. To open the show Johnnie warmed everybody up with “Who’s Makin’ Love To Your Old Lady.” From then on the show grooved. The backup orchestra was ex- cellent along with four of the prettiest nicest sounding backup vocalists around. John- nie did all of the hits and in between did his famous bumps and grinds. He had total control over the audience because when he asked the sisters to scream, they respon- ded enthusiastically. “Somebody’s Gittin’ It,” his new single was well-received along with ‘‘Runnin’ Out Of Lies” off his "Eargasm” LP. For the finale Johnnie naturally did "Disco Lady.” The place went wild, enough said. J.l. Conway Twitty/ Loretta Lynn LONG BEACH ARENA, CALIF. — Very few country singers have been as honored as Loretta Lynn. The beautiful lady from Butcher Holler, Kentucky has won virtually every award to be handed out for country music, and has been voted one of the most admired women in the country. One reason for Ms. Lynn’s success has to be the sense of identification that people feel for her. The lady has a sense of realness that comes from deep within, and reaches out to touch the listener. The songs composed by Ms. Lynn are generally about homey subjects that a large number of people can identify with, such as “Coal Miner’s Daughter,” about her poverty-stricken but happy childhood; “First City,” about jealousy; or “One’s On The Way,” about the tribulations of a small-town housewife. Some people undoubtedly find her tunes corny, probably because they hit a little too close to home. Ms. Lynn possesses the richly emotional vocal quality to make her songs believable and enjoyable. Altogether, the lady is a total original—one of the few in music today. Conway Twitty is one of a group of fifties rock-a-billies whose careers have since turned down country roads. Most of his big hits, such as “Fifteen Years Ago,” and “Af- ter All The Good Is Gone,” have that Presleyesque flavor that separates them from the run-of-the-mill country song. Twitty has a rich and varied voice with sen- sual overtones, and uses it to best advan- tage on the sexy love songs like “I See The Want To In Your Eyes” and “Touch The Hand." Conway and Loretta are the premier duo in country music today, with numerous hit singles and albums on MCA records in the last six years. THE GREAT ESCAPE — Passing through town recently, arranger, producer and Atlan- tic Records artist Gene Page described the inspiration for a cut on his “Lovelock” album, “Escape To Disco. ” He was sitting in a sauna bath with a psychiatrist friend, who aired theories of the discotheque as a place of “escape” and “release of pent-up anxieties. ” Page tried to effect these feelings with sound. Later in the day, Page fielded questions from the press, recalling that Barry White’s “rap" over the phone to his wife was equally effective as any heard on record . . . Mark Radice, who was recently catapulted into the limelight as emergency lead singer for Brass Construction and now has his own album and single out on U.A., has been around popular music for most of his 18 years on earth. His father was a recording engineer, and he can remember Jimi Hendrix in the studio. Radice penned Dion’s current single “Hey My Love" when he was 13. POINTS WEST— SMOKE SIGNALS — Dream Merchants Unlimited of Atlanta has joined forces with the T-Shirtery, a big distributor of what their name implies, in a new merchan- dising scheme which will aim at the same market that's been so responsive to High Times Magazine. The two firms are now producing rock 'n rolling papers with album graphics on the outer cover and ad art on the inside of the paper package. Dream Merchant president Norman Penfield says the plan will offer artists “triple value. " Not only will the product promote albums and concert appearances, but it’s an additional royalty source as well. The papers will be marketed in retail record stores as well as traditional outlets that service an estimated 30 million A mericans with some 200 million packages of rolling papers a year. First two acts involved in the promotion gimmick are Camel and the Atlanta Rhythm Sec- tion. For further information, phone Norman Penfield at (404) 434-8794. C4SHBOX RsB R&B Ingredients An interesting situation arose after analyzing the charts this week. What seems to be occurring is a heightened awareness by both pop and black programmers into both pop and R&B product. 'Disco Lady. " by Johnnie Taylor and "Boogie Fever, " by the Sylvers are the only two singles to have gone platinum so far in 1976. Both records were #1 onthe Cash Box pop and R&B charts. It seems that both record and radio people are becoming more knowledgeable of both areas and see how important it is to be conscious of crossover potential. Pop groups like the Doobie Brothers, Boz Scaggs, Elvin Bishop, David Bowie, Bee Gees and Steve Miller are all getting heavy black AM airplay. So are Johnnie Taylor, Lou Rawls, Natalie Cole, Tavares, Wild Cherry etc. on the pop side. The record buying public seems to be ready for this crossover situation and both record and radio people are preparing themselves for it. Hottest news of the week is that the Jackson Family LPis already in the can. It was produced by Gamble & Huff. Also learned that Theodore Pendergrass is going to do a solo LP. He will not be with the Blue Notes. Gamble & Huff will be producing the Teddy Bear. On the other hand Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes are negotiating with Gamble & Huff for their next LP. . .Also made an error last week, the new Miracles LP "Power Of Music" was written by both Bill Griffin and Peter Moore. Pete, not Bill produced the LP . . . Sorry . . Jermaine Jackson’s new solo LP on Motown is being readied for shipment at any time. The Parliaments are inches away from going platinum with their "Mothership Connection," LP. Tavares high on both charts with their LP and single can be seen on the Dinah Shore Show August 4th The brothers are happening . Archie Bell and the Dreils are off to Brazil for a major tour. After that they’re headed for Africa. Their new LP will be out shortly . The Commodores have added a horn section to the group so that their sound will be that much richer when they perform live . . . Isn't their LP the hottest thing happening? . . Jean Cams, the fantastic vocalist on the 1st Norman Connors LP is just finishing her LP for Philly International. Jean is managed by Billy Ward, formerly of that great group of the past, the Dominos. Rapped with Lewis Grey last week about the upcoming Earth, Wind & Fire show at the Rose Bowl. Grey said the gate will be one million dollars and this show at the Rose Bowl will be much better than the one Hollywood Bowl because the whole city of Pasadena is involved. Security will be tighter than at last year's show. Tickets will be scaled from 8 to 10 dollars. There will also be a special V.I.P. section. There won't be festival seating but assigned seating just like for football games. Grey is interested in adding the O'Jays to the show, but so far hasn’t received word from the group. Also learned that the Commodores may be doing the show . . . Grey commen- ted that the promotion business has changed dramatically over the past few years. "Today's promoters are businessmen. It's getting tougher and tougher on the guys that don't know the business. The key to success in the promotion business is in being organized. You need to have a top staff that know how to organize and present the best show possible. I'm finding out now that promoters, agencies, groups and managers are working closer together to bring the best possi- ble show to the public ... I feel that the upcoming Earth, Wind & Fire will be one of the biggest and best concerts of the year . Joe Fisher, program director at WCKO and past president of the Florida chapter of NATRA feels the organization needs a lot of changes. "First off the location of the con- vention is horrible. I can't afford to go, and I’m a program director. How can other air personalities do it? The organization does need a lot of help. I do like the idealism behind an organization like NATRA but for the past five or six years, the older mem- bers just bicker, argue, and fuss and nothing gets done. The organization has never acknowledged any of the younger programmers and given them a chance to participate. Also there has been too much in-fighting between the members from the north and the south. NATRA has not changed with the times, everyone in black radio has tried valiantly to grow except the NATRA organization. I think that NATRA should also try to be more self-sufficient as an organization without depending on record companies for help. When the record companies are involved, they mus- cle in. I would like to see a convention where I and my radio colleagues could inter-relate and learn.” Bernard Miller, program director at KNOK in Ft. Worth feels NATRA could be the answer, but that it doesn't do anything for its members. “I don’t see NATRA focus- ing in on the needs of the program directors and jocks. I would have liked to attend if they had seminars, where I could have sat down and talked shop. However, I have to stay on top of my station and really don’t 40 Cash Box/ July 31, 1976

On Jazz McCoy Tyner heads back into the studio shortly to begin a new LP. For the first time, the Milestone star will take a serious view toward overdubbing. There will be three horns (including Gary Bartz) and each horn will do some doubling. Sonny Rollins also ready to begin his next Milestone. Patrice Rushen, Billy Cobham and Lee Ritenour are scheduled to be on the date. Improv Records president Bill Hassett is also owner of the Statler Hilton Hotel in Buf- falo. The Downtown Room of the hotel re- cently finished a successful all-jazz run featuring several major artists. The room will open again September 7 with more jazz but during the current season the room was Top jazz vibraharpist Lionel Hampton receives his seventeenth consecutive win in the vibes category of the 1976 Playboy Jazz & Pop Poll. Bunny Natalie hands the award to Hampton at the Playboy Club In New York. Hampton is currently completing a three week tour of Europe. the source of live recordings for Improv by Charlie Byrd and Marian McPartland. The Vermont Jazz Festival at Waitsfield will host many big name groups July 31 & August 1. Scheduled to appear are: Dave Brubeck with Two Generations of Brubeck, Maynard Ferguson, Buddy Rich & His Killer Force, Bill Evans Trio and John Payne Band. The Sunday show will have George Benson, Chuck Mangione& Esther Satterfield, Gary Burton's Quartet and the Jack DeJohnette Directions. Coverage of the event will appear in a coming edition of Cash Box. Veteran arranger Wade Marcus will ap- pear with his own LP in the next Impulse release. Impulse GM Esmond Edwards preparing sessions with B.B. King and Sonny Criss for fall release. Mike Mantler's LP “The Hapless Child" is just out on JCOA. New Music Distribution Service handles the album. Muse president Joe Fields is very high on his current Woody Shaw LP "Love Dance.” This label has made dramatic positive changes in its cover act. The latest covers on Woody Shaw and Cecil Payne are knockouts! July must be Sonny Stitt month. Apart from the Cash Box picks on Catalyst (“Forecast: Sonny & Red”) and this week's pick "Stomp Off Let’s Go" on Flying Dutchman, there are new Stitt LPs coming from Muse and Prestige. The Prestige set is the last featuring Stitt with Gene Ammons and, in addition, piano ace Junior Mance is in the band. Springboard International through its Trip label will continue to issue Mercury material. Next up are Les McCann, Max Roach and a previously unissued set by Eddie “Cleanhead” Vinson. T rip is also into new recording with a Frank Foster LP produced by Foster's former Count Basie sectionmate Billy Mitchell. Xanadu releases for August will include Barry Harris, Sam Most and Sam Noto. The Harris set was done live in Japan. The Audio Fidelity August release will have three new LPs on Chiaro-scuro (Lou Stein, pianist Joe Turner and the Kenny Davern-Bob Wilbur Soprano Summit) and three on BASF: "My Ship" by George Shearing, “Sentimental Journey” by the Singers Unlimited & The Robert Farnon Orchestra and a set from Monty Alexander titled “Love And Sunshine.” Reports have it that reed man Charlie Mariano has com- pleted a BASF set with Jan Hammer and Jack Bruce in attendance. Among the latest Vanguard releases are "Color Visions” by guitarist Roland Prince and a double set entitled “Great Blues- men/Newport” featuring the likes of Lightnin' Hopkins, Sonny Terry-Brownie McGhee and John Lee Hooker. The blues set is vintage 1 959-1 965 and was recorded at the old Newport Festival in Rhode Island. Savoy will issue a double set of jazz from Los Angeles in the 1940’s featuring Hampton Hawes, Dexter Gordon, Art Pep- per, Helen Humes and others. The next Arista/Freedom release will include New York Mary, The John Payne Band and Archie Shepp among others. JazzAlbumPicks BACKGAMMON — Art Blakey & The Jazz Messengers — Roulette SR 5003 — Producer: Fred Bailin — List: 6.98 The key to any Art Blakey LP is the front line. Here with veteran Hardman on trumpet and young monster Dave Schnitter on tenor sax Blakey has a great front line. The eight titles contain a mixture of new material and revivals (“Whisper Not" and “Blues March”) and everything is done in the best Blakey tradition. Schnitter has “Georgia On My Mind” and “I Can't Get Started" as features. He sings quite effectively on the former. The hard- driving rhythm is never a problem with the leader booting everyone along. Certainly the best Art Blakey of the decade! STOMP OFF LET’S GO — Sonny Stitt — Flying Dutchman BDLI 1538 — Producer: Bob Thiele — List: 6.98 Sonny Stitt is certainly one of the most recorded jazzmen but he rarely fails to deliver. The music here is stretched out jazz standards by Ellington, Parker and Luis Bonfa but there is added excite- ment in the two trumpet team of Lew Soloff and Jon Faddis and the presence of great drummer Louis Bellson. Stitt has equal time on alto and tenor sax and the quality of all four selections is quite high. Stitt always benefits from the attendance of strong supporting players and here he is frequently in- spired. A different kind of Stitt record but one that is bound to please his fans. He has help from his regular rhythm section and special guests Budd Johnson and Milt Jackson. The key to ap- preciating Roy is the knowledge that he is not con- tent to rest on his laurels and that music is a continu- ing challenge to him. Whether the tune is an old favorite (“The Heat’s On”) or a bossa nova (“Recado”) or the blues the fire is always there. Johnson has a beautiful spot on “The Heat’s On” and Jackson shines in his solo opportunities. Another fine Pablo LP and one that adds con- siderable luster to their excellent mainstrem catalog. LONG GREEN — Donald Byrd — Savoy/Arista SJL 1101 — List: 6.98 This reissue finds Donald Byrd leading his first recording session in 1955. Through originals such as “Long Green” or the often-heard Gershwin stan- dard “Someone To Watch Over Me," Byrd displays a rich and elegant tone with relaxed and confident phrasing. The participating musicians are four- fifths the beauty of this recording, with the piano ex- pertise of Hank Jones and the memorable bass solos of Paul Chambers combined with the work of modern percussion innovator Kenny Clarke and the tenor sax of Frank Foster. This album has l>t“e similarity to Byrd’s current jazz and pop- success, but his name may have served a wide audience to a “new” world of music Cash Box/ July 31, 1976 43

On Jazz Certainly the jazz success story of 1 976 is George Benson. His initial Warner Brothers LP “Breezin' ” continues at the top of the Cash Box jazz chart while his most recent CTI effort "Good King Bad” moves up to number four. The beauty of Benson is that all this acclaim has not gone to his head. He is still the basic warm guy who burned up the world with Jack McDuffs group in the middle 60’s. And he hasn't forgotten his compadres either. When Grant Green made his first Eastern appearance in several years at Newark’s Key Club, Benson was there to renew acquaintances. Considering his amazing sales streak, could it be possible that reissues from Verve, A&M or Prestige might appear? Speaking of reissues Roulette is continu- ing to march with their Echoes Of An Era series which will soon have new additions by Jackie McLean, Randy Weston, John Handy and others. Betty Carter’s first album under her Roulette pact will ship September fifteen. Her own trio will provide the backing. New LPs from Jan Garbarek and Pat Metheny in the current ECM release via Polydor. Also from Polydor are the Verve reissues which have an interesting recurr- ing motif in the art covers. The complete mural is shown on the back of each LP while an excerpt makes up the cover for each album. Bob Koester’s Delmark label out of Chicago promises the first LPs from the Un- ited masters in the fall. Kicking off the series will be sets from Tab Smith, Paul Bascomb.and Chris Woods. Muse will release five LPs late this month headlined by Pat Martino and Sonny Criss. Also appearing will be the latest from pianist Joe Bonner, vocalist Eddie Jeffer- son and keyboard stylist Cedar Walton. Jazz has rarely been well captured on film but if Bruce Ricker has anything to say about it all that may change quickly. Cash Box had the opportunity to see some footage from Ricker’s unfinished film on Kansas City jazz. Among the featured per- formers are Count Basie and his Orchestra, Jay McShann with big band and small group and the great bluesman, Big Joe Turner. While the style for the full color film will be documentary, the relaxed at- mosphere allows the musicians to be loose and natural. The music is dynamite also and Ricker has already sold some Joe Turner soundtrack material to Norman Granz. One of the most interesting LPs of recent vintage is Sandcastle 1030 “New Orleans Jazz Brunch.” The music is by the Alvin Alcorn Trio and is very nice indeed, but the kicker is the inclusion of some fabulous N.O. recipes inside the double-fold jacket. It seems that the Alcorn trio is regularly featured at the jazz brunch atCommanders Palace and the LP serves to promote some fine music and also the fine cuisine at the restaurant. The Smithsonian Institute will issue retrospective sets on Duke Ellington and Dizzy Gillespie this fall. The Ellington is 1938 vintage while the Gillespie set will focus on Dizzy away from Charlie Parker. Also in the works from Smithsonian is a multi-record Fletcher Henderson package. JazzAlbumPicks DEE GEE DAYS — Dizzy Gillespie — Savoy/Aris- ta SJL 2209 — List: 7.98 John Birks Gillespie founded the Dee Gee label witd Dave Usher in 1951, and until the company’s masters were picked by Savoy some years Ihter, he was able to exercise a degree of creative control previously unrealized working with other com- panies, during a time when bebop was often ex- ploited for its commercial potential alone. This dou- ble set includes vocal blues, some early examples of Dizzy's experimentation with Afro-Cuban motifs, and some exciting all-out blowing featuring the likes of tenorman Budd Johnson, Art Blakey at the drums, Milt Jackson on vibes, and John Coltrane, alto sax. NORMAN GRANZ JAM SESSION/THE CHARLIE PARKER SIDES — Verve VE-2-2508 — List: 7.98 (Dist: Polydor) Here is one of the great jam sessions of all time. The roster of artists was picked from the cast of Granz's touring troupe Jazz at The Philharmonic and includes Charlie Shavers, Flip Phillips and Os- car Peterson. But the key ingredient is the inclusion of the three most important alto saxophones of the time: Charlie Parker, Johnny Hodges and Benny Carter. The music is basic fare: two long blues, a medley of ballads and an uptempo outing on “What Is This Thing Called Love.” There is scarcely a mo- ment of less than great music and in his “Funky Blues” solo, Parker has left a masterpiece for all time. SOPRANO SAX — Zoot Sims — Pablo 2310-770 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 7.98 This is Zoot's first all-soprano LP and it is a major event for jazz. Unlike other musicians who may take up another horn for the purposes of picking up an occasional double, Zoot has mastered the straight saxophone more completely than anyone since Sid- ney Bechet. The eight-tune set is heavy on stan- dards with“Ghost Of A Chance” and "Someday Sweetheart" being especially appealing. Solid sup- port is rendered by Ray Bryant, George Mraz and Grady Tate. A beautiful album. Weeks On 7/31 Chart 1 BREEZIN’ GEORGE BENSON (Warner Bros. Fronting a nine piece band here, he struts with bold assurance through a program of five original melodies. Among those lending support are Rene McLean and Billy Harper but it is the leader who impresses most with his bright as a dia- mond tone and bristling execution. The title track at twelve and a half minutes contains a striking exam- ple of this great musician at his best. DREAMS SO REAL — Gary Burton Quintet — ECM-1-1072 — Producer: Manfred Eicher — List: 6.98 Gary Burton seems to be coming alive in his ECM recordings. There is a much more natural flowto his music now and this program of six Carla Bley originals brings out his creative best. His current band has two guitars, bass and drums and it serves to showcase his talents as well as any of his previous groups. The music alternates between laid-back ballads and highly charged energy music. Packac ing is very classy with plastic-lined inner sle and, of course, there is extraordinarily rich ded sound that is a hallmark of this labs'. Cash Box/August7, 1976 27

Heard from a reliable source that Leon Haywood has delivered his new LP to Columbia . . . that's soul. jess levitt Jim Maddox: Maverick Or Innovator by Jess Levin LOS ANGELES — Jim Maddox, program director at KDAY in Los Angeles, is one of the new breed of young black program- mers that is creating a new era in black radio. Maddox has taken KDAY, a former AM rocker, and turned it into one of the most progressive black AM stations in the country. Last week Cash Box interviewed Maddox about black radio in 1976. Black Radio Black radio has gone through some in- teresting changes lately. Black stations around the country are playing more LP cuts, more jazz and are quicker to pick up on crossover records. Maddox said the reason this is happening is that more and more black radio stations are becoming aware of their own needs rather than the needs of the record companies. “Radio sta- tions are realizing that it is their purpose to serve the community. Our primary concern is not to make the record companies happy; just because their A&R depart- ments choose a certain single release doesn't necessarily mean that I have to play it. I think the time has come in black radio where programmers are not afraid of being badgered by record companies. We won't be made guilty if we don't cooperate with them. They can’t wave the time buys in our faces. We are not being paid by the record companies and they know it.” A New Day Maddox also pointed out that black radio is not the same type of entertainment vehi- cle as it was in the fifties and sixties. “In the fifties and sixties black radio was into public affairs and gospel hours on Sunday. Now in the seventies the mood of the public has changed to where they want to hear more music. Jim Maddox tr 42 consistently all week. Public affairs and news are still important, but we make these spots short and they have a lot of impact when they are on.” Progressive On the subject of being progressive, Maddox said that really depends on your market and how far you can open up your audience. “You have to be very careful of what you play, because you may do too much too soon and turn a portion of your listeners away. We're into formula radio to a degree, more music, a personality-oriented jock, not a wailer or screamer, but a guy that can relate to his audience. However, even if you want to call it formula radio, we try to disguise it. We like to bring familiarity to the air; however, it is important to keep the people guessing, so that they don’t know that an O'Jays record is coming up. Free-form radio is not where I am at. I like a system and organization.” LP Research Lately the trend around the country in black radio has been to add more LPs and LP cuts. KDAY was one of the first to make this move. “After a year’s research in our market, I was finding that most of our listeners were more and more affluent, had a higher level of education and were buy- ing more LPs than singles. They had the money to buy LPs, and were doing it because the LPs are better bargains in comparison to singles. Our audience is primarily 18 to 24 and 25 to 34. We’re low in teens. These older listeners usually are more loyal in buying their favorite artists. So what I've done is not to do anything too drastic in programming; however, what I think I have done is refine and polish what we were doing in the beginning. We will still play singles, but stay away from the marginal ones. I only want to play records that benefit KDAY. I’m not interested in helping out A&R departments that are tell- ing me what to play. If it is right for us then we'll play it,” Maddox said. Maddox also feels that it is inevitable that more white artists will be crossing over. “Right now the general market is better able to accept both black and white artists. Both artists are producing good product that really doesn’t fit any category. It’s just good music. I see more and more black AMs getting into more white pop records, but not to the point where their stations will lose their black identity. Black stations like ourselves will keep our identity because our news and public affairs still primarily address themselves to black people. A lot of the racism, though, will be erased through this easier crossover situation. I think it’s kind of criminal that I don't receive every LP that comes out — white, black, jazz, classical or whatever. Plus I also think that our biggest competitor, KHJ, should get every black LP that is released.” NATRA While Maddox feels that people in black broadcasting need their own professional organization, he doesn’t feel that is NATRA. “I like the concept of the organization; however, I understand why they have little support and low attendance. They don’t have any seminars and they never seem to get anything accomplished. I personally like less talk and more action. I would like to go to a convention and share ideas with the rest of my colleagues in the field, but NATRA doesn’t feel the same way I do. I think they need to clean up their act. I’m not going becausel'm in the last part of my ARB period. I don't have time to go down and party. The only way to stay on top and be consistent is to add the hottest records week in and week out. The people that con- trol NATRA are the old line of broadcasters, and they fail to realize that there is a whole new breed of young programmers who are very dedicated and very professional. These people have not kept up with the times. I personally have too much work to go down to Antigua and play games. Being a programmer is not a 9 to 5 job. It’s a pro- ject by project job. I will gladly get behind any black organization that is serious about getting things done. I think it's a little sad that most of the jocks at our competitor KGFJ are not closer to us. I'm not into any diabolical plots; however. I wouldn't mind discussing improvements for the better- ment of black radio with them. I think a NATRA could be a great organization if they restructured it so that we as com- municators could come together to im- prove and enhance our industry.” ADDITIONSTO R&B PLAYLISTS WBUL — BIRMINGHAM #1 — Lonely One — Special Delivery You To Me Are Everything — Real Thing — UA Love Myself — Bill Cosby — Capitol Fifth Of Beethoven — Walter Murphy — Private Stock Jive Talkin’ — Chaka Khan & Rufus — ABC Come Get To This — Joe Simon — Spring One Man In My Lifetime — Diana Ross — Motown Baby, We Better Get It Together — Barry White — 20th One For The Money — Whispers — Soul Train 38 to 22 — Play That Funky Music — Wild Cherry 19 to 12 — Rock Creek Park — Blackbyrds #1 LP — Commodores NEW LPs — Bill Cosby, Joe Simon, Emotions, Brother To Brother, Spinners WBMX — CHICAGO Entro — Graham Central Station — WB Come Get To This — Joe Simon — Spring Turn It Loose — Tyrone Davis — Columbia All Right Is All Night — Honey White — Haven #1 LP (tie) Bootsy Collins/Lou Rawls New LPs — Roy Ayers, Fatback Band David T Walker WORL — ORLANDO #1 — Getaway — Earth Wind & Fire Come Get To This loe Simon — Spring Lean On Me — Melba Moore Chance With You — Brother To Brother — All Platinum Life On Mars — Dexter Wansel — Phila Inti. Eric Carmen mo touring was one of the most important things for an emerging artist to do. “Every time you go out you make more fans. Eric's first tour as a solo artist lasted seven months, during which he had three days off at home in Cleveland. The second day he was home I called him and told him that he would have to fly off to a meeting of the Arista distributors to meet them and see how they work. He went; those things are important." Poses added that while on the road, Carmen visited radio stations and met the local Arista promotion and distribu- Lou Boorstein Dies MIAMI, FLA. — Lou Boorstein, who at one time some 1 5 years ago had one of the hot- test one-stop operations in New York, Leslie Distributors, died last week. He was 61 years old and collapsed in his doctor’s office. He is survived by his wife Eleanor and four sons. Bernie Boorstein, who owns Double B Records, the Freeport, Long Island one- stop, got his training at Leslie from his un- cle, Lou. tion people and did press interviews. He added that if there are important dates available which are less rewarding monetarily than others they will do them. “The money at this point is not what’s im- portant; we’re building for long range growth. Some managers try to grab it all while they can, but I expect to be working with Eric in eight, ten years.” Poses said that at the end of the next tour, which will begin in October, Carmen will have es- tablished his base. The tour will follow the release of his second LP in September. In light of Carmen's success in three dif- ferent areas of music, Poses was asked which of those directions he would pursue with the new album. ‘‘He's maturing musically, he’s grown up like everybody* else. If I had to put a label on it, I would say that he’s heading towards FM, though we’re not looking to lose the MOR audience. The direction comes by itself, and the people who listen to the various kinds of stations will pick what they like.” No Demo Tape Made Poses managed the Raspberries during their last year and a half together, when he said there was conflict in the group. This was partly because when the band put together the “best possible set,” according to Poses, Carmen ended up singing eight out of ten of the songs. According to Poses, Jimmy lenner (producer of the Raspberries and Carmen) and he always had in the back of their minds that Carmen would become a solo artist. When the time came to sign Car- men, his availability was made known but no demo tape was made. Poses feels that it is not fair to “peddle a tape." He was offer- ing a package of artist, producer and manager, and he had the interested com- pany representatives fly into Cleveland to listen to Carmen play some songs on his piano. “Clive Davis showed more interest than anyone, and within 24 hours his business people were back to me. The other thing was that Clive was building a new company; he had no superstars, and I knew I would get a shot.” Poses said that Davis heard Carmen perform four songs, among which were part of “All By Myself” and “Never Gonna Fall In Love Again,” Car- men’s first and second singles respectively. Poses was asked how important hit singles have been to Carmen's career. “Few artists will break, even strongly on FM, without a hit single. However, as far as Eric is concerned, I think the most important thing has been concert appearances. The promoters gamble on building the acts of the future. We in the industry tend to pre- hype ourselves, and not wait for the reac- tion from the public.” Poses feels that con- certs are one place where the public reac- tion to an act can be accurately sensed. ‘A Manager Is Like A Father’ Poses feels that the most important thing about managing is to understand the nature of the job. “Personal management is just that: personal management. A manager is looked on almost as a father, and you have to be as available as a father is. And that is seven nights and seven days a week.” Poses also thinks that too many business people and lawyers assume that there is no real definition of management, that it only involves managing business af- fairs. “A manager has to be as comfortable handling the creative and personal ends of the job, as the business.” He added that a manager must also be concerned with an artist’s future, which for Carmen will involve production in addition to songwriting. “Basically," he emphasized, “a manager has to watch over every facet of an artist’s career.” Retail LP Selling Prices i ? ALBUM REVIEWS TOM SNOW — Tom Snow — Capitol ST-11545 — ; Producer: Michael J. Jackson — List: 6.98 Tom Snow is a unique singer/songwriter whose j tunes deal with such diverse subjects as strange ! love and the lady whose old man is a traveling musi- cian. Snow is a literate song sculptorwhose vision is { ciear: he must convey his feelings through his music j — and we are fortunate enough to experience them vicariously. Backed by many good players such as John Klemmer and Waddy Wachtel, Snow creates very visual songs whose emotional content is far- j reaching. Programmers who’ve not already gone on | this record might flip to the “Most Added LPs” sec- | tion this week where they will find this LP prominen- tly displayed — think about it. BYRON BERLINE AND SUNDANCE — Byron Berline And Sundance — MCA-2217 — Producer: Ken Mansfield — List: 6.98 Byron Berline’s notable fiddle and mandolin chops are the outstanding feature of this LP, though it would be a huge oversight to neglect mention of his band, Sundance. The band is about as tight as a good country band can be — the tunes are pleasant, the vocals clean and uplifting and the instrumenta- tion quite nice, particularly the pickin’. This album will be warmly greeted by fans of the progressive country sound and airplay in that market and the AM market is sure to follow. “Sweet Wanomi” and “Laid Back Day” are fine examples of the album’s movers and ballads respectively. GENUINE COWHIDE — Delbert McCIInton — ABC ABCD-959 — Producer: Chip Young — List: 6.98 With the growing interest in straightforward music a la Bruce Springsteen, this LP should be a natural for acceptance on that level. Delbert McClinton’s vocals are stark and uncluttered with cosmetic frills — the perfect vehicle for his choice of material, which includes covers of such heavies as “Lovey Dovey,” “Let The Good Times Roll,” and the Leiber/Stoller classic, “One Kiss Led To Another." The instrumentation occassionally belies the age of the music, with some musicianship displayed on the part of McClinton’s back-up unit. FM progressives will have some fun with this LP, but the AM programmer is sure to find some picks here too. Yes, that’s a wallet on the cover and yes, that's a . . in the wallet. GOD HAS BLESSED OUR HANDS — Michael Wynn — Buddah BDS 5663 — Producers: Michael Wynn, Marian Lampkin — List: 6.98 A very nice collection of contemporary gospel tunes that lean well into the R&B vein. Michael Wynn, borther of the Spinners’ Phillipe, has a pure touch in delivering a touching gospel ballad or a powerful rafter-shaker. Background vocals provide further strength and velocity to this already intense album. A sure shot at the R&B market, this LP might also garner some favorable play on the pop playlists. "Am I Strong Enough” and the title track exemplify the tenor of this effort which is sub-titled "A Musical Tribute To A Peoples’ Struggle For E- quality.” HOWLIN’ WOLF — Howlin’ Wolf — Chess 2ACMB- 201 — Producers: Various — List: 6.98 Many rock innovators owe a great debt to the j early rural and urban bluesmen— their contribution in the form of influence cannot be ignored by those who have prospered thanks to the chops of heavies | like Howlin’ Wolf. This 2-record set on the Chess Blues Masters Series is an outstanding tribute to the work of one of the most influencial blues players of [ them all. The titles included herein are instantly ) recognizable — even by those who aren't old enough to remember names like Chester Burnett, Willie Dixon and Howlin’ Wolf: “The Red Rooster,” “Spoonful," “Killing Floor,” “Sitting On Top Of The World” and “Back Door Man.” A true collector’s | item. HAS ARRIVED — The Whole Dam Family — Soul International SLP-1Q3 — Producers: August Moon, Tyrone Thomas — List: 6.98 A clean soul offering that proves indisputably that The Whole Darn Family has, indeed, arrived. Dynamite horns and smooth string arrangements lay the groundwork for some very tasty up-front vocals that are augmented by clean harmonies and fine melody lines. Various instrumental solos lend a touch of excitement to a great selection of movers like “You Know That You Lied" and “Seven Minutes Of Funk." R&B and pop programmers will like this LP — it’s for listeners who like to boogie down. ARISTA IS POE’S ‘COMPANY OF THE YEAR’— Arista Records wasnamed “record com- pany of the year" at the recent Bobby Poe convention in Nashville. The award is based on the tabulation of ballots from record companies and radio stations around the country. Pic- tured are (I to r) Mike Klenfner, Arista vice president for national album promotion and special projects; Bobby Poe; Clive Davis, president of Arista Records accepting the award; and David Carrico, vice president of promotion. The award was presented in New York re- cently by Poe, who was there for the presentation to Davis and Arista Records. It’s a multi-format album, and has been accep- ted by adult contemporary stations as well as progressives." Commenting that the progressive sta- tions are concentrating on the “Devil Woman” cut, Cosgrave also cited at least two other cuts off the LP which are being played by American progressive outlets. Rocket Association Although MCA is in charge of the marketing for Richard’s product, the artist commented more about his association with Rocket Records. “Well, it all started quite by accident, really ... we knew the people at Rocket London," he noted, "and sent them tapes and they liked them. But they thought the U.S. exposure was im- perative for my career . . . and that’s basically where the people at Rocket came in. They’re so enthusiastic . . . it’s a small enough company to be personally involved with all of us.” But long before Rocket were Cliff Richard's days with the Shadows (his own group in England during the late fifties). "Those days are over now, of course,” he recounted. "We were making inroads on the British rock scene in those days, but based on the American scene. Wewerejust doing a British version of what was happen- ing in American music. We used material from Elvis, Jerry Lee Lewis, and other American acts that were hot until we built our own repertoire. Those were the original days and they were very exciting for us . . . you almost had to be 18 to survive the schedule we were on.” Songwriting What about Cliff Richard’s songwriting? "I’ve always been a person who sings songs, although I do write too. The producer for the current album wanted me to do one of my songs on the LP. But I didn’t because I felt there were other tunes that took priority over what I had done. But I also have enough sense to realize that no one else is gonna record my material because it's mine and I can doit anytime I want to. I'm not in a rush to record my own material, but the right time will come.” Of his manager Peter Gormley, Cliff said, “I seem to meet up with the right people at the right time. I’ve never had any big dis- agreements with him ... we meet, we talk business and we always come to an agree- ment on what we’re going to do in the year ahead. On Jazz DAVIS HOSTS JAZZ GREATS — Les Davis, nighttime personality on WRVR-FM, New York's all-jazz station, played host recently to Lenny White, Al DiMeola and Randy Brecker. The special open-ended discussion involved the three guests playing cuts from LPs that influenced their own styles. Seated left to right: Randy Brecker, Lenny White. Standing: Al DiMeola, Les Davis. jazz notes Weeks On 8/7 Chart A&M's Horizon label is readying eight LPs for September release. Included in the coming package are albums by Charlie Haden, Sonny Fortune, Don Cherry, Mel Lewis, Dave Brubeck, Jimmy Owens, Jim Hall and a new group, Karma. In the upcoming MPS/BASF release shipping August 15 is an LP by Oscar Peterson entitled "Oscar's Choice.” The material is previously unissued titles from a variety of Peterson sessions over the past few years. Also from MPS/BASF is a solo piano L,P "My Ship.” On this George Shearing makes his singing debut on “Send In The Clowns." All the people at Audio Fidelity who have heard advance pressings have flipped out over the veteran pianist’s vocal abilities! Verve is readying a Wes Montgomery LP package of live material that will include some unissued sides. In addition Verve is un-sweetening some tracks that originally featured overdubbed strings and horns! Irv Kratka at Music Minus One is blazing straight ahead with his two jazz labels, Inner City and Classic Jazz. Recent LPs by The Art Ensemble of Chicago and Stephane Grappelli-Jean-Luc Ponty are on the for- mer while things to come include Anthony Braxton ("Saxophone Improvisations- Series F”), Gato Barbierl-Don Cherry and a Randy Weston solo piano LP recorded last year. Classic Jazz recently issued a double ($9.96) set by John Kirby and will soon, in a major coup, issue for the first time in the U.S. the fabulous sessions of Mezz Mezzrow and Sidney Bechet recorded more than thirty years ago for Mezzrow’s King Jazz label! If all this weren't enough, Kratka suggests that everyone be on the lookout for a French pianist, Jean P. Moss, who will have an Inner City LP shortly. Irv says he definitely has an artist of star poten- tial here. JazzAlbumPicks THE COMPLETE GENIUS — Thelonlous Monk — Blue Note LA 579-H2 — List: 7.98 The entire Blue Note Monk (as leader) is an ex- ceptionally rewarding musical experience. The four sessionsfrom the 1940s are truly revealing, not only for Monk’s distinctive piano but for the excellence of his original compositions. Milt Jackson and Art Blakey are the sidemen most adept at interpreting the leader’s moods. Dealers should be aware that this material has only been available in phony stereo for several years and fans will want this convenient package in the original mono presented here. Another well produced Blue Note reissue. THE CHICK COREA/BILL EVANS SESSIONS — Stan Getz — Verve VE 2-2510 — List: 7.98 The combination of Getz and two of the major pianists of the modern generation makes for splen- did listening. Polydor has provided excellent pressing quality — a marked improvement on the originals. Perhaps the most outstanding track is "But Beautiful" on which Getz makes it most obvious that he is best on melodic material. Rufus Thomas stopped by the Hollywood Cash Box offices recently to play his new single, ‘‘If There Were No Music." And that’s not all that’s new with Rufus, he’s got a new label — Artists of America. This is the first single in recent memory in which Thomas busts out of the ‘novelty dance’ format; this tune is straight-ahead R&B and it’s got a good chance of crossing over into the pop market as well. Record Shop Talk: Separate Language ,r u Additions to Pop Radio Playlists .» der apparently was packed by a guy who strongly believed in fun and games. Middle Island — A middle island is not land surrounded by water. It is a way of dis- playing albums in the middle of a store. N.C. — No charge. Merchandise sent in free as part of a deal as in “buy five and get one at no charge.” N.C. is a second cousin of 'freebie.' On Hold — A term that means your ship- ment is not being shipped because of delin- quent or late payments, or no payments at all. Before every and all shipments to you a company credit man has to put his o.k. prior to delivery. If you are not up to date in your payments the credit man can hold up your order. When you call up to find out why your order has not gone out you are told that you are 'on the hold list,’ therefore, the shortened 'on hold.’ One Stop — A distributor who sup- posedly can service your shop with everything. Therefore, the phrase one stop. Your profit margin varies and so do your headaches. Payola — Illegal payoff in the course of promotion, primarily radio exposure. Plant — In this case, a person used to make a purchase from a new employee in order to test his honesty. Plug — Another word for hype. Promotion Man (P.R. Man) — One who is paid by a company or a distributor to plug, hype, push or do anything short of payola to make an album or hit single into a chart item. R.A. — Return authorization; a piece of paper from your supplier authorizing you to Izumiya Concert lr44 according to the program. The performance featured Izumiya alone in the spotlight. The fact that he neither spoke nor sang in English did not prevent stirring audience acceptance. Kalapana Ir44 however — a couple of hours in front of a videotape outfit would probably clear that up in a hurry. Jazz Notes fr45 ner, Rahsaan Roland Kirk, Clifford Brown, Maynard Ferguson and Gene Ammons. Let’s hope this latter set will include the sidesGene madewith hisfather Albert Am- mons. West coast trumpet man Don Rader has a new LP on the PBR label titled "Now.” Rader’s ex-boss Maynard Ferguson has nice words for the album in his brief sleeve note. A new label of Italian origin, Pausa, has an LP featuring Gerry Mulligan titled “GM Meets Enrico Intra." Also due shortly from this label is a Thad Jones-Mel Lewis LP recorded in 1973 and '74 in Europe. Vocalist Dee Dee Bridgewater is featured with the band. From All Platinum/Chess comes Woody Herman’s "Double Exposure’” James Moody’s “Moody's Mood” and John Klem- mer’s "Magic Moments.” These doubles are in the Chess Jazz Masters Series and in the Chess Blues Master Series we have sets from Howlin’ Wolf, Little Walter, Muddy Waters and Little Milton. The first three are straight reissues of doubles originally in the Chess 6000 double series while the Milton collection contains some of his biggest hits plus one side of unissued material recor- ded at The Burning Spear in Chicago. This label has the finest catalogue of post-war blues anywhere and let’s hope the success of the series will result in some of the great work by these bluesmen being issued on LP for the first time. There is plenty of it! return merchandise as per your request for a specific reason. Rainy Day Fund — Capital that is not used for operating expenses or purchas- ing, but held in escrow for emergency measures. Release — Webster says it has some- thing to do with tension. Schwann says it’s the monthly issue of new albums. Shyster — A brother-in-law to a factor. There are two slight differences. A factor is controlled by law thus enabling the shyster to charge more when he collects and to hit harder when he doesn’t. Also a factor gives his benefactor coffee or a drink in a glass. The shyster serves his in a cheap paper cup. Spiff — Extra money for sales clerks for selling specified items. Step Downs — A style of displaying a variety of albums on a graduating type wall fixture. Stiffs — See “bombs.” Switcheroo — A customer buys a record for under a dollar, and one at another shop for four or five dollars. At home he switches the two records from their jackets and br- ings back the more expensive purchase claiming the wrong record was inside the right outer jacket. Two Ten — A code name for a shoplifter or booster. This expression in a record shop is an all out alert warning that someone has been spotted who has all the earmarks of a professional thief. The “two ten" expression is the coinage of the phrase "Keep your two eyes on those ten fingers." Bartell’s New VP great way to expand my knowledge." Approached by KBEQ, Kansas City in late 1973, Rochelle Staab assisted in organizing the music, changing the format from progressive to rock, and hiring a new staff. Then in 1974, Ms. Staab set a different direction for the MOR format of WHEN, Syracuse and organized the music there. “I insisted on carrying out the basics," she noted, referring to format and music guidelines set down by previous station consultancy experience. “The station went from a number five in the market to number one and has been there ever since.” Are there any repercussions resulting from being a woman and holding the positin she does? Ms. Staab answered with an emphatic no. “I have never had a problem with anybody that I’ve worked with on anything because of the fact that I’m a woman. It may be a taiked-aboutthing now, but as long as anyone does his job and does it well, being a woman or man just doesn’t matter. What could be the dif- ference between working with me two weeks ago and working tor me, just because I’m a woman, or I’ve assumed a new position?” Future plans for Rochelle Staab? “I haven't set my next goal yet,” she replied. “I'm not going to stand still . . . media is a very exciting industry and I think someday I'd like to be the president of my own radio chain.” Staab mentioned that the first day after she became Bartell vice president, many of her friends called to give congratulations. "I remember wondering what I was going to do next. I don’t know that much about broadcasting sales yet . . . it’s really not at- tractive to me right now, but just as every sales person would like to program a radio station, I think every programmer would like to try to sell radio. That may be my next learning experience.” London Inks L.D. Pearl LOS ANGELES — London Records has signed L.D. Pearl to a recording contract, and their initial single, “Flying High With You” b/w “Kinda Love” has been released. Critics from Holland and abroad, as well as the public and some 330 participating musicians, were calling the event the most unique presentation of any jazz festival in the world. Lee Konitz spoke of a “52nd Street revived,” as the Dutch festival ran three consecutive days in six different halls and rooms concurrently between 6 p.m. and 4 a.m. In other words, one could hear and see Count Basie and his orchestra in one hall while Stan Getz or Dizzy Gillespie were playing another hall, Teddy Wilson in yet another. There were special halls for dixieland and avante garde jazz, a hall with continuous showings of jazz films and an exposition hall. Record companies had their own record market which attracted many thousands of Monte Carlo ‘Golden Rose’ To Chalkiris PARIS — Harris Chalkiris has won this year's “Golden Rose d'Antibes” award for his original French presentation of “Milady Lena” before a jury composed of French radio and television personalities. The festival lasts four days and is spon- sored by Radio Monte Carlo, The French station that covers exclusively southern France and parts of Italy. interested people. Business for Polydor, Phonogram, WEA, Dureco, CNR, Negram, EMI-Bovema, CBS, Inelco (RCA), Ariola and Munich Records was beyond expecta- tions. Among the artists appearing at the festival were Ray Charles, Count Basie, Lionel Hampton, Sarah Vaughan, Dizzy Gillespie, Stan Getz, Larry Coryell, Horace Silver, The Crusaders, Lee Konitz, John Lee Hooker, Memphis Slim, Randy Weston, Mighty Clouds of Joy, Teddy Wilson, Thad Jones/Mel Lewis, Cedar Walton, Illinois Jacquet, Sir Charles Thompson, Joe Albany, Frank Wright, Vic Dickenson, Bud Freeman, Beryl Bryden and many others. The Northsea Jazz Festival will be a yearly event in mid-summer. It is almost certain that the city of The Hague will give its support from 1977 on. Early September Sammy Davis Jr. will do a show at the Amsterdam Concertgeb- bouw, while Harry Belafonte is expected next November. The newly-signed Barclay artist Cathy Rosier was the guest of honor at the concert which closed the festival. Miss Rosier is a pretty French comedienne well-known for her brilliant appearances in top motion pic- tures. Hot Tuna is coming to perform in France for the first time. The event will take place at the Orange Festival. Chances are the group’s latest record will finally see French release with this performance. Ted Nugent, Quicksilver Messenger Service and Todd Rungren are also on the bill for the Orange Festival; all are doing very well in the French market and are looked forward to. TORONTO — If the Canadian government’s “forced airplay” policy has done anything for the domestic recording industry, it has been to take Canadian artists from out of the attic and into the front rooms of record stores and homes of the consumer. It may be less than ironic that one of the most successful independent record com- panies to blossom forth since the 1971 reg- ulations is Attic Records. Formed by Alex- ander Mair and Tom Williams in 1974, Attic has quickly become an exam pie for similar- sized operations to follow. Cash Flow The key to Attic’s success is partially due to solid financing. Mair and Williams (both former promotion men with multi-interna- tionals operating here) invested large per- sonal loans into the operation. Another in- jection came from the Canadian Enter- prise Development Corporation, an es- tablished investment company. Without being hampered by cash flow, Attic forged ahead with contracts and releases and by year-end 1975, had a catalog of a dozen albums and 33 singles. Beyond this, Attic became the first Canadian independent to attain a platinum LP with Hagood Hardy’s instrumental album, “The Homecoming.” Aggressiveness Next to cash flow, Attic has a reputation amongst retailers for its aggressiveness at the retail level. As one leading racker put it: “We never have any worries about stocking Attic product — the quality has always been excellent and they know how to get the con- sumer's attention.” Hagood Hardy was not an overnight suc- cess. The record was based on a master tape that had been turned down by most major recording labels and quite a number of independents before arriving at Attic. Both Mair and Williams saw something in its quality that others had been fearful of. They heard an established jazz musician with a highly commercial album tape that had solid MOR potential. As is true in the U.S., Canadian companies have been more concerned with the under-25 market than the over-25 segment. Therefore, the tape was simply “nice music,” as one dejected A&R director put it, to most of the potential labels prior to Attic’s involvement. Attic quickly culled the title cut as a single and started working the MOR stations. Reaction was slow but by the fall of 1975 over 100 stations were onto the record. At- tic then turned its attention to top 40 air- play. Meanwhile, Heather Murray, marketing head for the company, badgered retailers into giving her prime retail space for posters and mobiles on the Hardy deck. Following this, she was into the major retail chain stores checking to see if they wanted Hardy personal appearances and autograph sessions. Neglected by record companies and quick to see the potential in having housewives drawn into their stores, most agreed. The ball was roll- ing and the album and single sales picture began to snowball. ‘Consistent Flow’ The success of the Hagood Hardy album, according to president of Attic, Al Mair, opened the company’s eyes even more to the fact that a “consistent flow of product” is necessary for any company operating in the record industry. An arrangement was made toward the latter part of Attic’s first operational year with the non-profit Cana- dian Talent Library, an MOR-oriented sub- scription service which provides Canadian talent recordings. This arrangement has led to a number of release deals through Attic. Both Mair and vice president Tom Williams shrug off MOR when asked if this is the direction they are following. “We have an album by Triumph set for release any day now,” Mair said, “which is probably the heaviest rock act we’ve signed. We both (Mair and Williams) have a preference for lyrical music which, perhaps, is reflected in our signings.” Acts such as Ken Tobias, Larry Evoy (for- merly the principle voice in Edward Bear and an RIAA gold achiever with “You, Me And Mexico”), Shirley Eikhard and Frank Mills all fit into the softer rock fold and have proved, in each case, to be artists with strong crossover potential. Philosophy Continuing, Mair expounded on the phil- osophy behind Attic. “What we are trying to do is build a base in Canada for our own acts in the world market,” explained Mair. “We wouldn’t sign an act here unless we saw foreign potential. An example of this is Patsy Gallant. She has done very well in the past in the Quebec market and because of this she could do well in the French market. She is able to sing and perform in French and English, though we feel she has the ability to get out of the strictly French- speaking market and work anywhere. The Gallant signing is probably the com- pany’s most conspicuous to date. The first independent English-language label to look at the lucrative and well-endowed- talent province of Quebec, Attic jumped into the middle of the bidding spree to sign the attractive chanteuse. With her arm almost to another contract, Attic’s Tom Williams arrested the attention of her manager Ben Kaye, leading her to sign with the white-on-blue Attic logo. Advantages Mair sees advantages in not having towering talents such as Elton John and John Denver on the label. "Our advantage is that we can rise and fall with each suc- cessive artist. Our commitment is a one- hundred percent thing. Patsy could have signed with a major for a larger sum of money but by taking slightly less both she and her manager have that invisible advan- tage of dealing directly with the top people at the record company.” The Gallant deal calls for two albums per year over five years with singles. Patsy will record separate French language recordings for Attic although her first single in English, “From New York To L.A.,” is to be recorded in French for release shortly in Quebec. While Attic has been more fortunate than many in the independent field, Mair acknowledges that stations do have a ten- dency to reserve airplay additions for Can- Con discs and that getting chart positions is still “a problem." As Mair views it, however, “stations that hold back on charting Cana- dian discs, for whatever reason, are going to hurt themselves in the long run.” The goal of Attic over the next year is to solidify positions for artists Ron Nigrini and Shirley Eikhard. Ken Tobias, an es- tablished name with a rather poor track record prior to his signing with Attic, has since had three consecutive top 40 hits which, in turn, have quadrupled his stage earnings. Until now a club attraction, Tobias will headline his first Massey Hall date this fall in Toronto. Hagood Hardy's second album has just been released with 30,000 copies immediately on back order, meaning that he will hit the 50,000 copies necessary for gold certification with ease. The new LP “Get Up And Boogie" is currently charted across the country and expected to be gold within a week. Image Music, a division of Image Records, controls the publishing rights for Silver Convention material, most of which is composed by Sylvester Levay and Stephan Prager. Negotiations are underway for Silver Convention to perform in Australia later this year. Cash Box/August 14, 1976 59

INJAZZ Concord, an excellent quality label from the west coast, has two LPs just out. “A Pair To Draw To” features Herb Ellis on guitar and Ross Tomkins on piano. Tomkins is the regular pianist in Doc Severinsen’s Tonight Show band. Also on Concord is “LA 4” with Laurindo Aimeidia, Bud Shank, Ray Brown and Shelly Manne. Things to come on Con- cord include “Brown's Bag” by Ray Brown featuring Blue Mitchell, “Sunshine Ex- press” by the Bud Shank Quintet and “Hot Tracks" by the Herb Ellis-Ray Brown Sextet including Sweets Edison and Plas Johnson. A new LP in the traditional vein on the Down Home Cookin’ label features Sammy Duncan, veteran trumpet star, and a sextet from Atlanta. The Chess reissue series is being assembled by Dan Nooger and in his things to come he has several outstanding LPs. Look for LPs by Oliver Nelson-Lou Donaldson, Art Blakey-Max Roach and Trip Records has five new releases in its continuing reissue of Emarcy material. Featured artists are Gerry Mulligan, Roland Kirk, Eddie Cleanhead Vinson, Max Roach and Dizzy Gillespie. New from Prestige: Azar Lawrence, ex- McCoy Tyner reedman, with an LP titled “People Moving” featuring Lee Ritenour, Patrice Rushen, Harvey Mason and other west coast heavies. The second LP from the orchestra of Toshiko and Lew Tabackin is entitled “Tales Of A Courtesan (Oirantan).” It’s on RCA. The band is a big one, with eight brass and five saxes. Toshiko wrote all the original tunes. David Sanborn stepping, out with his new Warner Brothers LP “Sanborn.” The "Smile” title features guest vocals from Paul Simon and Phoebe Snow. Int'l./Epic PZ 34079) — 1 MOODY’S MOODS — James Moody — Chess 2ACMJ-403 — List: 7.98 Twenty-six titles from Moody’s early Chess association — 1956 to 1958. For some reason Moody never seemed to capture the groove blues feeling in much of the music here on later sessions. Vocalist Eddie Jefferson contributes some vintage vocals and Johnny Pate’s arrangements on the big band tracks are some of his best. The album com- bines virtually all of three Chess LPs into a package that consumers will be quite happy with. Out- standing titles include “Last Train From Over- brook,” “Stardust,” and "Flute ’N’ The Blues." A significant start for this new series. COSMOS —McCoy Tyner — Blue Note LA460-H2 — List: 7.98 This is previously unissued Tyner from 1969 and 1970. Three sessions are involved: one trio, one quintet with strings and one sextet including Gary Bartz and Hubert Laws. Just why this material has been held back until now is unknown but all Tyner fans will be interested. Of special significance is the original recording of “Song For My Lady,” but there are moments of magic in all eight Tyner composi- tions. Despite what must be enormous pressure, Tyner continues to go acoustic and his music always contains an integrity above and beyond the average jazz performance. JazzAlbumPicks ARTPEPPER McCOY TYNER EARLY ART —Art Pepper — Blue Note LA591-H2 — List: 7.98 With the death of Charlie Parker in 1955 there seemed two logical candidates for the major alto saxophone voice: Sonny Stitt and Art Pepper. Pep- per’s own problems seemed to get the better of him and he never gained the expected prominence. Yet these sessions from 1 956 & '57 show clearly that the talent was there. He is somewhere between Lee Konitz and Parker in his tonal conception but he has always been a hot player. The twenty-three titles contain an admirable mixture of originals and stan- dards. This will be a priority item for anyone who was ever into west coast jazz since the music has been unavailable for at least fifteen years. SKY STREET — Kenny Burrell — Fantasy F-9514 — Producer: Kenny Burrell — List: 6.98 Burrell’s Fantasy period has been somewhat less prolific than his stints with Verve, Chess and Blue Note and at the same time he has managed to stay with his best abilities and avoid the obvious crossover attempts. This date is small band and features Jerome Richardson on reeds and Kirk Lightsey at the keyboards. Originals from each featured sideman and Thad Jones make up the program. Burell is still a top guitar stylist and his many fans will be interested in his latest. 36 Cash Box/August 21, 1976

Cash Box recently conduc- ted a telephone interview with the group’s lead guitarist, Bob Parissi. Among other things, Parissi spoke of the group’s recent local tour dates with such heavies as George Benson and Santana. In the near future, Wild Cherry will be hitting the road to open the show tor the Isley Brothers. West coast appearances scheduled thus far include dates in Sacramento, L.A. and San Diego. C4SHBOX Heilicher Registers Gains On 14 LPs By Beach Boys Disc-O-Mat’s Low Typifies NYC ‘Price by Bob Speisman & Julian Shapiro NEW YORK — The Beach Boys have been a recording and performing phenomenon for more than 15 years, and now they have become somewhat of a retailing phenomenon as well. On July 17, "15 Big Ones,” the band’s first studio album since January 1973 ("Holland” was the last) entered the Cash Box “top 200 albums” chart at #97 (it is now #12.) Two weeks later, "Endless Summer," a 2-LP set released two years ago by Capitol, reentered the chart at #187 (it is now #88 with a bullet). Now, this week, "The Beach Boys In Concert,” a 2-LP set released three years ago, has appeared on the chart at #190. More Chart Appearances? There are indications that even more Beach Boys albums may reappear on the chart, as the band winds its way through the seocnd half of a three month, 36 city tour. This week, Heilicher Bros./JL Marsh, the nation’s largest rack jobbing operation and operator of 185 Musicland stores, reported major sales increases of 14 Beach Boys albums. Big August "Endless Summer,” which sold 1,100 copies during the week ending August 6, in- creased to 1,957 copies at the reporting branches of the Heilicher operation, which include all the Musicland stores and the en- tire rack jobbing operation. As a result, the album, which has sold 15,499 copies during the six months ending June 30 at Heilicher, moved from #17 to #7 on the company’s list of top selling LPs, which is based ex- clusively on sales monitored within the various corporate branches. "15 Big Ones” jumped from #20 to #1 1 on the Heilicher list as sales increased from 984 for the week ending August 6 to 1,649 the following week. Jumps "Spirit Of America," released in April 1975 on Capitol reached #151 from #193 the previous week. Sales increased from 201 to 297. “20 Golden Greats," an import album on Capitol which is the #1 album on the current Melody Maker chart in London, leapt to #170 from #490 with sales climbing from 186 units to 265 units. "The Beach Boys In Concert,” released in December, 1973, is currently at #180, up from #362 as a result of sales for the week of 253, more than double the previous week’s total of 114 10- Year Old Greatest Hits “Good Vibrations ... ”, released in July, 1975 is currently the #209 best selling album at Heilicher, selling 218 copies for the week. Last week it was #284 with sales of 137 copies. "Best Of The Beach Boys — Vol. 1,” released in June, 1966 on Capitol is at #260, having taken a substantial jump from #443. Lieberman purchased the store in July from Musical Isle of America, along with several other one-stops around the coun- try. The one-stop in St. Louis, which deals largely with black product, has been managed by T aylor for seven years. Lieber- man Enterprises, upon purchase, at- tempted to institute its controlled computer system, which it found inappropriate for its main customers, the small mom and pop stores. Being a mass merchandiser, Lieberman Enterprises must maintain stringent inventory control which is difficult at best, given a consumer profile more oriented to individual unit selection than mass purchasing. Fairness Commenting on the sale of The Soul City One-stop to Taylor, Lieberman told CB, "My St. Louis store had been losing customers, and since I really had’t intend- ed to change my operating system, I felt it would be fairer if Taylor purchased and operated the store the way he had operated it in the past. I felt it an ideal opportunity to allow a man who knows his business well to become an entrepreneur. I also feel I must mention this has nothing to do with tokenism — we made a business deal that benefited both of us." Black Community Taylor, who takes over operation of The Soul City One-stop, effective September first, discussed his feeling about the purchase as well as his operational game plan’ "We will be servicing the jukeboxes and the mom and pop stores with black and country product. How less? Specials run as low as $2.69 at certain times. And though Cohen maintains that he is staying out of newspapers for a while, a relatively recent ad in the Village Voice jazz supplement listed current $6.98 list CTI and Blue Note specials for $1.69 per LP. Two weeks ago, an in-store advertising campaign (signs on the windows) offered every album in the stores for $2.99. The sale was supposed to run for three days, Thurs- day, Friday, and Saturday, but, according to Cohen it ended at about 2 p.m. on Satur- day because the stores simply ran out of merchandise. “We disappointed some people, but we gave each one rain checks; we stand behind our operations." Explanation Cohen explained, "We manage to operate on a very low overhead; we run tight, be we’ve proved that it can be done with our prices. There’s no baloney, either. Every record that comes in here is on in- voice, and we pay our bills promptly, usually within 10 days.” As to the sale of the downtown store, Cohen denied that it was a foreshadowing of financial trouble. "We sold the store because it was too small. We sold it to a competitor who's been in the area for a while and we got a nice price.
