At the same time, Barry Manilow has renewed his recording agreement with the label. At a press conference called last Monday, Arista president Clive Davis ex- plained that the signings were not akin to FRONT COVER wmmammm ar< Ik- ba L By _Teai It’s not too often that really important bands come into existence whose personnel is drawn from the roots of other important bands. David Crosby, who used to be in The Byrds, and Graham Nash, ex-member of he Hollies, are a good example. Both men rly in their careers created a seminal body of work. Most musicians would be happy with just that. Not Crosby & Nash. They continue to ex- plore new sounds. Everything in their collective experience comes into play. They do not deny their roots; rather, they ex- pand, grow, and incorporate everything they’ve learned. Their ABC albums have attracted more than just a cult following — they are univer- sally accepted. And they take full respon- sibility for that acceptance; they educate their vast audience on issues of social con- science, as in their recent involvement with the “Save The Whales" movement. The committment is folded in with the art; in fact, Crosby & Nash are about to supply the music for a Jacques Costeau television special. And they just keep on going. No ‘Bought Contracts’ Davis was firm in his position that the ar- tists were motivated to choose the label for non-economic reasons, and commented that there were no “bought contracts," nor were the signings a result of “outbidding battles with other labels.” He commented in passing that both the Jefferson Starship and Fleetwood Mac were also under con- sideration at one point. WASHINGTON, D.C. — Schwartz Brothers, Inc. reported net income of $12,319 on sales of $5,305,037 for the second quarter ending June 1. These figures represent a recovery from the same period last year when the music merchandiser listed a loss of $83,026 on sales of $4,899,891. James Schwartz, president of the Washington-based company, attributed the improved performance to a variety of factors including a 20% increase in the firm's 15-store Harmony Hut retail chain. This represents the second consecutive quarter in which sales and earnings have been significantly higher than comparable periods a year earlier. As a result, for the six months ended June 30, Schwartz Brothers posted net income of $31,148 on sales of $10,536,529. Last year during that period the company declared a loss of $86,332 on sales of $9,582,976. In addition to its retail chain, Schwartz Brothers owns wholesale distribution and rack merchandising operations, all from New Jersey to Virginia. During that time, the com- pany posted a net loss of $21 6,000 on sales of $7,292,000. continueo on pg. 28 N.Y. Broadcasters Halt Proposed Telephone Tariff by J.B. Carmicle LOS ANGELES — The American Broad- casting Company, along with several New York radio stations, has filed a petition with the Public Service Commission in Albany, New York, to reject a telephone contest tariff proposal made by New York Telephone. The phone company’s proposal calls for answering devices to be installed in radio stations that generate "in- creased network usage” when initiating call-in contests involving station listeners. The tariff would affect the customer direc- tly; charging, him either a long distance or message unit rate when he successfully completed the call and received the recording telling him he was not a winner, to hang up, and not, try again. In the past, customers would only receive a busy signal. The extra lines provided by the phone company to the radio station will allow more customers to get through and be charged, thus the controversy. The radio stations contend that the phone company will create millions of dollars of additional revenue for itself and the phone company’s rebuttal is that someone has to pay for the increased usage of their network lines. Stay New Y ork Telephone wanted the answer- ing devices installed August 5, but a 30-day stay issued to ABC by the Public Service Commission postponed the action to Sep- tember 5. Rick Sklar is one of five New York broad- casters fighting the phone company proposal. The PD of WABC, New York, Sklar has been meeting weekly with representatives from WXLO, WHN, WWRL, and WNBC. “We want this tariff rejected and our petition (WABC's) calls for a hear- ing where alternate ideas could be dis- cussed," exclaimed Sklar. "The phone company is going to make a lot more money on this than what it will actually cost them. Making Money WWRL's general manager, Mark Olds, said the phone company would not provide a cost figure of the additional expense. "They say there are a lot of out-of-pocket expenses involved, but we can’t get them to tell us how much. We’re not asking how much they want to make, just how much it will cost. What they want is a whole new way of making money . . . and they are con- verting busy signals into a way to charge the customers by using these recording devices. We’re going to fight it tooth and nail and perhaps get our own hearing." Olds called the phone company a monopoly, saying, “They never like to be reminded of that. We are prepared to editorialize against them on the air because we think this practice will be unfair.” He also mentioned that this could be the forerunner of a national campaign by the phone com- continued on pg. 26 12 Albums Bow On Chart; Nine New Bullets Registered by Steve Ostrow and Julian Shapiro NEW YORK — Album chart activity has begun to accelerate once again with the debut of four LPs on the Cash Box top 100 chart, all with bullets. In addition, eight other LPs ap- peared on the list of the top 200 titles for the first time, five with bullets. The resulting total of nine new, bulleting LPs is the largest such total to be registered since July 3, when 11 albums entered the top 200 chart with bullets. "Hasten Down The Wind" by Linda Ronstadt (Asylum) debuted this week at #57, which is the highest first week showing of any album since “Spitfire" by Jefferson Starship registered at #43 on July 17. "Spirit” by John Denver (RCA), the follow-up to “Windsong,” which spent 44 weeks on the Cash Box chart, is at #85. It joins “John Denver’s Greatest Hits” which is at #172 after an incredible 165 weeks. Three Kiss Albums Charted "The Originals" by Kiss (Casablanca), a 3-LP repackage of three earlier Kiss albums, ap- peared at #93, and thus becomes the third album by the band currently on the charts. "Kiss Alive," a 2-LP set, is at #74 after 47 weeks, and “Destroyer,” their last studio effort, is at #126 after 22 weeks. "Waking And Dreaming" by Orleans (Asylum) is the fourth new entry into the top 100, bowing at #97. Other albums receiving bullets their first week on the Cash Box top 200 chart are: "Bigger Than Both Of Us” by Hall & Oates (RCA) at #130; “American Flyer” (UA) at #143; "Disco Train" by Donny Osmond (Kolob/Polydor) at #174; “Get Up Offa That Thing” by James Brown at #177; and “We Can’t Go On Meeting Like This” by Hummingbird (A&M) at #183. In addition, three albums appeared on the chart for the first week, but without bullets. They are: "Beach Boys In Concert” (Brother/Reprise) at #190 (see separate story on page 7); “Life On Mars" by Dexter Wansel (Phila. Int’l/Epic) at #193; and “Earl Klugh" (Blue Note/UA) at #194. Highest Top 100 Debuts In Month Not since July 17 have as many as four LPs debuted in the top 100 (six debuted during that week). On July 24, no new additions to the chart appeared that high; the highest placed album that week was "Wild Cherry" at #139, which has since catapulted to #13 with a bullet this week. The following week, “Happiness Is Being With The Spinners” was the sole new entry into the top 100 at #95; it is currently #38 with a bullet. A week later, “Diana Ross’ Greatest Hits” appeared at #79, climbin’ three weeks later to #26 with a bullet. On August 14, two albums entered the top 100 upon release, the first time that occurred in a month: "Music, Music” by Helen Reddy at #89 and “Best Of B.T.O. (So Far)” at #97. The former has since risen to #49 with a bullet; the latter has reached #51 with a bullet this week. Last week, entry into the top 100 reverted to its once-a-week pattern with the lone emergence of “This One’s For You" by Barry Manilow, at #67, which this week is #32 with a bullet (the large jump due in part to a debut of #1 2 at Heilicher Bros., the nation’s largest rack jobbing operation.). Chart Movement Foreseen Further evidence of a more fluid chart situation is relfected in an examination of the top 10 albums. For the first time since July 31, there is a new member, as “Silk Degrees” by Boz Scaggs moved from #13 to #10 with a bullet, supplanting the Beatles' "Rock 'N' Roll Musi: It has been on the chart for 25 weeks. EPICANDASSOCIATED LABELS: somebody who’s really been around —a session man, say, now recording his first album for himself. Somebody like HERB PEDERSEM,a premier studio musician from L.A. who’s played on more hit albums for more super- stars than probably anyone else around. We told him it was time to step out from behind those other people. One debut album, coming up. A new album called “Close-Up” brings BONNIE KOLOC into sharp focus. The lady from Chicago has a lean, clean sound, mixing pop with jazz and rock with scat and coming up with something very special. Definitely a grand lady of rock in the making. Which brings us to the hottest new act anyone has going at the moment, WILD CHERRY. Their production com- pany Sweet City was the one that came to us. They’d heard we were the best around for sales and distribution. We broke them first on black radio, spread them to top-40—and ended up with bullets in all three trades, sales figures nobody can believe . and a guaranteed top-five tune that’s look- ing hard at the #1 spot. Their first album is outselling every single on the street except one: their own. The trend for white music making it on black stations is skyrocketing — the only place we’d ever consider being is out front, setting the pace. GILT BY ASSOCIATION Epic doesn’t have a monopoly on im- pressive success stories, though. The method that works so well for the parent company-and for the artists —carries right on through to our associated labels. At BLUE SKY RECORDS, the word is new directions. JOHNNY and EDGAR WINTER, than whom few people are more together, are even more together than usual for their first joint effort. The brothers Winter share star billing, musical and production chores for an album that has to be a standout in two particularly lustrous careers. It’s called “Together,” of course...EDGAR WINTER’S partners for his next solo album are perhaps even more intriqu- ing; GAMBLE & HUFF. This album is still in the studio/songwriting stage, but get ready for it. JOHNNY WINTER pro- ducing MUDDY WATERS— Muddy’s just signed to Blue Sky. And the DERRINGER gang doses it out, with the loud, tight, bright, young, raucous, irrepressible spirit of rock and roll. “Derringer” is the new album by the hottest new band on the road this year. Britannia still rules the air-waves, at least if VIRGIN RECORDS has any- thing to say about it. MIKE OLDFIELD reminds everyone just how talented he really is With the release on Virgin of his magnificent first album, “Tubu- lar Bells.” (That’s the music that did so much for a little film called “The Exorcist.”) Mike outdid even himself on the follow-up album, “Ommadawn”; every time you play it, you hear some- thing new. Any band coming out of Liverpool deserves particular attention, but SUPERCHARGE would catch interest if they came out of nowhere. And they’re very far indeed from nowhere. Album is“Supercharge”-d, too. And BOXER, the band that’s knock- ing everybody out for the count, first in their native England, now here in the States. The big news at CARIBOU RECORDS is a Very Important S DENNIS WILSON, of America’s most legendary band, could have gone any- where for his first solo project. He came to us because we don’t rubber-stamp our acts— and because we can make it happen for an artist whether he’s an international superstar or somebody just starting out. New on Caribou: JAMES VINCENT, i here are a lot of people who have been called “virtuoso guitarists,” but James redefines the words. His first album for us is Space Traveler’’ — he was signed and nurtured by James William Guercio and Larry Fitzgerald, and they should know. In the studio again: L.A. EXPRESS. Some of our biggest success stories ever are called PHILADELPHIA INTERNATIONAL, TSOP, T-NECK and INVICTUS RECORDS. Before they brought T-NECK to us, for instance, the fabulous ISLEY BROTHERS were a musical byword — but they hadn’t sold more than a quarter-million albums total in their long career. Now they average five times as many albums, every time out —and there’s another LP on the way that’ll up the averages even more.

Radio Unites On Tariff « pany, if the New York proposal was ap- proved and enacted. New York Telephone marketing manager Ray Baxter explained the phone company’s proposal. "The answering device will help to reduce the volume of calls our network will have to carry,” he noted. “The recording will tell the caller that he did not win and to not call back.” Reimbursement According to Baxter, one way to assure that listeners do not call back to jam the lines even more is to charge for all calls to the recorded message. “It reimburses us for use of the network. Something had to be done," Baxter related. “People picked up telephones while these contests were being run and couldn’t even get dial tones. We’re just trying to avoid needless calls.” Baxter said the New York network phone lines were never set up to handle the sud- den impact usage resulting from radio sta- tion call-in contests. “Ten thousand calls may be generated at one time," according to Baxter, “but the broadcaster will only be responsible for paying for ten lines. We’ll furnish the additional lines, but someone has to share in the cost.” Experiments Experiments were conducted using the answering devices at some radio stations last year. "WXLO was very cooperative, along with other stations,” he explained. “We did two tests. The first trial proved the equipment worked. The second provided us with the methodology to make broad- casters look like their telephone use was just like an ordinary businesse’s use because we provided the extra lines to han- dle the increased usage in a normal man- ner. In other words, the broadcaster was not incurring a cost unequal to other businesses’.” Baxter said that the cost of providing the service will bring down the amount of revenue made from charging the public. Charles Herndad, an information super- visor in public relations for New York Telephone, added, “Everybody should be able to make and receive the calls they want to. When people couldn’t get through to hospitals and other places because they couldn’t get a dial tone, something had to be done.” Misinterpretation Both Baxter and Herndad reiterated that no customer would ever be charged for a busy signal. “This was a misinterpretation picked up by the media but it’s not true,” said Baxter. Cash Box contacted other radio stations who were also protesting the proposal. WHN’s program director Ed Salamon com- mented, “We’re unhappy with it, obviously. It doesn’t seem to be an equitable means of sharing the cost.” WNBC's general manager, Perry Bascom, noted, “We have joined with WABC in filing a petition before the Public Service Commission. We are taking the same stand as WABC and are requesting relief from this proposal.” More Revenue Bascom also mentioned that the phone company has the option to allow long dis- tance calls, rather than message unit calls, to sweep through the answering devices, creating even more revenue for itself. “It's also going to affect our public affairs programming. Should customers who call in on those shows be charged as if they were playing a contest?" questioned Bascom. WXLO general manager Rick Devlin said his station has filed a separate petition against the proposal, also. “We’re definitely gonna fight it,” said Devlin. Public Service Commission spokesman Francis Rivett told Cash Box that the filings by the radio station were “in hand." He noted that the Commission hadn’t had time to act on it yet because “our staff is still analyzing the proposal itself and the radio station petitions. The staff will either accept the phone company proposal and submit it to the Commission, turn it back to the phone company for revision, or order a hearing before the full Commission,” said Rivett. Time Needed The enactment date for the phone com- pany proposal is September 5. But, ac- cording to Rivett, another postponement seemed likely because the tariff and rate division of the Public Service Commission would need time to decide what course to take. As New York Telephone battled for enactment of the proposal and New York radio stations petitioned against it, the fight continued. Theoutcome won’tbeclear until September 5. Industry Viewing Variety Of Of Black Mktg. Techniques seemed to epitomize the theme of un- mitigated determination Cash Box found evident in many of the black professionals we spoke to. Separate Departments One sore spot that many representatives encountered was pointed out by John Levy, an attorney and manager who currently represents Nancy Wilson: “Every label seems to have separate promotional departments for R&B and pop artists. Black artists usually fall into the R&B heading, no matterwhat their musical direction. I always found it curious," remarked Levy, "that an artist like Nancy Wilson was placed in this category.” A few of the managers CB spoke to felt that black artists are getting an even better deal than white acts. Ron Strassner, manager of Parliament, Bootsy's Rubber Band and New Birth, thinks there's a new trend in music: "Record companies are recognizing that black music is experienc- ing an exciting and big change, expanding into what I call “black rock,” said Strassner with conviction. “The impact upon the in- dustry is similar to that made by 'Woodstock' years ago. The labels are anx- ious to strengthen their black rosters to be part of it. There are so many different types of black music and audience tastes that it’s getting harder for those who used to lump all black artists together to ignore it. As a manager, I’ve noticed a lot of things chang- ing the last two years. Black music is a vital and growing market." Audiences are leading this trend towards declassification, in the opinion of Joyce Bogart, Donna Summer's manager. "Even though Casablanca, Donna's label, has always been aware of the broad scope and appeal of black artists, some industry per- sonnel were not. Audience demand and buying tastes are turning those heads around.” Al Ross, manager of the Sylvers, thought certain labels were slower than others in recognizing this change. “I’m new to the record industry," Ross noted, “but it seems to me that some labels are more supportive of equally or less statused white acts. Some people think the ‘English invasion’ is still where it’s at and respond accordingly when it comes to sponsoring press receptions and promotional ventures.” Same Contract Lee Young Jr., general counsel of ABC Records, informed us that ABC uses the same contract forms for pop, country and R&B acts. Contracts may follow the same form but percentages, advances and promotional budgets are negotiable. CB found that much controversy exists around the promotion of product by black artists. Radio, always the industry’s prime road-to- gold, is still a powerful vehicle for exposure and sales. Most of the individuals CB spoke with placed great value on “crossing-over.” Aside from selling more records, “cross- overs” make it possible to achieve a wider audience, and thereby build an artist’s strength and longevity. The latter is, of course, a universal industry goal. Nikki Randall of Capitol Records market research division recently compiled statistics on R&B/pop "cross-overs." Her research showed that of the top ten records that appeared on the R&B charts in 1975, only one did not cross-over. Of the total of two hundred and twenty-four records that appeared, only twenty-eight percent did not cross-over to the pop charts. “Those that didn’t make it,” said Ms. Randall, “were largely regional R&B hits and were low ranking on the R&B chart list." It seems to be common practice among pop stations to wait until a “black sound” record has reached a certain position on the R&B charts before going on it. Con- sensus is that labels have accepted this and promote their black artists first on R&B sta- tions. Salter Disagrees Columbia’s Lome Saifer disagrees with this approach. “It’s not the color of the artist that determines how we promote a record at CBS, it’s the sound. We must also realize that R&B is a big, important market in itself. Many white artists, like Boz Scaggs, AWB, David Bowie and Elton John have looked to cross over into it, and done so successfully. Some records just have a certain feel to them,” Saifer noted. Otis Smith mentioned that pictures of the artist are not sent out with ABC’s DJ records. Smith felt that programmers listen to the music. They know that many white listeners tune into KDAY and KGFJ (two black L.A. stations ) because they like music and want to attract these listeners as well. But Sid Maurer, manager of Brass Con- struction and B.T. Express thought that in- dustry logic deems it necessary for a black artist to prove himself strongly on the R&B LP Cut Increase 5 albums is the fact that the album product has so greatly improved in the last few years, a trend which he sees continuing. In summary, there has not really been a drastic change in black programming, sim- ply a gradual evolution to more sophisti- cated attitudes. Record companies are naturally interested in making money, and the sale of album product does exactly that. Consequently, the more exposure album product gets on the air, the more sales can be generated. Development of an artist’s career and the life of the album is depen- dent upon the single, so by no means is the single on its way out. Yet with the increased LP cut exposure artists are now receiving much greater enthusiasm for new product is being generated at the all-important con- sumer level. charts before being broken in other areas. Limited Playlist And Al Ross wonders why quality, across the board product has to wait 8-10 weeks to break R&B before being properly promoted on pop stations. “I’ve gotten the impression that certain stations have limited playlist space allotted to each per- former. We recently had a situation where the new Sylvers’ single ‘Cotton Candy,’ was not put on pop stations because 'Boogie Fever’ was still on rotation and getting heavy requests. But when an artist like McCartney or the Doobie Brothers is hot, the singles flow one after another. The j Sylvers are a bunch of really hard working j kids. They appeal to all markets and i deserve a chance to develop that poten- j tial,” remarked Ross with emotion. Scott Shannon, vice-president of promo- | tion and media at Casablanca Records and a former Atlanta DJ and programmer, ex- plains that many pop stations only add one or two black records a week. He said the reasoning is that pop stations, from the j term “popular,” deal with a wideformat and | audience and don’t wish to oversaturate their listeners with too much of any one sound. Diana Ross or the Fifth Dimension J are not considered “black sound” artists. He also added that the black market has a | more solid buying base and so there are I many less turnable hits than in the pop market. Reorganization Recently Motown Records, a primarily black rostered label, initiated a special pop promotion reorganization to break artists on a broader level. And in an effort to con- centrate maximum promotional efforts, some new companies are experimenting with a method whereby a record is promoted on all stations in a region as soon as it hits R&B locally. 19 — Magic Man — Heart Industry Eyes Black Marketing Strategey sound are a true criteria for promoting any record, black artists still find a readier ac- ceptance at R&B stations. The DJ’s and programmers are more accessible to new product by black artists. Bernie Gross, Al Wilson's manager respects the labels right to break a record as it sees fit. "That’s their business and they know the field. I guess R&B is where the door is open first to a black artist,” Gross acknowledged. However many black stations are narrowing their playlists. Mike Upton, own- er of In-Tune Distributors and former senior vice-president of United Artists Records, opined that this will make it even more difficult for new black artists to break R&B, and therefore exceedingly rough to get that “cross-over” pop exposure. Ron Strassner expressed a rare opinion on promotion of his black artists product. His theory is to concentrate building an ar- tist on black stations. "If a cross-over comes, that’s fine,” ventured Strassner, “But I don’t go out looking for it. There’s a tremendous black audience out there to appeal to.” Discos Important Discos have become an increasingly im- portant area of development for the promo- tion of black artist. Saifer gives them credit for making it easier to break an R&B record at this particular time. As does Ms. Bogart who enthusi- astically said, “Discos have made an in- credible impact on the industry. Donna’s first hit, ‘Love To Love You, Baby,’ broke first in the discos as an unusually long cut, and then spread across radio nationally. Discos are bringing all kinds of people together to dance and have fun. They’ve contributed to making audiences more aware of music.” For The Record «. club has opened its doors out in the Valley (Encino, to be exact). It’s called the Cafe Concert and it’s open to all types of acts — rock, country, comedy — whatever. Call (213) 996-6620 for details . . . WORK TO MAKE IT WORK — Three local Los Angeles rock groups decided that it was high time that L. A. provided some sort of exposure for unknown acts. Therefore, members of the groups called Pop!, The Dogs and The Motels have joined forces to produce their own concert. The event, which the novice producers have dubbed Radio Free Hollywood, will be held at Troopers Hall on Tuesday the 24th. Don’t let the name of the event fool you — the boys do intend to charge admission . . . and while we’re on the subject of off-beat concerts — Elton John’s recent appearance at Madison Square Garden erupted in chaos when several members of the piano man’s business team pran- ced on stage clad in costumes depicting various fruits, vegetables and assorted goodies such as a banana, a strawberry, a carrot and an ice cream cone. Sources report that the rather comical visual interlude was not anticipated by John, whose shows are generally very tightly choreographed. Throw in a cameo appearance by Kiki Dee and you’ve got a pretty tantalizing banana split! . . . HIT THE ROAD, JACK — Harvest recording artists Be- Bop Deluxe, currently touring the Continent with Jethro Tull, are soon to return to the States — in person and on disc. The group’s third domestic LP, “Modern Music," will be released Sept. 13, to be followed by the American tour in October, November and Decem- ber . . . Canadian music-makers Heart are also slated for concerts throughout the month of October, including a four-nighter with Logglns and Messina at the Universal Ampltheater in L.A. Other acts that Heart will be paired with on the tour include Jeff Beck and The Beach Boys . . . With a performing record that spans half a century to his credit, Rudy Vallee debuted at the Playboy Club in Century City for a five-night engagement . . . CH . . CH . . CH . . CH . . CHANGES — The new Eric Clapton album on RSO, "No Reason To Cry,” which was scheduled for September release, has been delayed til Oct. 1 so it will coincide with Clapton’s scheduled tour of the U.S. The LP features some harmony vocals by Bob Dylan. . THE REEL THING — Sunset Sound is playing hostto Rita Coolidge and Jackson Browne — both are finishing up LPs . . . The Village Recorder reported that Columbia artists S.S. Fools are putting the finishing touches on a new single while The Band polishes off a segment for the King Biscuit Flower Hour . . . Erstwhile Doors guitarist, Robbie Krieger, has signed with Blue Note and is currently laying tracks for his debut solo effort for the label at Devonshire Studios . . . Island’s blue-eyed soul man, Robert Palmer, is curren- tly working on his forthcoming album, “Some People Can Do What They Like,” with producer Steve Smith. The LP is slated for a mid-October release . . . Al Stewart has just emerged from the studio after having completed his new LP, “Year Of The Cat,” for Janus. Their debut LP will be released in September. album, Palladium might have become a new Capricorn. But when a record com- pany starts a project like that, it’s really creating its own little monster. “After all,” insisted Andrews, “how much money can they really afford to dump into Palladium Records knowing that in three or four years I'm going to say to them, ‘I want a million dollars if you wantmeto stay.’ Keep- ing this in mind, it's only natural that Warner Brothers product is going to get worked and if it happens at Palladium, great. If you can wield enough economic power, like a Capricorn or an Asylum has now, you can demand that your product is worked. But at the time we were in no position to be mak- ing demands, besides it’s just not realistic to expect them to dump tons of money and time into something when they know that they're just creating a monster. When I ap- prised them of the situation, they told me, ‘give us one more album and if we can't bring that record together we'll write you a release.' And that's exactly what they did — the album didn't come together and they wrote us the release." According to Andrews, that’s when the label shopping began. “We had decided to leave Palladium with Warner Brothers because I wanted my artist to be one of the number one acts at a label again so he would receive the attention that he deserves. Without our own label to worry about, we knew that a company would see that if they'd build us, they would stand to make some money on us, rather than just creating somebody to bitch at.” Management — A Tough Game Gets Tougher "The manager's job is getting tougher and tougher,” related Andrews, “for- tunately for us, all the guys we had known when we were with Capitol way back in the beginning had become influencial ex- ecutives, so we didn’t have to prove anything to anybody. They knew what kind of people we were — that we were hard workers.” ad with no prices listed). He then summarized: "Working the road is your key to the top. It’s definitely the hardest, but it’s also the best.” Prefacing his statement with a broad grin. Punch Andrews resumed: “Like I was saying, it's really getting tough for a manager to break a new act. For example, even FM airplay is getting tough to get — no, I shouldn't say that it’s getting tough, cause it's always been tough — now it’s brutal. And agents — sure a lot of them will sign you, buttheywon’tdoanythingforyou. They’ve got a lot of acts to book, so they’re not likely to take a new act with nothing go- ing for it in the way of sales and throw it on a Z.Z. Top or Kiss, or Rolling Stones tour — they’re just not going to do it,” he emphasized. "Unless you’ve got creden- tials, meaning sales, you’re really up a tree." Bringing all of these elements together in one definitive statement, Seger concluded, “If you're a new act without any product, the only things a record company has to look at are your live performance and manage- ment. There is absolutely no doubt that the two are equally important. You can have the best band in the world but if the record company thinks your management is flaky and they’re going to have trouble with them, you might as well forget it.” Cale Sets Tour LOS ANGELES — Shelter recording artist J.J. Cale is set for his first major concert tour of the United States in three years. The tour will take Cale throughout the Western U.S., as well as into Canada, beginning Sept. 1-2 at Ebbets Field, Denver. The Cale tour will coincide with the release of his fourth album for Shelter, “Troubadour,” produced by Audie Ashworth. markets surveyed, including five major markets embraced by Korvettes. And In New York Meanwhile, in New York, where the "price war" among record retailers con- tinued its low profile, jockeying for optimal position remained the week’s most impor- tant concern. Korvettes retained at least a share of the front running spot with its list of “super specials,” at $2.99 each, expanded to seven in the Sunday edition of the New York Times. The albums offered were “Ten Percent" by Double Exposure, "Wild Cherry," “Silk Degrees” by Boz Scaggs, "Good King Bad" by George Benson, "Juicy Fruit” by Isaac Hayes, “You Are My Starship” by Norman Connors, and “Love, Life & Feelings” by Shirley Bassey. In addi- tion, newest albums by the Andrea True Connection, Marilyn McCoo & Billy Davis, Jr., Grand Funk Railroad, and Walter Murphy were available for $3.54 each. Four days later, the 30-store area chain added “War’s Greatest Hits," to its list of $2.99 specials, as well as four 2-LP sets from Buddah Records (The Best Of . . . Sha Na Na, Lovin' Spoonful, Monty Python, and The Essential Paul Anka). The albums involved were latest releases by the Ritchie Family, Beach Boys, Helen Reddy, Jefferson Starship, Barry Manilow, Diana Ross, Lou Rawls, David Bowie, and, in- terestingly enough “War's Greatest Hits.” Quantities were limited to 100 of each title per store, and one of each per customer. In order of largest to smallest, they were: New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Philadelphia, Detroit, San Francisco, Wash- ington, D C., Boston, Dallas, Pittsburgh, Long Island, Houston, Baltimore, Cleveland, Atlanta, St. Petersburg-Tampa, San Diego, Miami, Denver and Cincinnati. However, These are not the nation’s 20 largest markets, according to Standard Rate and Data. “We wanted to get the 20 top markets," explained an official of Media Records, "but we found out that certain ones weren’t subscribers to our service, either last year or thisyear.” Consequently the firm had to extend itself to 26 cities to arrive at its list of 20 top markets. The six cities not included in the survey, and their relative positions on the Standard Rate and Data list, were St. Louis (13), Newark (15), Minneapolis/St. Paul (16), Anaheim (19), Seattle (24), and Milwaukee (25). M.ENTONSTAGE ForTheRecord Jefferson Starship/Jeff Beck with Jan Hammer NASSAU COLISEUM, LONG ISLAND — Jefferson Starship has continued to suffer from an uneasy, split personality throughout its oftentimes stormy recording career. Spawned by Paul Kantner’s desire to explore more freeform, loosely defined musical directions, the band reached a nearly fatal level of acceptance, until resurrected by Marty Balin several years (and three albums) ago with a succession of love songs. “Caroline,’' “Miracles,” and the presently charted “With Your Love” (#18, bullet), all written by Balin, have vaulted the Starship to a level of popularity un- precedented for the members since Kantner, Balin, and vocalist Grace Slick flew on the more down-to-earth Airplane. The Starship may be the current vehicle, but judging from a recent performance before an overtly enthusiastic, demonstrably young crowd, the ride is less than easy. Just as the Starship has faced recurring identity problems in the recording studio, so do they generate obvious comparisons with their former incarnation on stage; and these problems are more serious. Initially, after only several songs, one is struck by the sound of two really distinct bands. Without Balin’s lyric input, the Starship tends to revert to the overindulgent musicianship that characterized earlier ef- forts; however, with the joining of Balin’s voice to Slick’s and Kantner’s, the vocal symmetry and resultant harmonic textures that made this grouping so unique become apparent. This need for a continuous, more highly organized and developed stage persona becomes more urgent with the musical ad- ditions of ex-Quicksilver Messenger Ser- vice member David Freiberg on bass and assorted keyboards, and rock ’n’ roll stylists John Barbata on percussion and Craig Chaquico on guitar. The performing skills are certainly there, but tend to com- pete with each other rather than integrating to create any semblence of the dynamic in- terplay that was a trademark of the Jeffer- son Airplane. Occasionally the parts meshed, and when they did, the results were varying degrees of exciting. Grace Slick’s reading of a slow blues accompanied solely by Peter Sears's excellent acoustic piano was particularly well-received. “Cruisin’,” from the successful “Spitfire” album, was a similarly effective vocal showcase, this time for Balin, and could prove to be a potent follow-up to their current single. An exten- ded version of "St. Charles” featured some lively guitar playing, but it was “Have You Seen The Saucers?” that proved to be the instrumental tour-de-force for the evening, highlighted by a multi-chorded bass solo by the versatile Sears. Jeff Beck, with the aid of the Jan Ham- mer Group, opened the show. While Beck’s guitar work was, at times, outstanding, the bulk of the performance tended to be aim- less. j.s. Felix Pappalardi/Joan Armatrading ROXY, LA — Felix Pappalardi and Creation, a Japanese rock 'n' roll band Pappalardi encountered at a rock festival in Japan in 1975, brought their music to the Roxy recently. The group opened the set with : "Preacher’s Daughter,” a powerful tune from their latest album. The melodic guitar \ riffs provided by Kazuo Takeda highlighted I the show, as Takeda transformed his lead guitar into a blues instrument B.B. King would envy. Pappalardi’s vocals were well done, but on some tunes the lyrics were in- ! audible, with the group’s instruments at what must have been full volume. Per- cussive shading, including two drummers who went crashing through “Secret Power" j to a crescendo ending, received the best ! response of the night. Flash, Daybreak, Sugar, and Thunder, as the Creation mem- | bers are dubbed, are fulfilling their desire [ to make U.S. audiences aware of them by putting together with Pappalardi, veteran of Cream. Youngblood and Mountain, one of the best rock and roll shows for any venue, large or small. Music, whether influenced by the East or West, is the universal language, and Felix Pappalardi and Crea- tion provide a much clearer meaning for that language through their music. Although Joan Armatrading squandered a chance to rap with her audience, her brand of modest rock was well performed before newcomers to the Armatrading name. The paucity of female guitarists notwithstanding, Ms. Armatrading's R&B overtones on “Love And Affection,” and her acoustic accompaniment on "Tall in The Saddle,” a powerful love lament, show- cased a vocal telent reminiscent of Phoebe Snow only stronger. Joan Armatrading's name will be heard again. j.b.c. Ian Matthews/Graham Parker BOTTOM LINE, NYC — With a voice impec- cable in range and clarity, and a solid band | of session men behind him, Ian Matthews has emerged as a song-oriented solo artist who exDands the dimensions of his presen- i tation with careful attention to instrumental elements. Matthews blends musical styles with a reference to his former affiliations with Fairport Convention and his own Southern Comfort, combining folk, pop, jazz and blues influences. While the cultists were relentless in their demand for old material, Matthews kept the set in an orbit close to his latest album on Columbia, “Go For Broke,” while delving into the past and future as well. The current single, Van Morrison’s “Brown Eyed Girl,” was charac- | terized by the delicately arranged lead and harmony vocals that pervaded the set, | while a yet unrecorded selection, ten- tatively titled “The Shuffle,” was more than “lyrically bizarre,” as Matthews put it. Adding a harmonic twist to a simple blues beat, the band’s expertise wrought a simple form into something unusual and arresting. All the solos were short, to-the-point state- ments, yet each piece reached a crescendo all its own. Matthews obliged the bottle- thumpers with one request, “Simple Tigers Will Survive." While he no doubt has written many songs that cultists will always de- mand, there is no reason why he shouldn't be able to combine his compositional ideas with the rich combination of colors and tex- tures afforded by good arrangements and excellent musicians, to create more varied but equally memorable moments. It wasn’t Graham Parker, but guitarist Martin Belmont of his band the Rumour who offered a “quieter number," “Gypsy Blood,” to the members of the audience who were tired of dancing. While few among the staid opening night gathering actually were dancing, Parker's brand of British R&B never stops dancing within it- self. “Back To School Days” is a non-stop uplift through each chorus, while “Lady Doctor” is almost a cool-blues shuffle until it explodes with Parker’s shouting vocal delivery. Another dance form he experi- ments with is reggae, turning out an authentic product with "Just Something You’re Going Through,” and using the rhythms in a blues fusion for “Don’t Ask Me Questions," which ends his Mercury album, "Howlin' Wind," with a wailing, haunting chorus. While Parker will inevitably be compared to Springsteen and other figures of the Asbury Park scene, he has much of his own style to offer, especially English blues-oriented musicianship. p.d. EAST COASTINGS — Power to the Pyramid — Those of you who have been trying to con- vince your friends of the mystical power of the pyramid structure and who have had to put up with a lot of snide comments because of it, take heart. It seems that the Record Plant, primo New York recording studio, has just built a new 24 track mixing room which features a pyramid-shaped chamber which rises high over the glass ceiling of the room. Several books have been published lately extolling the age-old mysterious powers of the pyramid, which is supposed to collect cosmic rays in a manner which gives it amazing preservative powers. Small pyramids are sold and used to keep razor blades sharp for months and to preserve food Record Plant engineers claim that the pyramid room has unusual acoustical properties which they are unable to explain. Coastings suggests they leave a pizza in the room for a few months and see what happens. RHODES RETURNS — During his recent stint on Scott Muni’sWNEW-FM radio show here, during which he blasted New York Times critic John Rockwell. Elton John played an old Emitt Rhodes cut and asked the audience if anyone knew of his whereabouts. He got his answer from a listener that the former ABC recording artist has surfaced as an a&r man for Elektra-Asylum Records in Los Angeles. Rhodes will also act as a staff producer, and one of his key projects is the utilization of the ill-fated Countryside studio in the San Fernando Valley. That studio was once a key E/A project under the aegis of former Monkee Mike Nesmith . Queen will play a free concert in London’s Hyde park, scene of the 1969 Rolling Stones free concert. Other shows have been held in the area of the park since them, but none as big as the Stones show. This concert is scheduled to have five acts, and the organizers are trying obtain the use of the same area used by the Stones, the Cockpit by the Serpentine. Sounds like an appropriate place for a show by either group . . . Several members of Bonnie Raitt’s road crew were arrested on the Jersey Turnpike for possession of one or another controlled substance on the day of the recent concert in Central Park. Ms. Raitt was reportedly following the equipment truck when it was stopped, and then followed her boys to the police station to help out. The equipment was held fora time, her boys for longer, and she and what was left of her crew arrived at the park not much more than an hour before showtime. Those attending were treated to an appearance by Elton John, resplendent in baseball cap. He sang “I’m Btowin’ Away" with Bonnie, and played piano on another number. Also joining the hoot was David Bromberg, members of opening acts Muddy Waters’s band, and Martin Mull, who repeated his “Let's give her a warm hand on her opening" intro from a Raitt show of a year or so ago . . . At Bruce Springsteen’s recent Red Bank concerts, he referred to saxman Clarence Clemmons as “Mr. Hollywood." This was a reference to Clemmons’ featured role in Martin ("Taxi Driver") Scorcese’s upcoming movie musical “New York, New York." Clemmons is co-starring with Liza Minnelli and Robert DeNiro, and portrays a sax player . . Franki Valli added to Elton John’s collection of glasses the last night of his Madison Square Garden concert series by presenting him with a pair which featured a season in the corner of each lens . . . Robbie Krieger, former guitarist with the Doors, is recording an instrumental album for Blue Note Records. Krieger is producing the alubum, which features top L.A. studio musicians. “Light My Fire," the Doors biggest hit single, was authored by Krieger . . . The b-side of Steve Miller’s new single, "Rock ’N’ Me," is the old Miller song “Living In The USA. "After the initial pressing of 200,000. a more recent cut will be substituted . . . Jimmy Carter was pictured flying to L.A. with John Denver in last Monday's Daily News. Tony Orlando garnered himself some neat publicity during the recent Republican con- vention in Kansas City. Nancy Reagan had just made her entrance into the hall, thus prompting a vociferous Reagan demonstration. The band then for some reason struck up " Tie A Yellow Ribbon 'Round The Old Oak Tree, "and Orlando, who had been sitting in the Ford box, began to trip the light fantastic with former Martha Graham student Betty Ford, thus drawing the TV cameras and much of the attention away from Mrs. Reagan. Jack "Backstage" Ford was later photographed on stage in Kansas City with Orlando, wearing an old leather flying helmet. Does Jack know more than he’s telling about various methods of flying? . . . Three-fourths of the original Monkees re-united onstage recently at, of all places, Disneyland. The touring and recording group of Dolenz, Jones, Boyce and Hart (two ex-Monkees and their producer/songwriters) were joined by ex-Monkee Peter Tork. Tork is now teaching under his real name, Thorkelson. Dave Clark, leader of the Dave Clark Five, was in the audience. Another L.A. reunion occured recently when Spirit was joined onstage at Santa Monica Civic by original members Jay Ferguson and Mark Andes. The one-time reunion was “just for the hell of it” according to Randy California, who organized it . . . Carole Sager and Marvin Hamlisch recently co-produced an Aretha Franklin session during which she recorded their song "Break It To Me Gently." Members of the Dwight Twilley Band stopped by the CB office last week while in town promoting their ABC/Shelter LP "Sincerely," and the upcoming single “Could Be Love." The band will rehearse at Shelter headquarters in Tulsa in preparation for a tour in Sep- tember. Reaction in Tulsa, which is also Twilley’s hometown, was that the cuts on the album were too short. POINTS WEST —Joan Baez joins Bob Dylan for two previously unrecorded tunes in his upcoming NBC special, “Hard Rain," on September 14 at 10 p.m. The two harmonize on Woody Guthrie’s “Deportees ” and the traditional “Railroad Boy.” Dylan is currently in a New York studio working on the final mix of the “Hard Rain” LP which, reportedly, contains some of the songs that will be on TV and some that will not. The show was produced by TVTV in association with Dylan’s own television production company, Streaming Eagle Productions. The taping took place at a Rolling Thunder concert in Fort Collins, Colorado on May 23 . ONJAZZ Get well greetings are extended to LA saxophonist Teddy Edwards, who is recovering from stomach surgery. Benefits for Teddy were recently conducted at several LA area clubs including Jimmy Smith’s. Singer Patti Austin, who has provided many a background vocal on CTI, makes her debut on the label in an LP titled "End Of A Rainbow.” Ms. Austin wrote eight of the nine songs and CTI regular Dave Matthews did the arrangements. New from Monmouth Evergreen: Duke Ellington’s “Black, Brown and Beige” by Alan Cohen’s band. The LP was recorded in England and features a big band of English musicians. Jack Kleinsinger’s “Highlights of Jazz" shows continue in New York. Next up is a COUNT 72 — Program director Barney Lane of jazz radio WRVR-FM, New York, holds the microphone during an interview with Count Basie. Interview highlighted an all-day programming tribute to the famous musician on the occasion of his 72nd birth- day. The day also featured a solid four-hour block of the Count's music, hosted by jazz historian Ed Beach. program titled "Jelly Roll, Joplin, James P and Others” with Dick Hyman, Vic Dicken- son and Pee Wee Erwin in the cast. The show will be at Loeb Student Center of New York University, September 22. Miroslav Vltous, former Weather Report bassist, is working on his first Arista LP at Secret Sound Studios. Vitous is producing as well as featuring his own electric and acoustic bass. In addition he'll be playing guitar and a variety of keyboards. Bill Evans and Tony Bennett will be recording together again. The album will be for Bennett's label, Improv, and Helen Keane will produce. Recording begins in San Francsico in late September. Jazz returns for a second season at the Santa Barbara Jazz Festival October 1, 2 and 3. Artists set at this point include Dizzy Gillespie, Supersax, Stanley Turrentlne, John Klemmer, Joe Williams and the Don Rader sextet. Tony Williams Lifetime’s long awaited LP “Million Dollar Legs” has appeared. Recorded in Colorado, the band features Allan Holdsworth, guitar; Tony Newton, bass and vocals; Alan Pasque, keyboards, and Williams on drums. Talk about George Benson power! His late 1960's A&M session "The Other Side Of Abbey Road" appears on our jazz chart. Who said you had to repackage in order to sell catalogue? Reedman Pee Wee Ellis, to Savoy. Ellis who came up in the James Brown organiza- tion and has lately served as conductor for Esther Phillips, will begin work on his first LP shortly. Houston Person’s "Pure Pleasure” is his first for Mercury. Jimmy Roach arranged the LP and it was Roach who was responsi- ble for Person’s “Disco Sax” hit of last year. In the biggest leap on the CB jazz chart of recent weeks, Roy Ayers “Everybody Loves The Sunshine" cracked a top ten that has changed little in the past few weeks. Ran into Cotillion's Willis Jackson on the street recently. The veteran tenorman has a new LP due any moment. An interesting (and X rated) profile of veteran jazz and blues producer Ralph Bass appeared in a recent edition of Blues Unlimited. Bass, at sixty-five, has managed to survive the likes of Herman Lublnsky, Syd Nathan and Leonard Chess, all of whom he served in fine fashion. Bass, located in Chicago, is now working with T.K. Productions. One of the most interesting vocal LPs of recent times is "Quire” on RCA. Quire is a choir under the direction of Chrlstlane Legrand, formerly of the Double Six of Paris, and The Swingle Singers. The LP contains no instrumental accompaniment and the material ranges from Meade Lux Lewis, Erroll Garner, Duke Ellington, into Bill Evans and Dave Brubeck. This one has to be heard to be believed! There have been orchestrated disco tracks, all-star blowing dates and then there are his own small band perfor- mances. Billy Cobham, Kenny Barron and Hugh McCracken assist the leader in able fashion during the course of four Carter tunes and two additional ti- tles. Carter’s artistry shines through every moment of this disk and the result is one continuous display of the creative gifts of this fine musician. JAKE HANNA — Kansas City Express — Concord Jazz CJ 22 — Producer: Carl Jefferson — List: 6.98 This is an especially pleasant visit to small band Basieana circa 1930-1947. Hanna is an excellent drummer for this groove and with the likes of Richie Kamuca, Bill Berry and Nat Pierce for the soloists the set could hardly go wrong. But the big surprise is the return to disk of Many Ann McCall, one of the era’s finest vocalists. Very nice cover art and ex- cellent sound are a part of the Concord tradition. For the band, try “Robbins’ Nest”; for Mary Ann try “Wrap Your Troubles In Dreams.” HOT TRACKS — Herb Ellls-Ray Brown — Con- cord Jazz CJ 12 I Producer: Carl Jefferson — List: 6.98 Concord has managed to present some excellent mainstream jazz over the past couple of years. Most of the artists are involved in studio work so the chance to step into a full blown jazz date generally brings out the best in those present. Ellis and Brown should need little introduction by this time, as both were members of the best Oscar Peterson trio. Plas Johnson and Sweets Edison form a most effective front line and there are originals from all four men. Quality jazz timeless in nature. BAREFOOT BALLET — John Klemmer — ABC 950 — Producers: Stephan Goldman and John Klem- mer — List: 6.98 This artist has a considerable following amongst rock and pop fans (in case you wonder why he ap- pears on ABC instead Impulse), but make no mis- take, he can play! Of the nine titles Klemmer also wrote eight (Janis Ian’s “At 17" is the other). The acoustic performances are likely the best of Klem- mer’s career and it is good to hear him relying less on effect. For those partial to the other side c Klemmer, “Whisper To The Wind” w Should be a strong seller. Cash Box/September 4, 1976

Twelve to three Willie Johnson, from WENZ . . . three to six Bob Terry (Nighthawk) from WLIB in New York, ... six to ten Barry Richards returns to the station from WMOD in Washington D.C. ... ten to two Bernle Harris, from WFEC . . . two to six Mike Evans, from WRAP in Nor- Continued on pg 52 ip W /? - : J \r zk staffer's Buy Direct by Cookie Amersors LOS ANGELES — More black retailers are buying directly from the manufacturer than ever before. Where previously the black retailer was almost overlooked by the manufacturer, he is now a. more viable force in the industry. The survival rate of the black retail store is unquestionably reaching new heights. They’re moving more product, making larger profits, and handling credit better than in the past. Taking its Place Henry Allen, president of Cotillion Records, told GB “the black retail store is definitely taking its place in the industry.” Stores are now more frequently being in- cluded in the company advertising and getting more display materials, because the manufacturer realizes the black retailer is becoming a more integral part of the record business. Allen also stated that by purchasing directly from the manufacturer the black retail store has a larger profit margin, is able to increase its volume and handle finances more effectively. Allen also maintained that several of the smaller mom & pop stores are banding together, forming co-ops so that they too will have the buying Continued on pg 46 Reflections SM Black Skip Miller has been appointed national director of R&B promotion at Motown Records, replacing Bunky Sheppard, who recently left the company to form his own label. Within the next two weeks, WMOT Records will be releasing a new Blue Magic LP en- titled “Mystic Dragon.” Jermaine Jackson’s plan to buy out Madison Square Garden and give a free promotional concert has been nixed by the New York City police department. The tickets would have been handled on a first-come first-serve basis, which the police department felt would create problems they would be unable to handle. Savory Records will soon be shipping its largest gospel release of the year. The release will include a new LP by James Cleveland which should be his biggest yet. Radio: Lyn Tolliver will be taking over as PD at WJMO in Cleveland, replacing J.J. Jefferies who is now PD at KSOL in San Francisco. Survey Probes Black Retailer Plight n 53 dimensions to the area of white crossovers in sales. Jimmy Foster of Jimmy’s Record Rack mentioned that "anything they play on the radio sells.” Likewise Mary Randall of | Lee's Records felt that “if black stations | play them (crossovers) then they go.” The I best examples of crossover sales at these stores seem to be AWB, Wild Cherry, and KC and the Sunshine Band, with some J stores having good luck with Gino Vannelli I and The Rolling Stones. Even though in-store play does help it does not accomplish the same results that demos do. Nonetheless, this seems to be the best compromise that the “mom and pop” stores can come up with at the mo- ment. Ads The black community in Los Angeles, as in many other major cities, has a number of publications such as “Scoop” which are devoted to the events and happenings of the community. Many of these papers are distributed to the community free of charge and usually have reasonable rates for ad- vertising. Since these papers deal ex- clusively with the black community and cost little or nothing to the consumer, they seem to give the retailer the best buy for his ad- vertising dollar. Some of the community conscious retailers leave these papers on their counters, but CB found that few stores utilize these publications to their own best interest. Gary Holmes indicated he had 500 hand- bills printed to stimulate slow business. Holmes said, “Response to the handbills was excellent.” He increased the effect of the handbills by staying open on Sunday when many of his competitors were closed. Holmes stated that his is progressing slowly into store advertising so as not to get ahead of his means and that he next plans to try FM radio ads since they are less expensive than AM ads. Larger R&B outlets in L.A. have often brought current hit artists into the store on weekends. Few "mom and pop” stores are able to do this, but those who have tried were usually satisfied with the results. Sometimes however the situation may get out of hand. Frank Johnson spoke of one incident that occurred when he hosted the Jackson Five at his store. Police had to be called to direct traffic and crowds were so great that his store had to be closed for the day. Calvin Anderson of VIP Records said that his store solves this problem by “know- ing who to let come in.” Anderson said that they "try to give the average group a break” and that people are always excited about meeting recording artists. Roland Boyd at R&S Records brings this concept a little closer to the means of the smaller independent dealer. Boyd is a musician himself and often brings his guitar Stevie Wonder Promotion also planning a tribute to Stevie on the Mid- night Special, to include film segments and obtain additional national attention. Next, Tucker revealed that he will institute a fan club, organized by him separate from the what the record company had previously organized. In outlining how the club will be handled, Tucker stated, “There will be a club application in every album. A nominal fee will be charged, and each member will receive a Stevie membership card, a beach towel, T-shirt and shoulder bag, which isfar more in value than the nominal mem- bership fee paid.” Sesame Street Starting in October, there will be an ad- ditional member to the muppet family on Sesame street. There will be a blind mup- pet by the name of Stevie. There is also an additional film called “Birthdays of To- morrow” filmed in part last may on Won- der's birthday, where people from seven- teen nations were represented in conjunc- tion with the bicentennial. This film will be and amplifier into the store on and plays the current top tunes. This at- tracts the people in the area (especially when business is slow), and often keeps people in the store for a longer period of time when they might normally stay. With so many aspiring young groups in the black community this could be the “mom and pop” stores answer to the appearance of the established artists ar larger stores. Anderson’s idea that his VIP store is “always trying something new and dif- ferent” could be useful to smaller outlets. Unique Approaches Some small R&B outlets in L.A. have had the foresight to capitalize on areas of sales that larger stores neglect. This may be specializing in gospel, jazz, and oldie record sales or utilizing the smaller store's ability to deal in used records and trade- ins. One store CB contacted brought a large number of cutout LPs from record companies for less than a dollar. The dealer is able to sell these albums for $2.49 and capitalize on the fact that an artist’s entire catalog sells better when a new album is released. The same dealer sells the current LPs for $3.99 Add-on sales of non-record items in small stores is a proven way to boost profits for most R&B independents. The high profit margin on incense, posters, and needles for phonographs increase the life of many stores which seem to have been hurting this summer. Still, many stores fail to display these items to the best advantage. Independent R&B stores in L.A. are definitely being affected by low prices of larger outlets and in most instances seem to be doing little to really improve their situation. Even though conditions in the community do not point towards a big growth in these outlets, it seems that some attempt must be made to incorporate com- munity support. While opinion differs widely as to the best way to enlist such community support, it would appear that, for now, many black in- dependent retailers are dissatisfied with their lot, but confused about which way to turn. The need for greater exposure, adver- tising and free goods support from the manufacturer, co-op advertising dollars, and central purchasing power all point to a climate ripe for change. Erroll Dophin perhaps summed the dilemma up best when he said "someone has to be paid" to pull it all together. Itmayturnouttobeinthe best interests of L.A.'s independent black retailers to find such an individual. New York’s Hitsville co-op has offered the retailers in that market an alternative and though L.A. retailers claim they are in need of relief, it appears that, for the time being, they'll have to settle for what they’ve got. Seven Major Manufacturers Indicate Holiday Campaigns Nine Japanese Executives Comment On Summer Sales TOKYO — As evidenced by various sales reports, the Japanese summer season (as a whole) did not turn out to be as strong as first expected. A variety of reasons were of- fered for this slow pulse. Here are some comments from various industry ex- ecutives, as gathered by the Cash Box Tokyo office. Nippon Phonogram Mr. Koizumi, managing director of Nip- pon Phonogram, said “slow recovery from the recession, the low rise in wages among the big Japanese companies this spring and the delay of a summer bonus, have brought on a ‘saving mood’ among con- sumers. This is the reason summer sales were not active." Polydor “No big hits or leading music,” said Mr. Fujita, chief of the Polydor sales section. "These factors brought on a slow summer. We may be wrong in expecting strong sales in the summer seasons of the future.” Tokuma Mr. Kuwata, managing director of Tokuma Music Industries Co., pointed out that “this summer season was the worst, in the absence of a superstar who can attract the buyer. This was equally true with Japanese as well as foreign music.” Victor Musical Mr. Ohta, chief of record business for Victor Musical Industries Co., disclosed that “the clearup of the economic climate has not yet come. Few retailers could be ex- pected to show rising sales." Toshiba-EM I On the other hand, Mr. Mizuguchi, chief of sales promotion for Toshiba-EMI Co., of- fered a different opinion, that “Japanese record makers didn't make full efforts to ex- cite consumers.” CBS-Sony Mr. Matsuo, chief of the CBS-Sony business section, came to the conclusion that "neither the summer nor the Christmas season can be expected to compare with other months from here on out. On the con- trary, we have to pay attention in order to realize constant sales through ail months of the year.” Crown Mr. Tsuyuki, chief of Crown Records’ business section, stressed that an active ef- fort toward consumer appeal is inevitable. “If the makers and retailers sell records aimlessly, favorable results shall never be realized.” Warner-Pioneer At the same time, Mr. Hirokane, chief of business management for Warner-Pioneer Co., commented, “Surely concerts are very effective in raising sales; our company is going to concentrate on that area in the future.” King Finally, Mr. Shimizu, chief of the business section of King Record Co., held that "without big hits or leading music, we can’t draw consumers to the music in- dustry, because the record business is a fashionable one. CBS-Sony Diversifies With Lemon Orchard TOKYO — In a move indicative of an expec- ted push into diversification of industrial in- terests, CBS-Sony Record Co., Ltd. of Ja- pan has established a new company, CBS- Sony California, Inc., which will raise and export lemons. The firm has acquired a 900-acre orchard in Ventura, California and enters production with $7,400,000 in working capital. Four Japanese and four Americans will act as executives under CBS-Sony president Norio Ohga, who will preside over the interest. Expected output for the first year has been set at $1,300,000. Yano Selected JASRAC Director TOKYO — Ryo Yano, a verse maker, has been elected a director of Japan’s Associa- tion of Authors and Composers (JASRAC). Yano succeeds the late Yutaka Kadota. TOKYO — Four students of the Yamaha Music Schools in Japan, selected for the cream-of-the-crop Junior Original Con- cert, have returned home after a tour of southeast Asian cities. The four, all girls, were invited to perform in concert by the National Theater Trust in Singapore and the Yamaha Music School of Singapore. On July 29 the group videotaped a 30- minute color TV program for Radio Televi- sion Singapore (RTS), a national TV chan- nel, and the program was aired as a sepcial in Singapore. TOKYO — With the summer season falling somewhat short of what had been hoped for, the music industry here is expected to lay emphasis on the Christmas and New Year seasons to increase sales. At least seven of Japan’s major record manufacturers have disclosed the direc- tions of their campaigns for the upcoming holiday period. The four gave their public concerts at the Cultural Center of the Philippines on Aug. 7 and 8 as fund-raising events for the Philip- pines’ National Music Competitions for Young Artists, the sponsor of the two con- certs. With an audience of 2,000 each day, the Aug. 7 performance was videotaped by GTV-4, a Philippines TV station, and was broadcast nationwide on Aug. 1 1 . This southeast Asian tour is one of a series which began in 1972, taking various Junior Original Concert musicians around the world for the development of fuller in- tercultural communication through music. Columbia will unleash a “Scrum 8” Christmas sales campaign including eight series of foreign and domestic music as well as educational recordings. Highlighting the release will be “Golden Star Delux,” consisting of 27 albums by popular Japanese artists; “Golden Package & Special,” with TV caricatures for children; “Mood Music Perfection 2500,” including many original foreign hits; and “Jazz Perfection 60” will present best albums from five artists, among whom John Coltrane, Sonny Rollins and McCoy Tyner are included. Crown is also expected to release special records for the holidays, including "Best Series,” and “Final Series,” which will con- sist of hit music and songs from famous Japanese artists and movie music from the •U.S. and Europe. RVC has scheduled a special Christmas project to be spread over four release dates from October 15 to December 5. Jazz, “home music” and popular Japanese mu- sics are included. Victor Musical Industries Co. has out- lined that it will launch “New Twin Delux” from October through November 15. After that date, the company will release “Family A Mood Delux 3200.” These two series in- clude Latin strings, “Charming Easy Lis- tening,” Argentine tango, continental tango, “Marches of the World,” flamenco guitar, country & western, dixieland jazz and dance music. King Records is going to carry out “King Joyful Winter Sale” from October 21 through January 20, 1977, aimed at raising their Christmas and New Year turnover. This effort will include Japanese hit songs, famous foreign music and tapes. The Car- penters, Quincy Jones, Cat Stevens, George Benson and Glen Miller will provide some of the highlights. Following their “Golden Special 1500” and “Super Deluxe Mirage 3000” cam- paigns, CBS-Sony will accept orders on Ja- pan’s big artists, for a second Christmas re- lease. Aside from hit collections, old west- ern popular songs, famous rock and mov- ie music will be included in this second shot. Nippon Phonogram, intent on increasing Christmas sales, has set two series: “Spotlight On,” and “Gloria 1000.” Follow- ing these, “New York Latin” will be released. Through these, the company will offer Japanese popular music, classical and urban salsa from the U.S. JPRA Says June Jumps For Japan TOKYO — According to the disclosure of the Japan Phonograph Record Association (JPRA), the output of records and music tape for June, 1976 showed some increase in both volume and value compared with the same month of the previous year. Records 16,794,000 copies showed a 10% gain against the previous month of 15,295,000 copies and 1 5% more than the same month of the previous year. At the same time, this brought in 14,309,000,000 yen indicating an 1 1 % gain over the previous month of 1 2,- 935.000. 000 yen and a full 23% more than the same month of the previous year (11,- 648.000. 000 yen). In monetary terms, singles ac- counted for 3,272,000,000 yen, again, an 11% increase over the same month of the previous year. Also climbing, LPs sold 8,- 449.000 — 9% more than the previous continued on pg. 68 ‘Silent Price War’ Perplexes Japanese Mfrs., Retailers Open (And Secret?) ‘Service Tickets' Allow Customers ‘Illegal’ Discounts by Sachio Saito TOKYO — Just as in an American “price war,” the Japanese music industry is lately con- fronted with confusion in regard to retail record and tape price policies. Unique System In comparison with the U.S., Japan’s retail system is unique. Free competition through discount retailing is not practiced in this country. Prices are set in mutual agreement by contract between manufacturers and retailers; everyone is obliged to abide by these con- tracts when they conduct their business. Consequently, retail prices of records and music tape are the same throughout the country. In short, with no discount policy, the only room for competition at the retail level is through publicity, display and after-service policies. This has been the established commercial practice since the music industry began here. As a matter of fact, both the manufacturers and Japan’s Record Retailer’s Union (JRRU) are very eager to preserve this contract system. Violations However, this long-continued practice has recently been violated by a major super- market chain — outsiders to the JRRU — issuing “service tickets” to consumers who buy records from its shops throughout the country. Toward Purchase These tickets, issued by Daiei, the largest mass merchandise discount chain in Japan, are said to be worth 10% of the price of a record. When the consumer collects ten tickets, he can exchange them for a record. This amounts, of course, to a virtual discount sale. Thus, the JRRU has denounced the chain as an offender to the contract system. At the same time, the JRRU has asked Daiei to stop these discount procedures in order to preclude industry-wide confusion. ‘Well-Known Secret’ In answer to the JRRU, the supermarket chain charged that, for some years, a number of retailers under the JRRU umbrella have been offering similar “service tickets” on a private basis — to date, a well-known secret. If the JRRU can stop its own violators, says Daiei, ef- forts will be made to abolish the recent above-ground ticket policy. On the other hand, says Daiei, if even one shop continues “secret sales” in conjunction with or in any way connec- ted with the JRRU, Daiei will feel “obliged to keep a ‘service ticket policy’ as a counter- measure.” Prior to the appearance of these problems at the supermarket level, the JRRU held general meetings and branch conferences throughout Japan in order to pass resolutions in favor of abolishing the service ticket policy at the retail record level. This attitude by the JRRU is, of course, based on a firm desire to keep the contract system intact. Chaos, Pitfalls JRRU opines that, if the system is broken or abolished, as a consequence much chaos and many pitfalls will beset the Japanese music industry at both the manufacture and retail levels. Notwithstanding such resolutions and projected control measures by the JRRU, the service ticket concept has by no means expired yet. JRRU, in actuality, is pessimistic about its chances of eliminating this so-called illegal practice among record retailers. Hence, their communication to the supermarket chain, as one music industry executive pointed out, "has not much persuasive power.” ‘Silent War’ Judging from these circumstances, the service ticket policy (discount sales, in effect) will quite probably continue both openly and secretly. This is the conclusion of the majority of the Japanese music industry. In other words, the “silent price war” is on in Japan.
