Matter Of ‘Pure Economics’ LOS ANGELES — “It’s pure economics,” said Playboy Records president Tom Taka- yoshi, talking about the benefits of in- dependent distribution. “We prefer the in- dependent route. We like the association.” That association has been going on ever since they released their first record in January 1974, and Playboy was underway, with Takayoshi’s self-acknowledged help from the indies. Playboy has a small roster of acts, and it’s intentional. “We want to be able to give vice president and general manager; Barry Resnick, director of national promotion; and Melvin Moore, national R&B promotion. our artists the proper concentration,” Taka- yoshi remarked. “We don’t want to over- extend ourselves. “Many of these are new acts,” Taka- yoshi continued, “and we count on the in- dependents for ideas — promotion and marketing. Whenever we’re planning a national campaign, we discuss every facet with them before we finalize things.” Playboy, coming out of a period of finan- cial hardship, is in the middle of a period of breaking new artists, and the president feels that the independents have a “great personal stake” in his company’s success: “Every sale means something to them. When they sell an album it’s money that comes directly to them.” Branch distribution, according to Taka- yoshi, is an expensive proposition, and he's presently satisfied with the service provid- ed by the independents. In the last couple of years, Takayoshi has seen “tremendous growth on the part of independents. I think it’s definitely in the cards for the indepen- dent to be a major factor in the industry within the next few years.” Takayoshi did not want to speculate on the current market share held by the in- dependent distributors, but expected that in the future they would hold much more. Great Northwest Opens i LOS ANGELES — Great Northwest of- ficially opened for business on June 1 of this year. The Seattle-based company is run by president Jerry Dennon, a former regional and national record sales and promotion man, record distributor and producer. He is assisted by Lou Lavinthal, former chairman of the board with ABC Records & T apes Sales, and Stan Jaffe, for- mer executive vice-president of ABC Records & Tapes Sales. The basis for the firm is artist manage- ment; this is handled by a wholly-owned subsidiary, the Omega Management Co. Great Northwest is actively developing its manufacturing arm via the Great Northwest Music Co. label. The aim of the label is twofold: first, to regionally release and test market product, primarily singles, that then can be leased to major labels for national distribution and, secondly, as an indepen- dent label for its own national releases through a network of selected independent distributors. Vee Jay Began, Stays, With independents LOS ANGELES — Beginning with indepen- Ms. Chiappetta plans on using indepen- dent distributors when the company was first getting started in Chicago in 1955, Vee Jay International, under the guidance of president Betty Chiappetta, will stick with them as it once again attempts to become a major power on the recording scene. “From the earliest days of Vee Jay, in- dependent distributors have supported us,” said Ms. Chiappetta. “They took us from strictly an R&B label over to the pop field. Unlike other distributors, ours didn’t try to pigeonhole our acts into specific categories; rather, they tried to get them airplay and sales wherever they could.” Ms. Chiappetta said the distributors would often pay in advance in order to allow Vee Jay to continue everyday functioning because they believed in and admired the label and its artists. “The financial and promotional support they gave us,” Ms. Chiappetta reflected, “really paid off for them when we landed the Four Seasons and the Beatles.” Vee Jay’s president is counting on the same kind of help from her distributors to- day, as her company doesn’t have any promotion staff of its own and has yet to deal with radio stations on a promotion level: "Many of our distributors are the same ones that Vee Jay was using when it first started. They’ve helped us in the past and I know they’ll help us now.” dent promotion people to help out whenever and wherever necessary: “A small label has no other way to go. We can’t afford to have permanent promotion peo- ple in every area but we can afford to bring someone in* when necessary. They can generally do a better job for you because they're in constant contact with other labels and the important people.” Started in Chicago, Vee Jay was one of the first black-owned record companies to become a major corporation. Known for its , longevity of product, Vee Jay specialized in R&B, jazz and gospel sounds, watching as each of them crossed over to the period’s pop playlists. In the mid-’60s, the company, facing many internal problems, went under. In 1967, current president Betty Chiappetta, along with Randy Wood, acquired the com- pany out of bankruptcy, moved it to Bur- bank, California, and began reassembling the pieces. Licensing the catalog until its feet were regained, Vee Jay is presently set to release its first new product in more than a decade. The company now has four labels — Vee Jay, Pollie, Dynasty and Epitaph — and two music publishing companies — Donna Lee Music (ASCAP) and Peglari Music (BMI). m INDEPENDENT DISTRIMJTION 7(» Letters To The Editor Editor’s Note: The following are two letters to the Editor, offering two views of independent distribution. The first, by Ralph Kaffel of Fantasy, traces the history of indy distribution. The second, from a new small manufacturer, takes the indies to task for what he considers their failure to assist him. Kaffel Traces History Of Indies LOS ANGELES — Central, Diamond, Hart, Modern, Milton’s, Buckeye, Record Sales, Record Merch, Pep, Chapman, Merit, Hitsville, and California Record Distributors were some of the firms that lined both sides of Pico Boulevard, L.A.’s record row in the fifties. Every then-existing label, except Columbia, Capitol, RCA, and Decca was utilizing independent distributors. Indy dis- tribution was entrepreneurial, very com- petitive, very primitive, and very exciting. The manufacturer was very much in the driver’s seat and the pressure to change distributors was constant. The early dis- tributor was a small business, seldom em- ploying more than 10-15 people. He was very product and promotion-oriented, as he had the total responsibility for sales and promotion in his market. The ability or in- ability to break records became a part of the distributor’s reputation, and was a primary reason for label switches. The volume was modest by today’s standards, but overhead and rents were low, and gross profit high, averaging 23-24% in the late fif- ties. Credit risks were few, a large part of the business was over-the-counter cash, and receivables were pretty evenly spread. The arrival of the oft-maligned rack- jobber in the early sixties signaled the gradual but steady downward slide of the distributor’s mark-up, which eventually (in ’68-’ 69 ) shrank to 12-13%. Local en- trepreneurs, very often underfinanced, jumped into the rack-jobber/one-stop business, generating large volume but of- ten folding leaving distributors with huge bad debts. Some labels, too, were folding, others selling out. Eventually, Atlan- tic/Atco, Warner/Reprise, ABC/Dunhill, Elektra, Polydor, Coral, Mercury, London, Blue Note, Epic, World Pacific, Liberty, and many others became unavailable to independents. The distributor, faced with credit risks, a shrinking product base, and deteriorating profits became the training ground for potential personnel for manufacturers, who by then realized that they had to assume a greater share of responsibility for their sales and promotion. L.A. was very fertile soil. My old company, which I co-owned with Jack Lewerke, was the school for Stan Bly (Arista), Marty Kupps (Lifesong), Gil Bogos (RCA), and Bob Ursery, Bob Mercer, and Bob Kirstein (Fantasy). Jerry Moss, Russ Regan, and Lee Laseff were all at one time associated with Record Merch in promotion capacities. The uncertain indy distribution picture in the late sixties motivated new labels to seek distribution arrangements with majors as an alternative to the independent route, thus further eroding the product base. I think the nadir for independent distributors came in 1970-71. No new labels seemed to be emerging, retail structure was weak, catalog sales slow and credit risks great. The advent of the super-retailer in 1972 was one of the signals of the turnaround. Emergence of such labels as Arista, Casablanca, TK, 20th Century, Private Stock, CTI, and Lifesong, the reversion to independent distribution by UA, London, and Monument, the choices made by Chrysalis and Island, and the continuing commitment by A&M, Motown, and Fan- tasy, all point to a bright and secure future for the independent distributor. He has gone through some tough changes and emerged stronger than ever. Not all sur- vived — distribution is not nearly as com- petitive as it once was — but the ones that did are the cream of the crop. Independent distribution is now large, efficient, finan- cially responsible, capable of moving almost unlimited quantities of product with great speed, just as well as, if not better than, branch operations. 1976 has been a banner year for the independent dis- tributors and labels, and 1977 looks even better. Maybe it’s just nostalgia, but the one weakness I still see in the system is the lack of sensitivity to, and involvement with the music itself at the highest executive levels of some distributors. I hope that changes, for if and when it does, the sky’s the limit. ralph kaffel Ralph Kaffel is president of Fan- tasy/Prestige/Milestone. He has an exten- sive background in independent distribu- tion, having owned and operated (with ex- partner Jack Lewerke) California Record Distributors, Merit Distributing Corp., Hitsville, Inc., and United Tape Corporation from 1954 to 1969, with Kaffel joining Fan- tasy in 1971, and Lewerke becoming ex- ecutive vice-president of Record Merchan- dising in Los Angeles. A Second View: The Indies Are ‘Whores’ To The Editor: Regarding your letter dated October 27, 1976, “The Independent Distributor Has Been Unjustly Maligned In Recent Years.” I have known and respected you for the past twenty years, but it is quite evident from your letter that you know absolutely nothing about what the independent dis- tributor does for the record industry. Having worked for independent record manufacturers who dealt only through in- dependent distributors, I think that I am most qualified to enlighten you. in addition, as you know, I started my own independent record label this year, and have gone the route of the independent distributor for the product that I have released. As far as I am concerned, the indepen- dent record distributors, every one of them, are the biggest whores in the world. They do absolutely nothing for the manufacturer until the manufacturer makes the record a hit, and after the record becomes a hit, the independent distributor will put a gun to your head and ask for 20% in free merchan- dise in order to distribute the record in his territory. As you must know, to break a new artist, or for that matter a new release by an es- tablished artist, takes a ton of promotional effort by the manufacturer. The distributor usually has a token promotional staff that does not do anything except mail out the samples that they receive from the manufacturer, and this is only a duplication of what the manufacturer does himself. It is incumbent upon the manufacturer either to put regional promotional people on his payroll, or to engage the indepen- dent promotional people that are available in order to properly promote a new release or a new artist. The distributor comes in only after the fact. How many independent distributors do you know of that ever took an ad in Cash Box to advertise a new release or a new ar- tist? If I sound bitter about the independent distributors of the record industry, it is only because I have had to live with them for the last few months. (Or I should say I have had to live without them.) Would you believe that they do not even extend you the cour- tesy of talking to you on the phone?! It is the most frustrating feeling when you try to contact the distributor that you appointed to distribute your product, and they do not want to talk to you. I can go on and on, but I think I have made my point. If you are really interested in what makes the independent distributor tick, you and I ought to get together. I can tell you things you will never believe. Kind- est regards. Signed Indies Fighting For Their Artists: DeJoy LOS ANGELES — Ed DeJoy, vice presi- dent and chief operating officer of Janus Records, attributed a large measure of Janus’ success to its system of indepen- dent distribution. "The indies,” stated De- Joy, “really fight for you and your artist.” Discussing the possibilities of distribu- tion, DeJoy postulated that for Janus branch operations would be too expensive a venture. “With our independents,” he continued, “it’s almost like having our own branch system. The people who work in in- dependent distribution are people who have grown up with the record business. They are aggressive and experienced.” Indies have broken records for Janus, according to DeJoy — most recently in the Seattle and Philadelphia markets, “it’s almost like having your own branch,” he revealed, “without having to support it. We're backed up completely with these ex- perienced, aggressive record people.” DeJoy allowed that branch operations were “terrifically effective” as well, but not necessarily so for an independent label. “Our business is the independent’s busi- ness,” the v.p. explained, “so if we’re suc- cessful, they’re successful. It’s as simple as that.” An interesting aspect of independent distribution, according to DeJoy, is that the indies have a choice; there are a lot of labels to work with. “If they believe in a product,” he stated, “they’ll go out on a limb for it and order more records initially that are im- mediately sellable.” PIP Tied To Pickwick LOS ANGELES — One of the advantages enjoyed by PIP and one of the reasons for its success is its almost exclusive dis- tributor, Heilicher Brothers. “We’re with one of the best,” said Sonny Kirshen, who is responsible for national sales and marketing for PIP. Since HeMicher maintains such a large presence in the distribution business, they are in a position to do a complete job in terms of working with and serving PIP, ac- cording to Kirshen. Independent promotion people are also an integral part of PIP’s overall push to sell records. “We use independent promotion men to enhance the promotion effort,” Kirshen declared, “especially depending on which type of artist or record we are try- ing to push.” Airplay Prime Factor Kirshen believes that airplay is the prime factor leading to getting the records in the stores. Today, he says, with what he con- siders to be fewer independent distributors and many more labels, independent promotion people are a necessity in the business. “The resistance,” he said, “on the part of the independent distributors to in- dependent promotion people is so minute, that it’s hardly worth talking about.” In- dependent promotion people, he added, are a necessary aspect of the total record business. JazzAlbumPicks BENSON BURNER — George Benson — Columbia 33569 — List: 6.98 This is some super music reflecting Benson’s first regular band with occasional guests. It dates from 1966 or '67 but doesn’t sound at all dated. The guitar playing is crisp and inventive throughout, and the support from organist Lonnie Smith and baritone man Ronnie Cuber is top-notch. While there are ele- ments of R&B, even gospel, the emphasis here is most often on straight-ahead hard cooking. There is no limit to George Benson's ability as a guitarist but when he stops out over a strong 4/4 as he does fre- quently here, he becomes much more than a pop- ular artist of the moment. . iSHBOKR&B Reflections ’N’ Black John Smith will be vacating his post as national R&B promotions director at United Ar- tists to join Blue Note Records as vice president of marketing and sales. Filling the slot at United Artists will be Eddie Levine, who is at present handling national promotion at Blue Note. L.A. Mayor Addresses Record Retailers: Motown Sponsors by Cookie Amerson LOS ANGELES — Motown Records recen- tly sponsored a breakfast meeting of various record retailers from the south cen- tral area of Los Angeles to Initiate an official rapport with City Hall. Mayor Tom Bradley addressed several biack record retailers and other small business owners to explain City Hall procedures as they relate to the small businessman. Several represen- tatives from the mayor’s office attended the meeting in support of the mayor’s discus- sion of monies available to the small businessman as a loan through the city government. Small Business Administration The representative from the Small Busi- ness Administration discussed with atten- dees procedures of obtaining a small business loan either to expand an existing business or to start a new one. Because of the past reputation of SBA loans being almost impossible to obtain, step by step policies were explained to rebut negative attitudes. Adrian Dove, director of the mayor’s Office of Small Business Assistance, held a question and answer session, responding to anything not covered in SBA loan discussions. Bridge The Gap Louis Wilson, executive director of iM- PAC (South Central Improvement Action Council incorporated), explained how his organization has helped bridge the gap between the individual seeking a small business loan and the SBA. Wilson told the gathering “IMPAG was formed to assist the small businessman or woman in qualifying for the SBA loans, and also to educate the minority entrepreneur in obtaining managerial expertise through classes of- fered by the organization.” Representing Motown Records was press and publicity director Bob Jones, who explained the company's involvement by stating, “Motown can certainly identify with the small businessperson because we were once there ourselves. We are fortunate to be in the position we are today, and we’re happy to be involved in this community affair.” rv ^ f 0 Jk- p Mlrfnm fi 11 i - J mCk * ' 1 i K * \ MELBA TO PLA Y MET —Buddah recording artist Melba Moore will be featured in a one- woman show at the Metropolitan Opera House, presented by Danny O’Donovan and “Big Blue Marble" (ITT’s public service television series for children) on December 12. Boston Gets Platinum NEW YORK — "Boston,” the first album by the group of the same name, has been cer- tified platinum by the RIAA. The album, on Epic Records, attained the million unit sales plateau in eleven weeks. FRONT COVER I i Norman Connors can claim a breadth and depth of experience that few other artists can boast of. Beginning a career as a drum- mer involved in mainstream and avant- garde jazz, Connors has crossed over to the R&B and pop markets as musical direc- tor of his own recorded works. His latest Buddah Records album, "You Are My Starship,” nears its eighth month on the j Cash Box top 100 pop albums chart, peak- ing within the top 40. The single “You Are My Starship” reached the number one position on the Cash Box top 100 R&B singles chart. Early in his career, Connors played drums with Leon Thomas, Billy Paul, Archie Schepp, Sun Ra, Jackie McLean, Sam Rivers, Lou Donaldson, and Charles Earland. He joined Pharoah Sanders in 1971 touring the world as well as recording i five albums with him. Connors began : recording as a bandleader the following year, with two solo albums on the Buddah- ! distributed Cobblestone label, “Dance Of Magic” and “Dark Of Light.” The players on these sessions number among some of the best-known names in today’s jazz, in- i' eluding Stanley Clarke, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Jean Carn, Herbie Hancock, Ron Carter, Gary Bartz, Eddie Henderson, Alphonse Mouzon, Airto and Hubert Laws. As part of an all-inclusive Norman Connors catalog program, Buddah has recently reissued both these albums. As sales for the most recent album near the figures required for gold certification, Connors continues to involve himself in varied projects, including production of a new group on the Buddah label, Aquarian. Two of the featured vocalists on his last two albums, Phyllis Hyman and Michael Hen- derson, have both signed solo contracts with Buddah. Norman Connors’ next album, coming shortly, will be entitled “Romantic Journey.” INDEX Album Chart 1-200 53 Album Reviews 25 Classical 26 Country Top 100 Singles 32 Country Top 50 LPs 30 FM Analysis 17 For The Record 36 International Section 50 On Jazz 37 Looking Ahead 46 Monthly Chart Share 28 New Additions To Playlist 18 Pop Radio Analysis 21 Radio Report 16 Regional Album Activity 24 R&B Top 100 Singles 39 R&B Top 75 LPs 38 Singles Bullets 22 Singles Chart Top 100 4 Singles Reviews 23 Talent On Stage 36 A&M ‘Nadia’s Theme’ Makes Impact At Franklin Music by Ken Terry ATLANTA, GA. — “Only once in a blue Copyright Renewal Date Looms As Crucial Issue by Rebecca Moore WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Copyright Of- fice is seeking comments on a proposed date current copyright holders may first give notice of their intentions to renew or terminate contracts with publishers. Com- ments are due by December 15. The new copyright law gives an extra 19 years to copyrights in their second 28-year term. When a copyright has expired, the owner has five years to give a two-year notice of his or her intention to reclaim ex- ploitation rights, but the new law also says an owner cannot file notice before Jan. 1, 1978. Crucial Date For some copyright owners, or their heirs, the earliest date they can file their two year notice is crucial. Copyright, renewed each ye# by Congress since 1962, has already used up many of the extra 19 years of life. If owners can file notice before 1978 — and thereby reclaim the copyright before 1 980 — they may have an extra year to milk their work before copyright time is up. At this point, no one is sure if a notice filed with the Copyright Office this Decem- ber will mean that an owner can renew or terminate his or her contracts in December of 1978, the earliest date after the two year waiting period. The Copyright Office is pro- viding notice forms and is accepting such notices. But it is not making any promises. NEW YORK — The F.W. Woolworth Com- pany reported income for the third quarter ended October 31 of $23.9 million. The figure represents a 4% decline from income of $24.9 million during the comparable period last year. London Changes Label Design NEW YORK — London Records has an- nounced a new, four-color “sunrise scene” label which will appear on the company’s 45 records. The new label will be utilized on all London 45s pressed after January 1, 1977. Singles from Hi, Threshold, Mach, Buk and other London distributed companies will retain their own labels. Jimmy Buffett Signs New Pact With ABC LOS ANGELES — Jimmy Buffett has re- signed a recording contract with ABC Records. Buffett and his Coral Reefer Band are currently in Miami’s Criteria Studios putting the finishing touches on Buffett’s upcoming ABC album, “Changes In Latitudes, Changes In Attitudes,” set for January re- lease. LA One-Stop Moves LOS ANGELES — West Coast Music Sales, a Los Angeles one-stop, has moved to 727 West Venice Boulevard, Los Angeles. moon does an album come along that you can really blow out like this,” remarked Lee Durham, manager of Franklin Music’s Perimeter Mall store, in a recent phone interview. He wasn’t talking about the new album by Stevie Wonder. Nor was he referring to Elton John’s “Blue Moves” or to Led Zeppe- lin's current soundtrack. The album Durham was discussing is one that has out- sold all of those top-charted items in Franklin Music’s three Atlanta stores: the A&M version of “Nadia’s Theme” with the hit single on it of the same name. In the Perimeter Mall store, Durham es- timated 250 copies of “Nadia’s Theme” have been sold in the past week. This is considerably more units than any other album has sold except for Boston’s debut LP “and things like that,” said Durham. Vaughan Jones, record manager at the chain’s Lenox Square location, stated that her store moved 600 copies of “Nadia’s Theme” last week; in comparison, she said, “we usually sell about 400 copies of our #1 album” within the same time period. At Franklin Music’s Cumberland Mall store, 150 copies of the A&M album were sold in a week. Consolidated sales for the nine month period climbed 12% to $3,569 billion, from sales of $3,183 billion for the comparable period in 1975. It’s a monster down here.” Special Sale All three managers agreed that a con- tributing factor to the current sales spurt on “Nadia’s Theme” was a special 10-day sale which began on Nov. 17. As of that date, Franklin Music lowered its selling price on the $5.98 list LP from $3.99 to $2.79/$3.79 tape. However, as Rubin pointed out, his store had been moving 90-100 units of the album per week even at $3.99. And Durham noted that “we had sold out of it numerous times (before the latest sale), but now it's doing even better.” Durham explained how the decision had been made to lower his store’s price on the A&M version of “Nadia’s Theme.” “We had that and the Arista (solo version by Barry DeVorzon) at $3.99 on the same rack just to see which would move better. And it showed up that the A&M one was stronger, so we went in heavy on it.” Durham cited in-store play as one of the major factors in the album’s current success at the Perimeter Mall location. “Besides the single, the rest of the songs on the album are pretty good, too. And it just moves out real well. I put it on last week when we had good adult traffic in the store. Well, I sold five copies — it was just like blinking my eyes.” What kinds of customers are buying this album? “Straight WASP’S,” Durham answered without hesitation. “Strictly your adult ‘easy-listening’ (fan) and young teens. They’re all clean-cut all-Americans: girls from 14 to 18 (years old), and above that, suburban housewives and so on. Your prime example is the people who listen to AM pop radio.” Ampex Releases 2nd Qtr. Stats REDWOOD CITY, CA. — Ampex Corpora- tion reported net earnings of $2.8 million for the second quarter ended October 30, a declinefrom last year’s second quarter ear- nings of $3.6 million. However, last year’s second quarter included a $2.4 million pre- tax gain from the sale of a facility. Increase Ampex’s second quarter sales increased from $66 million in 1975 to $74 million this year, a 12% gain. For the six month period ended October 30, Ampex reported earn- ings of $4.6 million, compared with $5.2 million for 1975, a figure inflated by the facility sale. Ampex net sales for the six month period rose to $139.3 million, from $129.7 last year. ALBUM REVIEWS HEJIRA — Joni Mitchell — Asylum 7E-1087 — Producer: Henry Lewy — List: 6.98 Joni Mitchell's latest work is more of the same. There’s no real surprises here — the same ethereal melodies, sensitive lyrics. The production is effectively spare, and she has at times a real bite to her vocals; she’s playing around with phrasing a little more. All of the cuts will doubtless be played heavy on FM progressives. “Black Crow,” an uptempo tune with a lot of life to it, could get some AM pop spins. A STAR IS BORN — Barbra Streisand, Kris Kristofferson — Columbia JS 34403 — Producers: Barbra Streisand, Phil Ramone — List: 7.98 The soundtrack from the upcoming film of the same name, this is sure to be a big album for some time to come. The marriage of the two voices is not without a special magic: Kristofferson’s gruff vocals mix well with Streisand’s sweet ones on tunes like “Lost Inside Of You.” If the movie is half as good as the record, this should be a real blockbuster, appealing to vir- tually all markets. THE BEACH BOYS ’69 — The Beach Boys — Capitol ST- 11584 — Producers: The Beach Boys — List: 6.98 Although virtually all of these tunes are available in previous incarnations, this is a live set, and none of the tunes is without a new twist. “Bluebirds Over The Mountain,” for example, is given a powerful reading, and those harmonies are just what you’d ex- pect them to be. Listen for this live version of “Good Vibrations” to stir upcoming FM waves, and there are a lot of singles possibilities here, maybe a re-release of “God Only Knows” or “Aren’t You Glad.” THE HUSTLE AND THE BEST OF VAN McCOY — Van McCoy — H&L HL-69016 — Producer: Van McCoy — List: 6.98 This package is just what the title indicates — some of the best disco around; indeed, a couple of the tunes gave the new genre a real boost at its inception. Along with “The Hustle” McCoy gives us “Disco Baby” and “Disco Kid.” A great package for the winter selling season, this is also an indispensable aid for any disco programmer. There’s also a terrific version of “Theme From Star Trek” where Van really lets loose. THE BEST OF THE CRUSADERS — The Crusaders — Blue Thumb/ABC BTSY-6027/2 — Producers: Stewart Levine with The Crusaders — List: 7.98 The Crusaders are really remarkable musicians — each can work as many sessions as he likes; however, when they play together, there’s a unique group magic. These two disks have been assembled from the five previous LPs, and there’s a lotfor any jazz, R&B or progressive programmer to choose from. With this package available, the catalog should move along with it, and The Crusaders will assume a rightful share of record sales. HEARD YA MISSED ME, WELL I’M BACK — Sly & The Family Stone — Epic PE 34348 — Producer: Sly Stone & Sylvester Stewart — List: 6.98 Splitting the production credit with himself, Sly Stone has made a successful return to the recording arena. The songs here are extensions of where he left off— smartly arranged funk and R&B, with a smattering of jazz and pop influence that’s sure to cross this over onto a couple of charts. The title cut is filled with melody; the tune is fresh. “Nothing Less Than Happiness” seems like a great singles choice, along with the poignant “Family Again.” WAYLON LIVE — Waylon Jennings — RCA APL 1-1108 Producers: Waylon Jennings & Ray Pennington — List: 6.98 What with the tremendous recent acceptance of “outlaw” country music in the pop scene, this live Waylon Jennings album should get across-the-board play and sales. Other writers represented are Kris Kristofferson, Willie Nelson and Jimmie Rodgers’ “T For Texas.” The band is in fine form, with steel ace Ralph Mooney supplying perfect counterpoint to Waylon’s choppy, hook-filled lead work. Display in retail outlets is a must. LET ’EM IN — Billy Paul — Philly Int’l./CBS PZ 34389 — Pro- ducers: Various — List: 6.98 Taking the title from the cut penned and recently sung by Paul McCartney, Billy Paul shines in this attractive package which was overseen by Gamble and Huff. The style of the LP is inherent in “Let 'Em In”; Paul’s high, sweet vocal accentuates certain phrases to highlight nuances that you never thought ex- isted before. “I Trust You” by Gamble and Huff is a killer, with obvious, attractive hooks that could cross this one pop. WHERE WILL YOU GO WHEN THE PARTY’S OVER — Archie Bell & The Drells — Philly Int’l./CBS PZ 34323 — Producers: Various List: 6.98 Archie Bell & The Drells have come up with another album of solid funk cuts, recorded (where else?) at Sigma Sound. The single “Nothing Comes Easy” is included, and there are other cuts, most notably the title track, that could easily have singles success. R&B programmers could safely choose anything here. Disco jocks will pick up on “I Bet I Can Do That Dance You’re Doin’ .” SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE! — The Not Ready For Prime Time Players — Arista 4107 — Producer: Michael O’Donoghue — List: 6.98 A comedy album, this contains many of the highlights of the first couple of seasons of NBC’s popular late night show. Danny Ackroyd does an imitation of our next president and the three women in the cast provide a f ifty-ish homage to Chevy Chase — besides being hilarious, the music is really good. Progressive programmers should put this one in the front of their comedy bins and use it often. Retailers should display — this is a perfect item for the season. THE JAMES MONTGOMERY BAND — James Montgomery Band — Island ILPS 9419 — Producers: Allan Toussaint, Marshall Sehorn — List: 6.98 A renovated James Montgomery leads his new, capable band through an album of funk and blues produced brilliantly by Allan T oussaint and Marshall Sehorn. This stuff is a lot better than the records a lot of more famous groups are churning out: it has style, wit and substance. “City Music” is a powerhouse cut that should get a lot of FM exposure — Montgomery’s harp play and singing is first rate throughout. no:S JOHN HAMMOND: SOLO — John Hammond —- Vanguard VSD 79280 — Producer: Maynard Solomon — List: 6.98 John Hammond is one of the best blues singers and players in America today, and on this album (recorded live) is hard evidence. He takes tunes by Muddy Waters, Robert Johnson, Elmore James, and the like, and infuses them with soulful, frenetic slide work and aching, right-on-target vocals. In-store play is mandatory for this artist; although Hammond’s been around for quite some time this is his finest album in years. SWEET BIRD — Lani Hall — A&M SP 4617 — Producer: Herb Alpert — List: 6.98 This album is worth the purchase price alone for its definitive version of “Send In The Clowns.” Stanley Clarke, one of the world’s great bass players, is ultimately sensitive to both the needs of the tune and Hall’s vocals. In an album well produced by Herb Alpert, Hall does eight other tunes with equal flair, in- cluding Joni Mitchell’s “Sweet Bird” and Michael Franks’ “Mr. Blue.” This is a case of carefully chosen material; all of these would be right for FM play; “Send In The Clowns” could get some top 40 spins. MELODY MAKER — Hugh Masekela — Casablanca NBLP- 7036 — Producers: Hugh Masekela & Stewart Levine — List: 6.98 Masekela delivers some smooth disco-jazz numbers, high- lighted, of course, by his fine horn work and well-arranged backing instruments and vocals. There's an imaginative, hook- filled version of "The Best Of My Love,” along with some mellow pieces suitable for jazz and progressive radio. There’s a real latin flavor here that cuts through even the most standard disco arrangements. A pleasing album, this should show up fast on pop and R&B sales charts. CHORDS OF FAME — Phil Ochs — A&M SP-4599 — Producers: Various — List: 6.98 This is a bargain two-pocket set that’s made up of the best stuff that Phil Ochs ever recorded. “I Ain’t Marchin’ Anymore” is given a fine electric reading, and the tunes progress logically to his last single for A&M — “Here’s To The State Of Richard Nixon.” With thoughtful liner notes by Ed Sanders and the vast body of work included, this should be a heavy seller for Christmas and for future catalog sales. TERRY CASHMAN — Terry Cashman — Lifesong LS6006 — Producers: Terry Cashman & Tommy West — List: 6.98 A slick pop album, this solo effort by Cashman should find a quick home in many markets. The tunes are, without fail, plea- sant to listen to, with good lyrics and production. There are a couple of AM singles shots, as well as MOR and FM possibilities. Look for "Baby, Baby I Love You” to get play on both bands, and “We’ll Be T ogether,” a beautiful ballad, to get concentrated FM spins. Henry Gross lends a hand on electric guitars and gives the record extra spark. ' Cash Box/December 4, 1976 25

On Jazz The joy of jazz was never more evident than at Carnegie Hall (20) for the Woody Herman 40th Anniversary Concert. Graduates of what one commentator called "the college of Woody” were heavily on dis- play: Flip Phillips, Chubby Jackson, Don Lamond, Billy Bauer, Sam Marowitz and Ralph Burns from the First Herd; Zoot Sims, Al Cohn, Stan Getz from the Second Herd; Nat Pierce, Phil Wilson and Jake Hanna from the Thundering Herd of 1963. Phillips was given more space than any of the early Herdsmen and he responded with some excellent tenor playing. He scored heavily on “Apple Honey,” “Sweet and Lovely” and the closer, “Caledonia.” Pete Candoli popped up for a brief duet with brother Conte and also contributed mightily when the audience called for high note trumpet. Phil Wilson on “Bijou" and Jim Pugh (“Everywhere”) saluted the late Bill Harris with some trombone solos. A highlight of the Second Herd portion occurred during the playing of “Four Brothers” when a gent in the front row start- ed dropping money in front of Getz, Sims, Cohn and Jimmy Giuffre. When Woody took the mike and asked “where are the hundreds?” the same fan responded — with hundred dollar bills! Zoot was very cool about scooping up the loot. The second half of the concert was devoted to the current band except for a pair of Getz specials. The entire cast assembled for a rousing finale to cap what was certainly one of the most exhilarating evenings of jazz in some time. Music Minus One has the first two Steeplechase LPs ready. Joe Albany and Horace Parian are the artists. The flow should increase and we can look forward to about three per week, according to Irv Kratka. Atlantic has signed trumpeter Don Cherry. Also on the Atlantic scene, Herbie Mann recorded in Germany with some members of Silver Convention. Columbia has announced the signing of Dexter Gordon. This is a bold step for Columbia, whose roster of jazz artists has been heavily weighted with crossover acts in recent years. Dexter, on the other hand, has been greeted with an outpouring of love and affection from his many fans during re- cent New York appearances. He has gar- nered more press than any other modern jazz act in recent memory during this latest tour. Big Joe Turner and pianist Lloyd Glenn have been a big success at the Cookery in New York. The sixty-five year old Turner still has strong pipes and, as owner Barney Josephson stated in a recent interview, “If we left the doors open, you could hear him a block away — without a mike.” Sarah Vaughn’s first Atlantic LP is being recorded on the west coast and will consist of all Beatles songs. CTI is ready with a new Grover continued on pg. 51 Rich To Perform At IRTS Holiday Show NEW YORK — Jazz drummer Buddy Rich and his group Killer Force will perform at the International Radio and Television So- ciety’s annual holiday show, hosted this year by New York jazz radio station WRVR. The show will begin at noon, December 9, at the Americana Hotel in Manhattan, with funds to be donated to the Bedside network. JazzAlbumPicks HUMMIN’ — Nat Adderley — Little David 1012 — Producer: Nat Adderley — list: 6.98 This is the first jazz LP from Little David and Nat’s first LP with his new band. It is a thoroughly contemporary set with plenty of space for im- provisation over a funky, percussive backdrop. There is good variety in the program, with reed- man John Stubblefield and pianist Onaje Allen Gumbs contributing originals in addition to the leader. Of particular interest are the title track and an intriguing version of “Theme From M*A*S*H.” There should be strong airplay potential for this album. J\jatyjddenlei{ o MISTER B. AND THE BAND — Billy Ekstine — Savoy/Arista 2214 — List; 7:98 This double-album compilation of 1945-47 sides has just about everything. This package contains some live perfor- mances with a splendid rhythm section (Wynton Kelly, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb) and some studio sessions by the same group. Completing the set are a pair of meetings with organist Jimmy Smith. Apart from the always stimulating playing the set is valuable for a display of Wes and co- horts in a straight ahead context for what ulti- mately proved to be the last time. Four of these performances had sweetened overdubs the first time around and Verve has decided to delete the trimmings in this package. An excellent decision. Cash Box/December 4, 1976 37

TALENTON STAGE ... - tj VEST— TAKING WALKS ON THE WILD SIDE — were two of rock n' roll's most popular spokesmen, who both dropped by to visit Cash Box last week. Lou Reed, along a ; members of his band, came by to chat between dates at the Santa Monica Civic and r poxy and told us that being with Arista Records has given him a whole new lease on fe Said Reed, "It had gotten to the point where I didn’t know if I wanted to make albums an v more, and when I got the opportunity to go with Clive I didn’t think twice about it. "As ;d left the offices, he ran into Ted Nugent in the lobby and the two struck up a lively con- sation about the technical aspects of some new guitars and shared anecdotes of life on the road. Nugent, it turned out, had dropped by to present David Budge with a gold record for his "Ted Nugent" LP. Nugent's Forum date last Wednesday (12/1 ) proved to be one of the year’s most raucous rock ’n' roll celebrations. However, beneath his demonic exterior, Nugent revealed himself to be a family man at heart: “ I only go out on the road for a few dates at a time. Otherwise I'd go crazy. After being on the road fora while I really appreciate getting home to my wife, baby daughter, and newborn baby boy." It looks like there's more than one rock ’n’ roll heart on the scene today . . . CHRISTMAS TULL — Chrysalis has released a limited edition of four previously un- released Christmas songs by Jethro Tull. The LP was sent to AOR programmers and will not be available commercially . . . The Odyssey Records chain has named The Chieftains as best group of the year . . The newAndrew Lloyd Weber and Tim Riceopera, “Evita,” is scheduled fora mid-January North American release by MCA. Mike Smith (ex-Dave Clark Five) and Mike d’Abo (ex-Manfred Mann) are among the artists featured on the record . . . Grace Slick and Skip Johnson were married on November 29, on a Maui beach at sunset. A traditional Hawaiian trio played the Hawaiian Wedding Song: after the ceremony, the festivities adjourned to a local disco where Pete Sears and John Barbata entertained with their own music . . . Thanksgiving was a good time at The Troubadour, with a lot of sur- prises for headliner Guy Clark. Some of The Hot Band showed up, along with Mickey Raphael, Dolly Parton, Susanna Clark, Rusty Wierand Nicolette Larsen- Levy (who sings with Commander Cody) . . . ’TIS THE SEASON TO BE SIGNING — The Big Wha-Koo signed with ABC, having just finished an LP with Roy Halee producing . . . Split Enz pacted with Chrysalis . . . Per- cussionist Bill Summers has signed with Prestige Records: his first LP, “Peel The Heat,” due in January, with guest appearances by Alphonse Mouzon, Paul Jackson, Charlie Meeks, Ray Obiedo and Mark Soskin . . . UA has inked British singer Adam Faith. Faith producing credits include Leo Sayer and Roger Daltrey, as well has a solid performing background in the early sixties. He appeared in Stardust, a film, with compatriot David Essex. . .MCA has inked Fresh; the group’s debut, “Get Fresh," will appear in January . . . Stallion, a five-piece Denver band, has signed with Casablanca Record and Filmworks . . . Lakeside, a nine-member group from Ohio that has been opening for the likes of Roberta Flack and James Brown recently in the northwest, will record for ABC Records, with an album due around the first of the year . . . GUEST APPEARANCE by Dusty Springfield, the first in a long while, with Labelle at Oakland’s Paramount Theatre . . . Neil Young and Ron Wood, on the other hand, did not sit in with Lou Reed at The Roxy, even though they seemed to enjoy the show . . . When Eric Clapton joined The Band on stage at Winterland, Robbie Robertson could be heard yelling “Come on!" at his friend, who accordingly stepped up the pace of his solo . . . REEL TO REEL — Jose Feliciano in at Cherokee, overdubbing and mixdowns. Jerry Wexler was in producing Bob Crewe for Elektra. Hollywood Stars are finishing up an album with Harry Maslin producing. Mike Curb and Mike Lloyd just completed the LP for Hero, an L.A. group on Mercury . . . Don McLean slated to write two original songs for Paramount Pic- tures’ upcoming “Fraternity Row.” The songs will be in the fifties mold . . . Thin Lizzy’s Brian Robertson severed an artery in his left hand just before he was to leave London fora U.S. Lizzy tour. The injury is not supposed to be serious, but Robertson will not be able to play the guitar for a month. The dates have been postponed until January . . . TAKE THE MONEY AND RUN — Steve Miller took his own advice and bought a ranch in Oregon: he’s building a $300,000 studio there. It’s a working ranch, with cows, chickens, goats, 26 horses and a barn. “I’ll have everything I need," Miller declared, “my animals, my hay, my studio. ” . . . “Friday With Frank,” a radio show devoted exclusively to the music of Frank Sinatra, just celebrated its 20th anniversary on WWDB in Philadelphia. Nov. 26 marked the 1,040th four-hour show; during that time, it’s reported, 41,600 Sinatra selec- tions have been aired . . . Stix Hooper and Joe Sample of The Crusaders appeared December 4 on the “Toys For Tots” telethon . . . Pure Prairie League will appear on the Dolly Parton television show . . . Bette Midler will sing the lead role Annie in a revival of “The Seven Deadly Sins, ” to be staged by George Balanchine for the New York City Ballet . . . John Mayall’s Nov. 23-24 Roxy gigs were recorded by Straight Ahead Sound’s mobile studio for his first “Live" LP for ABC . . . Al Kooper has set tour dates in support of his current “Act Like Nothing’s Wrong" LP. Three nights at New York’s Bottom Line are scheduled for the middle of this month; Kooper will hit The Roxy on January 5 . . . john mankiewicz EAST COASTINGS — How does success change a person’s life? Bruce Springsteen says his butler puts on his socks every morning, but doesn’t touch his sneakers, never his sneakers. Springsteen was guest forum leader at a unique after-hours college course called “The Making Of Superstars," given by Bob Spitz at the New School in downtown Manhattan. The visit was sort of an unexpected surprise to most of the people involved, and Springsteen spoke honestly on a number of subjects, never losing his sense of humor. He told the group that he has always wanted to marry Ronee Spector, and had such a crush on her that he would become transfixed by the sight of one of her records spinning on his turntable. Rock and roll records, he exclaimed, were meant to hit you straight on, not to “ping pong " in a confusion of hopping stereo channels. Would he ever work with Phil Spector? Only a possibility. Getting to the heart of Americana, Springsteen lashed out against oversized ham- burgers, claiming that the thinner variety, like MacDonald’s, were “where it’s at." Asked what he would have done had he not chosen the road to rock stardom, he said the number one alternative would have been baseball. BON VOYAGE — Many thanks to all who came by to toast the westward bound Gary Cohen. A list of visitors, as far as we remember, would include (in no particularly logicalor- der): hamish stuart, jim jeffries, carol strauss, margo knesz, barbara pepe, noel love, mitch kanner, judy libow, tuc eerim, irv biegel, ira heilicher, herbie corsack, dave morrell, bob small, larry king, howard rosen, beth rosengard, sheila schlanda, gunter hauer, lynn keller- man, art collins, larry herman, mike shavelson, kathy rowe, Steve leeds, donna sheets, susan wax, gail blackston, bill Swearingen, rick gale, bob sherwood. RICK SAYS YES — Speaking from Montreux, Switzerland, Yes’ manager Brian Lane has revealed the unexpected news that keyboard player Rick Wakeman will rejoin the band for touring and recording, while their keyboardist of two and one-half years, Patrick Moraz, has left the group for musical reasons to pursue a solo career. Wakeman will work with Yes (continued on page 45) The Band Dances Their Last Waltz; Bids Farewll Along With Friends WINTERLAND, SAN FRANCISCO — The whole thing sounded impossible. Thanks- giving dinner for five thousand people, waltzing to a full orchestra, The Band, plus more guest artists than you could remem- ber, all directed and captured on film by Martin Scorcese, a top-flight Hollywood (“Taxi Driver,” “Mean Streets”) filmmaker. Instead of riotous confusion, what emerged from all this will probably go down as the most exciting and well-organized event in pop music history. The dinner and waltzing worked fine. At 9:30, The Band kicked it off on a stage set with borrowed chandeliers and backdrops from “La Traviata.” Picking their most re- quested tune for the opener, “Cripple Creek” set the tone for a high-powered 90- minute set. For the last live concert, The Band played like never before. Often, critics have lambasted the quintet for play- ing “just like the record”; here, there were new solos (particularly from Robbie Robertson), newly phrased vocal lines — this is the last time, they seemed to feel, and we’re going to get it all said. “Wheels Of Fire” was played with a real vengeance; Robertson took a few extra bars on his solo and bassist Rick Danko supplied the essen- tial rhythm, as well as accentuating the melody with well-placed fills. This was, however, just the beginning. The band started calling on guests. Ronnie Hawkins (who fronted The Band when they were called The Hawks) came on for a rous- ing “Who Do You Love.” Hawkins strolled off the stage after the one tune, and Richard Manuel (The Band’s piano player) moved over to the second drum kit to make room for Dr. John, who slid into a jump-styled version of “Such A Night,” with The Band accompanying him like they’d been behind the Doctor for years. Indeed, this was one of the most startling aspects of the show. As the guests paraded on and off the stage for their short sets, it became clear that each member of The Band could adapt to wildly different styles — whether it was Muddy Waters’ blues or Joni Mitchell’s nebulous jazz melodies — it all worked. Paul Butterfield, Eric Clapton and Muddy Waters played some blues. Often, these superstar jams turn out to be soulless af- fairs — not so with The Band. Waters’ ex- tended version of “Caledonia” was packed with emotion, and Robertson traded some Jackson Browne/Orleans THE SHRINE, L.A. — Jackson Browne put the finishing touches on his current nation- wide tour here recently with a magically sensitive evening that went a long way toward further entrenching him as the premier musical troubadour of the ques- tioning 70s. Playing before an adoring, sell-out audience who cheered his every em- barrassed, boyish smile, Browne and band employed their golden California sound through a highly reputable retrospective of the singer/songwriter’s entire repertoire. While touching only slightly on his first two albums (“Doctor My Eyes” was in- cluded in the encore), Browne concen- trated on what many have called his finest, most cohesive LP, “Late For The Sky.” Every track from this album was played at one time or another throughout the eve- ning. Particularly soothing was a haunting “For A Dancer” duet featuring Browne on piano and David Lindiey on violin. Material culled from his current album, “The Pretender” (bulleted this week at #7 in Cash Box) included concert opener "The Fuse” and closer “The Pretender.” The new songs, echoing the same questioning vul- nerability as the bulk of his earlier work, (continued on page 45) great lines with Butterfield’s harp. Clapton sang “All Our Past Times,” co-written with Rick Danko. Neil Young played a loose “Helpless” and “Four Strong Winds”; Joni Mitchell played a fairly lackluster set of tunes from her new LP. It was Van Morrison who brought the house down with “Tura Lura.” Aided by The Band’s horn section (led by the versatile Howard Johnson), Morrison kicked into the tune, playing off the funky rhythm, in total control of the song and the audience. After Morrison, The Band played a cou- ple of tunes by themselves, aided only by the backing vocals of Neil Young and Joni Mitchell on the beautiful “Acadian Drift- wood.” Finally, at 12:30, Robertson an- nounced a 20-minute intermission. Bay area poets filled up the time with readings that ranged in quality from Sweet William’s ode to the Hell's Angels to Lawrence Ferlin- ghetti’s fine parody of The Lord’s Prayer. After the break, The Band turned in a fresh reading of “The Weight” and debuted a tune for the occasion, “The Last Waltz” (more interesting in spirit than substance). Robertson then introduced “a very good friend of ours," and Bob Dylan hit the stage, already strumming his Fender before he at- tacked the microphone for a slightly re- worked version of “Baby Let Me Follow You Down,” a tune from his first LP that had been one of the first to be electrified by The Band. Not stopping between songs, Dylan segued into three other songs, one (“I Don’t Believe You”) circa 1966 and two from the Planet Waves LP. The entire cast then assembled for an emotional reading of “I Shall Be Released,” with Ringo Starr and Ron Wood helping out on drums and guitar. Officially, this was the last tune of the night. Levon Helm and Ringo Starr, how- ever, had better ideas and they set up an irresistible rhythm that, like a magnet, drew the bulk of the players back on stage for some improvised riffing. The jam lasted for another frenetic hour; Eric Clapton chose this time to really step out, casually picking out searing funk leads to rhythm work laid down by the guitars of Neil Young, Robbie Robertson, and Dr. John. Robertson, not to be outdone, answered back in kind. After almost six solid hours of music, The Band and friends stepped off the stage; The Last Waltz was over. The Band had retired with extraordinary class. j.m. New York Philharmonic with Rafael Kubelik AVERY FISHER HALL, NYC — In the last of four performances of a program that was recently aired on national public tele- vision, the New York Philharmonic under Rafael Kubelik's direction showed why it is considered one of the world’s great or- chestras. At the same time, leading rendi- tions of works by Beethoven and Dvorak, the guest conductor demonstrated his forceful command and deep understand- ing of the music. Kubelik set just the right pace in Beetho- ven’s Egrnont Overture. Especially notable j here was the perfect balance between up- per and lower strings, the seemingly inex- orable expansion of the little second theme into a sonic storm, and the swiftly building excitement from the caesura j ust before the coda to the end of the work. The soloist for the evening’s perfor- mance of Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 3 was Claudio Arrau. In keeping with the pianist’s unusually romantic (by modern standards) style, Kubelik set a fairly slow tempo in the first movement's orchestral exposition, and drew a little extra rubato from the woodwinds. I JtlbumPicks l;PS’ HEAD — Flip Phillips — Choice 1013 — cei . Gerry McDonald — List: 6.98 a sleeper this is! Phillips, one of the major a the 1940s and ’50s is playing better than ever yet this is his first LP in more than a decade. Adding bass clarinet to his always impressive tenor he has fashioned an LP of superlative mainstream jazz. Whether it be mature balladry or up-tempo swingers, Flip demonstrates that he has lost nothing to the years. The program is heavy with standards but there are recent tunes mixed with old favorites and none is less impressive than the others. CHICK COREA—HERBIE HANCOCK— KEITH JARRETT—McCOY TYNER — Atlantic 1696 — List: 6.98 Two apiece by each of the major piano figures of the 1960s. Apart from the Tyner pair, “Lazy Bird” and “In Your Own Sweet Way," which are new, the material has been issued previously on Vortex or Embryo. With the exception of the Hancock titles (actually Ron Carter’s date) these performances are among the earliest work of each pianist. Consider- ing the very different direction taken by each man this is a fascinating return to the beginning when all were sidemen in bands led by others and (with the exception of Hancock) were still feeling their way in the music world. THE COMPLETE BENNY GOODMAN: VOLUME 4 — Bluebird AXM 2-5537 — List: 7.98 Producer Frank Driggs and annotator Mort Goode continue their marvellous documentary of the “king of swing” when he was at the apex of his popularity. This volume stretches from 12/30/36 to 10/22/37, documents the earliest alignment of Harry James with the Goodman band and also con- tains some splendid quartet items. But certainly the highlight of the collection is the original version of “Sing, Sing, Sing.” As Bluebird continues its chronology of the great bands of the swing era the momentum of the label should pick up con- siderably. This set should be attractive to older fans. THE VERVE YEARS (1950-1951) — Charlie Parker — Verve VE 2-2512 — List: 7.98 The first two sides are string sessions for the most part. Included are sometitles previously available in a JATP set. The last two sides combine small bop ensembles with some Latin material. While not the definitive Parker, this is still the master jazz creator in top form. The string titles are among the most listenable Parker performances for the layman and the bop titles demonstrate that Parker (in “Au Privave” and “K.C. Blues” especially) was able to create instant classics even into the 1950s. RED BEANS-JIMMY McGRIFF — Groove Merchant 3314 — Producer: Sonny Lester — List: 6.98 McGriff’s last outing (“Mean Machine”) was a solid hit and this album treads in similar territory. The Lance Quinn/Brad Baker arranging team is here once again and the Brecker Brothers add con- siderably to the proceeding (Mike has a peach of a tenor solo on the title track). McGriff is into four dif- ferent keyboards and the music has that disco- crossover feel to it. This one should be a good bet for the Cash Box jazz chart. LOUiS BELLSON’S 7 — Concord CJ25 — Producer: Carl Jefferson — List: 6.98 The Concord Summer Jazz Festival is the occa- sion for many of the LPs on this fine California label. While initially it may seem that seven pieces is a bit of a comedown from Bellson’s customary big band, this group, recorded at the festival, is a refreshing blast from right now. Stickout soloists are reedman Pete Christlieb and trumpet vet Blue Mitchell. Louis himself boots everything along with his vital drumm- ing and the results are a celebration of the modern mainstream. JazzAlbumPicks THE WORLD OF DUKE ELLINGTON VOLUME 3 — Columbia 33961 — List: 7.98 This set continues to fill gaps in Ellington’s Columbia dis- cography, concentrating as it does on material not available in other Ellington collections. This is the ’50s band and there is a good deal of previously unissued material. Outstanding among the selections are “Cop Out,” “Smada” and “The Sky Fell Down.” Certainly a must for Ellington fans. WILSON — THAT’S ALL — Phil Wilson — Famous Door 109 — Producer: Harry Lim — List: 7.98 This hard-to-find label has been producing excellent jazz IPs for the past few years. Wilson is given space to prove that he is certainly among the finest trombonists working today. A star of Woody Herman’s Herd circa 1963, Wilson spends most of his time teaching in Boston. Supported by a small band including Al Cohn and John Bunch, he displays extraordinary facility and feeling in an album that should be the talk of the town for trombonists. HELLO REV — Bill Berry Big Band — Concord 27 — Producer: Carl Jefferson— List: 6.98 This is a roaring big band comprised of LA studio players all of whom are familiar with large ensemble playing. There is a heavily Ellington tone to the program but there is no attempt to imitate. With stalwarts such as Blue Mitchell, Cat Anderson, Jack Sheldon, Jimmy Cleveland, Marshall Royal, Richie Kamuca and Dave Frishberg around, that is unnecessary. Ex- cellent recording and excellent music and another winner for Concord! GRANDPAWS — Jimmy Rowles — Choice 1014 — Producer: Gerry McDonald — List: 6.98 Rowles is a cutie. He gave up Hollywood studio work a few years ago to work New York clubs and play jazz. He has recor- ded frequently in recent years but it is unlikely that anything compares with his graceful wit and lyricism displayed on this disk. In addition to superb ballads (“Blood Count/Isn’t It Romantic,”) he sings an original, “Jam Face,” about a jazz dig- ging tennis star, in a voice that is effective while defying categorization. An outstanding effort all around. STRAIGHT AHEAD — Eddie “Lockjaw” Davis — Pablo 2310778 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 7.98 This is the very best Lockjaw in some time. Supported by Tommy Flanagan’s trio, he stretches out on nine tunes and emphasizes good standards for the most part. There is a vis- cerality in his playing that is timeless in origin but that always gets the message across. If strong virile tenor sax is the subject of discussion, Lockjaw will be among the first names mentioned. CARTER, GILLESPIe INC. — Benny Carter-Dizzy Gillespie — Pablo 2310781 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 7.98 Dizzy and Benny may seem an unlikely team but everything works on this album. The material contains pieces from each leader as well as a couple of standards and a Gospel tune (sung by drummer Mickey Roker). The grace and elegance of Carter is neatly balanced by the fire of Gillespie and for added significance Joe Pass and Tommy Flanagan make telling contributions. THE COMPLETE GLENN MILLER VOLUME 3 — Bluebird 5534 — List: 7.98 More nostalgia from Bluebird. This double record set con- tinues the documentation of the Miller orchestra from late 1939 and early 1940. While the jazz content of the band was minimal, Miller emphasized gorgeous arrangements (his own “Star- dust” is here) and a presentation of popular dance music that is simply better than any other band’s. Marion Hutton and Ray Eberleget most of the vocals and Clyde Hurley and Tex Beneke most of the solos. NOW’S THE TIME — Billy Mitchell — Catalyst 7611 — Producers: John Rowland & Billy Mitchell — List: 6.98 The former Basie and Gillespie tenor man fronts a small band recorded live in a Long Island club earlier this year. This is relaxed jamming with a firm functional rhythm section that allows the saxophonist (he also features alto and soprano) to stretch out on three originals and a groovy version of Charlie Parker’s title track. The sound is a bit muffled but the enthusiasm of the players (including Roland Prince and Earl May) comes through unobstructed. BOSS OF THE BASS — John Kirby — Columbia 33557 — List: 7.98 Kirby died in 1952 at the age of 43 so his name will not be familiar to many younger fans, but as an instrumentalist and combo leader (especially) he was a popular figure of the 1 930s. The collection is panoramic in that the first two sides feature Kirby as a sideman with various bands and combos (Lucky Mil- linder, Maxine Sullivan, Mildred Bailey) while the last two cover his famous sextet with Charlie Shavers, Buster Bailey and com- pany. It’s What You Value/Cracker Box Palace — George Harrison — Dark Horse/WB Simon BREflhs Drew Hands WRKO, 99XTape Of Springsteen’s Xmas Tune by J.B Carmicle LOS ANGELES — Although Columbia Records is unable to release any further Bruce Springsteen product because of legal ramifications, two RKO radio stations — WRKO in Boston and WXLO (99X) in New York — have added a live concert tape of Springsteen’s “Santa Claus Is Coming To Town" to their playlists. The tape, from a live performance Springsteen did in Boston just before Christmas last year, according to one source, was supplied to the two sta- tions by Paul Drew, vice president of programming for the RKO chain. Drew revealed to. Cash Box that he received the tape from Springsteen. 99X MD Joe Per- seck told Cash Box “phones are beginning to build on the novelty 'tern,” while WRKO MD Carol Singer added, “If it was a record and it was racked it would certainly sell in Boston.” Although the two RKO stations were playing the Springsteen tape, Stan Mon- teiro, Columbia Records vice president of Garland to PD WRKO Radio LOS ANGELES — Cash Box has learn- ed that CKLW program director Les Garland has resigned that position to become the PD of WRKO in Boston. Garland said he will make the move to Boston after January 1, 1977. Garland had been at CKLW for the past 1 1/2 years, having worked at WAVZ, New Haven and K100, Los Angeles before that. KIIS’ Charlie Tuna Resigns PD Position LOS ANGELES — Charlie Tuna, program director of KIIS, Los Angeles for the last two years, has resigned that position but will remain with the station doing his morning drive show. Tuna, who informed Cash Bc»o that there was absolutely no pressure from his family or station management to resign, cited long work hours and “diminished enthusiasm" for each job, since both re- quired his complete attention, as the reasons for his resignation as program director. “I owed it to myself and the station to give up one," Tuna reflected. “I guess I'm an air personality first and that's where I've decided to stay.” national promotion said there was “no problem” as far as Columbia is concerned. “We cannot release a record by Bruce Springsteen but we will furnish stations with a copy of the tape if they request it.” First Station 99X premiered the tape Friday, Dec. 3, after WRKO became the first station in the country to air the tape on Dec. 1. According to Carol Singer, Paul Drew had authorized her to play the tape on WRKO. Singer also noted that “Santa Claus Is Coming To Town" is charted at #28 on the station’s sur- vey this week. RKO national music coordinator Christy Wright, who said that RKO has no plans to play the tape on any of its other stations, ex- plained that New York and Boston are both markets in which Springsteen appeal has been strong in the past. Bennett Exits WNOE LOS ANGELES — Buzz Bennett has exited the program directorship of WNOE-AM, New Orleans, according to Eric Anderson, vice president and general manager of the station. Bennett has announced no future plans. Bennett, who had been at WNOE-AM for the last six months, had been asked by An- derson to program the station through the last ratings book, when former PD E. Aivin Davis left in September to go to WSAI, Cincinnati. KPOL-FM Switches To AOR Contemp. Format LOS ANGELES — KPOL-FM, an L.A. sta- tion that has programmed “beautiful music” since 1957, changed its format to “adult contemporary music” on November 22, according to Peter Newell, general manager of KPOL AM/FM. KPOL-AM will continue to program its beautiful music for- mat, but KPOL-FM, because of its format switch, will now be known as 94-FM, New P.D. Rodger Layng, formerly of KCBS-FM in San Francisco, joins the station as the new program director and Nancy Trabish, for- merly music director at Los Angeles’ K100, assumes the same position at KPOL.-FM. Newell also noted that Caron Brenner, another new addition to the station’s staff, will be handling the 3 pm-12 am airshift. Changes at WKTO (13Q), Pittsburgh. Ray Zoller promoted from jock to PD. He replaced Dennis Waters, who exits the sta- tion. Also, Jo Jo Kincaid joins the air lineup as 8-12 pm jock. Rick Donohue has been promoted from music director to PD at WZZM (Z-96), Grand Rapids. C4SHBOX R&B wMtmk Sonderling Plans Mass Appeal Jazz Format At WRVR by Cookie Amerson LOS ANGELES — The Sonderling Corp. has hired Dennis Waters as program direc- tor of WRVR in New York. Waters had been program director at 13Q in Pittsburgh for the past several years, and has an excellent reputation as one of the top research- oriented programmers in the country. Ef- fective December 27, Waters will begin at the station to initiate the changes in the for- mat. Mack Allen, national program director for the Sonderling chain, told CB, “We will initially sound out the marketplace, and in- stitute a carefully calculated rotation system.” All Forms Of Jazz Allen also stated, “The jazz library at WRVR is the most extensive I have ever seen. Because of its tremendous content, we have plans of putting the cataloging system on computer, so that all product can more or less be at our fingertips. Since the library must contain practically every piece of jazz product recorded, we will have all forms of jazz product within reach for our audience.” Research Waters explained, “We are planning the most extensive research ever for a jazz sta- tion, to gain as many listeners as possible. WRVR will be the first mass appeal jazz for- mated station in the country.” In elaborat- ing, Waters said, “The station has been designed for the jazz purist, but it is difficult for me to believe that only jazz purists listen to the station, and with this idea in mind ! feel we will be very successful in the New York market with the format we are plann- ing.” Sophistication With the sophistication of the radio listener continuing to increase, jazz orien- ted product has been enjoying increased sales across the country, Allen related, noticing an increase in jazz product being aired at other stations in his chain across the country, and added, “A new breed of musicians are surfacing that more effec- tively lend themselves to jazz as far as their expertise is concerned. There has been a tremendous growth in music through jazz musicians, and with the listening audience’s taste in music evolving towards the direction of jazz we may be witnessing a different trend in music approaching us.” WRVR has a signal that reaches an ap- proximate 75-five mile radius. They are a 50,000 watt station with their tower on top of the Empire State Building, giving them a welcome boost. O/C Honors Brock Peters, Donald Byrd and Dick Gregory were honored by the Oppor- tunities Industrialization Centers of America recently, at a concert preceding its 12th an- nual gathering. Upon release of his Island LP “Some People Can Do What They Like," Robert Palmer concluded a bet with his friend, Swiss pastry chef Robert Bourban, who promised Palmer that if his record made the top 40, he would bake him 200 of his special tarts. Bourban, who has been dubbed the ‘‘dean of tarts, "now has to own up; the album reached #35 on the Cash Box top 200 albums chart last week. For the reception following Palmer’s upcoming engagement at the Palladium, Bourban will fly to New York to bake the 200 (the number was chosen for its bicentennial significance) special fruit tarts all at once, a task that will take up to 36 hours straight and probably will earn him a place in the Guinness Book of World Records . . . Don Kirshner's Rock Concert features Elton & Kiki, Rod Stewart, Maxine Nightingale, Richard Lewis and Gary Muledeer (rerun). phil dimauro POINTS WEST — CHRISTMAS IS THE SEASON — for “Best of" packages, and this year is no exception in that regard. There have been, just in the last couple of weeks, such packages from Lou Rawls, Stephen Stills, John Prine, George Harrison, The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band, Mott The Hoople, Steppenwolf, Grand Funk Railroad, Shirley Bassey, Abba and Linda Ronstadt (to name just a few). The difference this year is that these packages are put together much better than in previous times. The song selections, for example, are, with few exceptions, intelligent choices. Sure, there’s not that much leeway when you’re choosing an artist’s big hits, but these packages are not just slapped together. Often (Aretha Franklin’s hits diskis a good example) the tunes are presented in chronological or- der, and there’s extensive label information — giving session dates, producers, etc. The artwork, too, is generally attractive, high class. This year, then, the release of a “greatest hits" package does not necessarily mean that the artist hasn’t been able to get it together for a studio album with new songs . . . Williams, who used to be in charge of the singer's production company, now takes management responsibilities . . . john mankiewicz Ad Agency Promotes Concerts (continued from page 20) a 60-second public service spot to promote subscription sales for the entire concert series. Beginning with a slide that showed the orchestra and a pitch for subscriptions, the ad concluded with 20 seconds of the Gurman and Murtha spot for Ohlsson. “It was a nice moving visual instead of just a picture of something,” commented Fran Levy, public relations assistant for the Baltimore Symphony. Possibly as a result of this ad, she said, “We broke all records for subscriptions this year. And we really didn’t have that much more publicity this year than we had last year or the year before, except for that one spot. Apparently a lot of people noticed it, because we ran over 9,000 subscriptions.” Levy added that the ad ran three or four times a day all through the month of August. Occasionally, TV stations even put it on “right before the 11 o’clock news. Since they felt it was a nice, professional- looking tape, they weren’t embarrassed to show it. Usually, they put our PSAs on at three o’clock in the morning when no one’s watching.” Not all of the promoters who were inter- viewed, however, were as enthusiastic as Levy about the new videocassette spots. Joan Johnson, director of Pequod Produc- tions in Santa Clara, California, said that, although the TV spots for Fodor were "very well-produced,” they had only helped her agency sell 550 tickets for a concert in a hall that can hold 2700 people. She believed that the commercials would have had a greater effect if Fodor’s name were better known. Charisma Is The Key Gurtman and Murtha emphasized that the television spots by themselves would not sell out a house. In New York, for exam- ple, the agency usually runs print ads both for season subscriptions and weekly con- certs by specific artists. Then, in the last four days before a show, they will utilize radio and television spots to stimulate impulse-buying at the box office. If the pic- ture used to make the TV slide for the con- cert announcement is the same one that appeared in print and on posters, Gurtman and Murtha have found, viewers will be more prone to recall the earlier messages than they would be if a different image were used. “The key to making a successful artist, in addition to talent, is charisma," remarked BernieGurtman. “So we try to merchandise charisma. And what better way to do that is there than television?” Singles Bullets (continued from page 29) #78 KISS — Added at WAKY, WERC, WJET, WBBF, WGCL, WLEE, KEZY. Last week added at WFOM.
