SINGLESREVIEWS picks of flicweek RICK DEES AND HIS CAST OF IDIOTS (RSO 866) Dis-Gorilla (2:58) (Stafree/Gold Top — BMI) (Manuel, Fisher, Hall) The king of toungue-in-beak music is back on the primate prowl, just in time for the latest spaghetti-King Kong extravaganza. This one fits the old formula, substituting fur for feathers, but there are some new hooks here, including Tarzan howls, jungle drums and some sort of demented cackle that pops up now and then. Following a number one golden duck, can he do it again? THE COMMODORES (Motown 1408) Fancy Dancer (3:40) (Jobete/Commodores Entertainment — ASCAP) (Lapread, Richie) The Commodores have come into their own with the most modern R&B/pop, com- bining influences of Sly and Wonder to make them some of the best representatives of Motown music today. Number 40 with a bullet on the Cash Box top 100 R&B Singles chart, this record crosses over to pop as well this week, at #90. PHOEBE SNOW (Columbia 10463) Shakey Ground (3:29) (Jobete — ASCAP) (Bowen, Hazel, Boyd) Ms. Snow’s interpretation of this Temptations hit is full of the twists and turns of her constantly creative vocal stylization. A lively record built upon a thumping bottom, this tune finds her taking off like never before. Made for pop/R&B crossover, from the album “It Looks Like Snow.” OZARK MOUNTAIN DAREDEVILS (A&M 1888) You Know Like I Know (3:15) (Lost Cabin — • BMI) (Lee) An easygoing, melodic ballad, this record’s sweet melody is driven home by the tag, which features a chorus sung in “na-nas” in a fashion that builds up dramatically and leaves the listener hanging on for more. First-quality pop music from a group that has proven itself in the top 40 singles field. 10CC (Mercury 73875) The Things We Do For Love (3:32) (Man-Ken — BMI) (Stewart, Goldman) Now a two-member composing/performing team, lOcc’s Eric Stewart and Graham Gouldman have come up with a pop record that combines the best of a strong Beatles influence with solid rock ’n’ roil and the luxuriant harmonies that characterized their past efforts. Not a simple pop record, but if top 40 could latch onto “Bohe- mian Rhapsody,” this fine music shouldn’t be too hard to swallow. HAMILTON BOHANNON (Dakar 4560) (Dist. Brunswick) Gittin’ Off (3:29) (Hog/Bohannon — ASCAP) (Bohannon) Bohannon’s attraction is the skill with which he is able to produce simple earthy arrangements built around the most basic chord patterns, while slick arrangements seem to be the trend. Made for disco play, the rhythm here is carried by percussive, muted guitar chords and a thundering fuzz bass. MIKE OLDFIELD (Virgin 9510) (Dist. Epic) Portsmouth (2:02) (Front Line — ASCAP) (Traditional, Arr. Oldfield) Famed hermit of the recording studio, Mike Oldfield explores the sound of Irish folk music here, as orchestral overdubs slowly build the simple tune into an extensive production. Makes its point quickly. Though this record will find its most comfortable slot at FM stations stateside, note that it was #14 among U.K. singles last week. CONSUMER RAPPORT & WING AND A PRAYER FIFE & DRUM CORPS (Wing And A Prayer HS 76) (Dist. Atlan- tic) A Holiday Gift (3:16) A cute record for the holiday season that kicks off with a disco sample of “Jingle Bells,” followed by an orchestral “God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen,” which leads to an upbeat lead vocal on “I’m Dreaming Of A White Christmas." The subsequent “We Wish You A Merry Christmas” introduces the finale, “Auld Lang Syne.” Sounds like an overture. OHIO PLAYERS (Mercury 73753) Happy Holidays Pt. 1 (3:27) (Ohio Player/Unichappell — BMI) (Williams, Satchell, Pierce, Bonner, Middlebrooks, Beck, Jones) “Hi, the Ohio Players would like to wish you the hap- piest of holidays,” a dulcet voice announces over jingling bells. A mellow R&B song with holiday lyrics follows, and the production and arrangement are quite satisfying. This is a Christmas record, but the group behind it still pulls in the R&B and pop station adds. THE TYMES (RCA 10862) Savannah Sunny Sunday (3:16) (Chappell) (Galdston, Thom) A slow, stately song from this top-notch group of vocalists. The instrumental arrangement is expansive, and the hooks are in the multi-layered chorus. Though the group’s home is the R&B airwaves, this record has pop and easy listening possibilities. BARBI BENTON (Playboy 6094) Needing You (2:54) (Butler/Chappell — ASCAP) (Jackson, Yancy) From the “Something New” LP, a song penned by Marvin Yancy and Chuck Jackson, composers of much of Natalie Cole’s repertoire. Ms. Benton is backed by in- ventive orechestration, and the song has definite possibilities. A Robert Appere production. WIGGY BITS (Polydor 14369) Ellie (3:17) (Pink Pelican/Unichappell — BMI) (Ricciar- della, Cerniglia, Castro) Pop-rock from Long Island played by a group that in- cludes bits of Barnaby Bye and The Illusion. Heavily dis- torted guitars pervade an overall ambience that sounds as if it were recorded in a huge, reverberant hall. The vocals are harmonized for the most part, with no strong lead dominating. For top 40 and FM playlists. JOHNNY MATHIS (Columbia 10447) When A Child Is Born (3:41) (Beechwood — BMI) (Jay, Zacar) From his “I Only Have Eyes For You” album, this single sets a holiday theme against a gentle, understated melody. The hook seems to be Mathis’ optimistic speech, a wish for the joyful season. Though this record is easy- listening by nature, it could get some top 40 play in the Christmas season. CARL DAVIS & THE CHI-SOUND ORCHESTRA (Chi- Sound XW904) (Dist. UA) Show Me The Way To Love (2:41) (Gaetana/Thesaurus — BMI) (Davis, Washington) A beautifully recorded grand piano introduces this record, a strongly jazz-influenced disco record that features weaving solo and section saxaphones. The only vocals are provided by a whispering chorus. For discos and R&B playlists. PAUL CLICH WITH CHOYA (Buddah 553) Linda, Write Me A Letter (2:38) (Buddah/Mr. Chris — ASCAP) (Clich) A lighthearted pop love song with an appropriately bouncing beat. The lead vocal is multi-tracked, a female chorus supports, and the arrangementglistens with bells and strings. Geared toward the top 40-youth market. TOUCH OF CLASS (Midland International 10754)(Dist. RCA) You Got To Know Better (3:25) (Diagonal/Ask Me — BMI) (Jackson, Jackson) Suggestive lyrics combined with a New York disco arrangement (by John Davis) makes this a solid dance record. The key to this single is tightness and crispness of sound, along with decidedly purposeful vocal deliveries. For the R&B airplay route. FAITH, HOPE & CHARITY (RCA 10865) Life Goes On (3:22) (Van McCoy/Warner Tamerlane — BMI) (McCoy) An uplifting song in disco rhythm from this three- person vocal group, benefited as always by the compos- ing, arranging and producing talents of Van McCoy. The group sings the entire lyric as a unit here, as one vocalist breaks off to improvise over the chorus. The soaring str- ings, terse horn comments and decorative percussion are distinctive. GATO BARBIERI (A&M 1885) Fiesta (3:30) (Irving/Leandro — BMI) (Barbieri) This record is described perfectly by its title. Acoustical guitars carry the chords, myriad percussion fills in the background, and Barbieri carries the melody line to sizzling levels on saxophone. Spoken Spanish syllables break the record into three sections, so the piece has a chance to build up a few times. Produced by Herb Alpert, all this record’s unusual sounds ring through true and clear. EARL KLUGH (Blue Note XW924) (Dist. UA) Living Inside Your Love (3:15) (United Artists/Klugh- moon — ASCAP, Roaring Fork — BMI) (Klugh, Grusin) The title track of guitarist Klugh’s most recent album, which made a top 20 showing on the Cash Box Top 40 Jazz Albums chart as well as crossing to pop. (The LP was re-added to the Cash Box Top 200 Albums chart this week.) The vocals and arrangement are commercial in nature, but Klugh’s work on the acoustical guitar stands up to the best. STEVE LAWRENCE (UA XW927) You Take My Heart Away (3:39) (UA — - ASCAP, Unart — BMI) (Conti, Conners, Robbins) Lawrence’s version of the love theme from “Rocky” is a bit slower and less disco-fied than the Epic/Sweet City release, though the modern drumbeat is mixed gently in the rear. It’s hard to say whether there will be a real cover battle, since this record is safely within the MOR category while the other leans heavily toward pop. For now, that is. GABRIEL KAPLAN (Elektra 45369) Up Your Nose (3:52) (Kapian, Prestopino, Roe) Kaplan enters as the preacher, with sound advice for relieving tension. Simply let your arms hang loose atyour sides, take a deep breath, and yell “Up your nose with a rubber hose!” The music never stops, and a melody line and a beat will take this farther than usual for a comedy record. Guest appearance by Howard Cosell. WEAPONS OF PEACE (Playboy 6093) City (3:09) (After Dark/Euwin — BMI) (Franklin, Hardy, Henderson, Jr.)) Hard rocking funk pursues the lead vocalist as he complains that the pressures of the city are “getting him down.” The chorus draws attention via catchy offbeats, while the whole song is arranged around a bass line that surfaces with crystal clarity as the other instruments drop off during a middle verse. A good fusion of funk and heavier rock sounds, this record is for R&B program- ming. PHILLY DEVOTIONS (Columbia 10462) It’s Gotta Be This Way (3:25) (Irving — BMI) (Hampton, Banks) For R&B stations, a ballad executed in a slow blues rhythm. Anchored by a solid bass voice, this vocal group’s harmonies are impeccable, set against an arrangement favoring strings. We don’t mean to make statistical comparisons, but this song is much like something the Manhattans might record. THE PHILADELPHIA STORY (H&L 4679) People Users (3:19) (Chappell/Unichappell/Boca/Raton — ASCAP, BMI) (McNeal, Weiss, Rubin) A “story” song in the debut single of this group. The people users are “born losers, love abusers.” Funky message music' in the style of the Temptations, this record is slated for R&B playlists. 40 Cash Box/December 25. 197(

Believe it — the first news trickled that Arista Records would release “The Mon- kees Greatest Hits.” JUNE As generally warmer weather began to bring members of the younger generation outdoors, the music industry devised profitable methods of herding them together. Summer, 1976 was the season of the stadium/arena concert usually held in the open air. Facilities seating over 100,000 were filled to the brim with all-star triple bills of touring artists such as Peter Frampton, The Grateful Dead, the Jeffer- son Starship, The Who and Fleetwood Mac. “Average-sized” stadiums, usually seating at least 50,000 patrons, saw ap- pearances of one headliner plus strong supporter bills that included the Eagles, Elton John, Kiss, Yes, Jethro Tull and ZZ Top. The large indoor arenas remained ac- tive as well, adding to a proliferation of large scale concerts that could safely have : ;"2 labeled "unprecedented.” Even June 5/George Benson GEORGE BENSON EWHOME NEW SUCCESS Mout* o 2 ‘-t: Hen Ungoag* Adopted NtdonwxfeXP Pw»Roundup Steve Leber, part of the Leber-Krebs team that manages Aerosmlth and other heavy touring acts, had to comment that the situa- tion was bordering on overkill. “There will be too many acts out there this summer,” he stated seriously. “The concertgoing public will have their fill of large concerts, and will start looking for something new.” MORE HEADLINERS — ABC Records created a stir by implementing a new policy aimed at curbing the high rate of returns. The program offered discount incentives to dealers who kept their returns below cer- tain prescribed levels ... A survey of retailers indicated that bar-coding was seen as an improvement . . . Increased pressing costs threatened a yet to be seen rise in the wholesale price of 45s . . . Lieber- man Enterprises set acquisition of Musical Isle of St. Louis, Transamerica’s rack arm. Shelter Records entered a distribution deal with ABC Records. IN WASHINGTON — Two significant developments occurred in the passing of the new copyright bill. The House of Representatives raised the mechanical royalty to 2% cents, and the House Judiciary Committee extended the copyright to life of the author plus 50 years, June 26/Beatles meeting the standard followed in most in- ternational markets. THE ROAD AGAIN — Perry Como set the first real U.S. tour of his career during June. He would play at the Westchester Premiere Theatre outside New York, his first live ap- pearance in the metropolitan area since an engagement at the Paramount in Manhat- tan in 1944. JULY Over one five-week period, 16 albums debuted on the Cash Box Top 100 Albums chart, an unusually large total. At the time of the issue dated July 24, four of the albums released in that five-week period had reached the top ten: the Beatles reissue on July 3/Olivia Newton-John Capitol, the latest releases by Chicago and Neil Diamond on Columbia and the most recent by Jefferson Starship on Grunt/RCA. The heavy pre-summer and summer LP releases by major record com- panies were being felt, while the rest of the (continued on page 108) Profile: Top New Artist of 1976 Heart For Heart, 1976 proved to be the year that the American-born rock group took its Canadian success back across the border. The result was a substantial charting im- pact in the U.S. market with “Dreamboat Annie,” their debut album, certified platinum and their top ten single “Magic Man" certified gold. The heart of Heart is the sibling duo of Ann and Nancy Wilson. Ann is the lead vocalist with a belting style somewhat reminiscent of Grace Slick and Nancy provides the music for their material. Both girls come from a musical background which led from classical to folk to rock. In addition to Nancy and Ann, Heart also in- cludes Steve Fossen, Roger Fisher, Mike Derosier and Howard Leese. The group was a fixture on the club cir- cuit until they caught the attention of a Van- couver studio engineer, who brought them to producer Mike Flicker. The next step was a contract with Mushroom Records and the first international hit record for the group, as well as for its fledgling record company. Cash Box/December 25, 1976

CONVENTIONS POINT WEST — CBS Records held its annual convention in Los Angeles, where CBS Records president Bruce Lundvall pointed with confidence to the company’s two certified platinum albums and one platinum single, in addition to 24 gold albums and nine gold singles, all awarded during the year’s first six months. At the convention Larry Harris, vice presi- dent and general manager of the newly- formed CBS west coast-based label Por- trait (the name had not been revealed at the time), discussed the industry trends which had led to the label’s creation. “There was a period way back, when, maybe a decade ago. New York was a far more creative cen- ter of music. Then the pendulum swung toward Los Angeles. Now, it’s swinging back to a balance between the two” ... At the RCA convention, held in San Francisco, company president Ken Glancy traced the history of RCA Records back to 1901, when the newly developed talking machine “sounded like a parrot with a sore throat, yet was a new art form.” Glancy further stated that at the company’s 75th anniver- sary, the first six months’ sales and earn- ings were the best in RCA history . . . MCA Records highlighted new product at its an- nual convention in Los Angeles. INDUSTRY LOSES MERCER - Johnny Mercer, songwriter extraordinaire and co- founder of Capitol Records, died at the age of 66. AUGUST Talent acquisition is a priority that de- mands the unfailing concern of A&R departments all year, but this past August it seemed that certain record companies were out to make the most of their artist Aug. 7/Spinners signings, and where formal announce- ments were not made, news of interesting artist acquisitions leaked to the press. HOME FREE — After a four and one-half year battle in the courts, John Lennon was granted permanent resident status in the U.S., following a final hearing at which Gloria Swanson and Norman Mailer testified as character witnesses. WITH LIBERTY AND JUSTICE FOR ALL — If you've seen the cover of ‘‘New Nation” by Roderick Falconer on UA Records, you’re probably afraid of the guy. Even Melody Maker, in a phone interview, asked him whether he agreed that the LP art looked “rather Nazi.” Falconer, really quite a gentle, if forcefully intelligent person, explained that his total image embodied in his lyrics as well as the other trappings, is one of “austerity and rejection of the pragmatic attitude of the sixties. " What pragmatic attitude? “That all pervasive decadence summed up in the phrase, ‘Do your own thing’. ” What about the notion that during the six- ties, especially at Woodstock, the young generation reached a peak of mutual love and self-respect that hasn't been seen since? Of Woodstock, Falconer says he enjoyed it, but in retrospect he feels it was a “false brotherhood, based on self-indulgence rather than self- sacrifice. "Not to let Falconer, the philosopher, seem too inaccessible, he is after all a musi- cian, one who has appeared under other names on other labels. He had good things to say about his producer, Matthew Fisher, whose “A Salty Dog" is one of his favorite rock albums, though he probably won’t work with Fisher on his next LP, due sometime near the end of January. Retailers say it is not unusual to have a young customer buying these art- ists at the same time. As far as recording the traditional styles of jazz today, there is plenty of activity about. Chiaroscuro, Concord, Pablo, Vanguard and Choice are only some of the labels. Active musicians who represent the best of swing and bebop are still being recorded. If there has been any decline in recording representative styles, it would be at the opposite end of the spectrum. Few traditional LPs are being recorded because there are not many musicians still alive who continue to play the style. The avant garde of the 1960s is not being represented by new LPs very often and several major art- ists of “outside jazz” inclinations are currently without contracts. Yet activity in Europe and Japan is taking up some of the slack. It is possible for musi- cians to make LPs for three or four different European labels during a tour. Japan has long had arrangements to record “name” jazzmen with U.S. contracts for exclusive Japanese consumption. European labels such as Black Lion, Freedom, Sonet, MPS/BASF, Steeplechase and Black and Blue are turning out quality jazz LPs every week oftheyear. If anything, the activities of European and Japanese labels seem likely to increase in 1977. In the domestic market, 1976 was the year that George Benson received the first- ever platinum disc by a jazzman. The year that John Handy returned to recording after along hiatus and made the bestselling LPin the sixteen-year history of ABC/Impulse. A year when Norman Connors made a major breakthrough. It was a year when more jazz records were issued than ever before; when more jazz records were reissued than ever before: when more jazz records were sold than ever before. It was, more than anything, the year that jazz became a marketable commodity. Fats Waller would have been flabbergasted. Tom Waits (continued from page 57) back-to-the-alleys patter that set all free to soar from suburban prison walls to the depths of his tarnished neon city. Unlike a Hollywood actor who dons his demeanor nightly, Waits’ persona is irrefutably tied to his character. His strong- est stage stance is the one of drunken story-teller relating distorted visions of acute comi-tragedy reality. Waits lives his character or, perhaps, his character lives him. Whether it’s hanging out at an all-night diner, a sleazy strip joint or a crowded bus station, all these experiences are brought to the stage via his desperado degeneracy. When Waits isn’t leaning against his mike stand, head angled and fingers fondling a cigarette between snaps, he stoops over a piano from where he slowly pumps out jazz- tinged ballads, backed by a rhythm combo. His voice, the heir apparent to Louis Armstrong, easily adapts itself to the even- ing’s sporadic themes. While there is a genuine feeling of ambivalence in the direc- tion of his work, Waits is a master craftsman, continually polishing and refin- ing his repertoire to reach that fine edge of calculated spontaneity. r.r. C4SHBOX R.B Music Research: Which Method is Most Accurate? by Cookie Amerson LOS ANGELES — In discussing the most widely used method of music research used by black-oriented stations across the country, the question of the reliability of the store report has arisen more than once. Basically these questions arise because of the general inconsistencies that occur in dealing with the record stores. Keith Adams, program director at KDIA in Oakland, cites the main problem being that many stores do not keep records of quantity of product sold. Adams explained that “many PDs must deal with knowing that they have several opinions of how product is doing, as opposed to knowing what rec- ords were actually bought from a store.” Donnie Brooks, WAMM, on his problem of not being able to speak to the same person every week, “There are many times that people have just been hired and are unaware of what is happening at the store. The store itself may try to hype you because they may have bought too much of a particular product. I try to combat some of these problems by spot checking my stores and actually going in and purchasing a record to see the operation at work.” Not Enough Time Store personnel complain that radio sta- tions call when they are busy with several customers and want them to spend several minutes on the phone discussing records. One west coast store manager told CB, “Many people in a record store may feel that they are only one store out of twenty that a station may be calling, thereby mak- ing their one report not that meaningful, so if they haven’t had time to do a list for the week, they may unfortunately just tell the caller something to get him off the phone.” Opinions “The method used by many stations in getting information from stores usually calls for an opinion by the store clerk who has no guidelines upon which to base that opinion,” noted Steve Gaspar, who has worked in several phases of the music business and now is editor of a research sheet entitled Audience. Sales reports should be taken on the actual amount of records sold, and not on a sales clerk’s opinion of how he or she may think the record is selling. Gaspar went on to explain a method he believed could triple the accuracy of infor- mation received from stores. “Radio sta- tions should set up a scale for stores to follow that would give the store clerk some criterion for information given out. For ex- ample, the top five records could be rated as excellent, the next five rated very good, and the last five rated good; anything below fifteen records should be rated either slightly above average or slightly below average. In using this method,” stated Gas- par, “resulting information would be more reflective of actual amount of records sold that week. When all reports all received, a point system should be attached to each block — for instance, ten points to the top five block, eight points for the next five, six points for the next five — to build a mathematical scale. Then simply add up the points to see what is popular in your overall market. With this method, accuracy should increase tremendously as opposed to the other method of asking the store clerk for an evaluation. This procedure calls for no decision making by store per- sonnel, thereby narrowing the margin that allows for personal taste and other factors that affect a station receiving good un- biased information.” When To Add “While the record buyers are usually the opinion leaders when it comes to music, thereby making the quantitative informa- tion received from store reports invaluable in letting a programmer know when a new record is starting to get action in his market,” states Bill Moyes, “sales results can be very misleading in telling you where a record should go once you have decided to add the record to your list.” Moyes heads the radio division of the Omaha-based research firm, The Frank Magid Co. The Frank Magid Co. has done marketing research for some of the top sta- tions in the country and has been in business for over twenty years. Moyes went on to explain, “Sales results cannot tel! whether a record should be added to the ’A’ or ‘B’ rotation list, or when it should go into recurrent and from there to gold. Also sales reports alone will not tell you when a record is reaching the initial stages of burnout. Once you have decided to add a record to your list the question of where to put it is best left to other forms of research such as a good call-out method, reporter groups and a little to request.” A call-out method of research, explains Moyes, can putyou in touch with yourentire audience, as opposed to just your record buying audience, as when you are only tak- ing store reports. “When we go into a sta- tion, in addition to call-out research, we work up a representative cross section of that station’s listening audience of approx- imately 200 people, cycling in fifty at a time so that we do not keep the same group of people, and have them report to us each week about records that have been added, have been on for a while, and ones we are thinking of adding. We also take requests, asking in addition to the traditional ques- tion ‘What would you like to hear?,’ which records they want to hear more of or less of and the ones they are completely tired of. Of course the results of your research can only be as good as your sample, so working up a good cross section of your listening audience is of top priority.” Random Sample Dennis Waters, program director at 13Q in Pittsburgh, whose background is as a research-oriented programmer, explained the intricacies of constructing a random telephone sample. “The initial sample should proportionately represent the pop- ulations of the areas covered by the direc- tors. An initial list of approximately 1,200 random telephone numbers can give you a working sample of approximately 100 peo- ple. A specific sampling formula should be used, e.g., one number from every third page of the directory. A tally sheet should be made up of results of every call made. The caller askes at random what stations a person has listened to during the past week. If the respondent indicates he listened to your station, you then find out if he would be interested in helping the sta- tion by filling out a weekly questionnaire that would be sent to him in the mail with a stamped envelope addressed to the sta- tion. “To determine the statistical reliability of your sample it should be broken down in the following categories: homes with dis- connected numbers, homes that were never reached, homes that refused cooperation, those that were not listeners of your station, those that were but refused to cooperate, homes that were sent questionnaires but could not be reached again, and homes that were included in your final sample." The Role Of Research At R&B Stations (continued from page 162) ter groups are a radio luxury meant only for large chains with thousands of dollars to spend on music research and do not in- vestigate using these methods.“But there are ways of getting around the high cost of music research,” states Waters. “Students enrolled in communications classes will work in a radio station for class credit and the local Junior Achievement chapters usually have people who will work for a minimum wage. Jay Cook at WFIL in Philadelphia has graduate students from Temple University making approximately 10,000 calls a day from his station. So good research is not as far out of our grasp as it may seem.” Behavioral Psychologist Gone are the days when programmers specifically relied on their ears in determin- ing what music they would play, declared Caspar. “In this day and age of sophistica- tion, we realize that as a person gets older and is exposed to more and more product, his taste in music may change, but most assuredly he must continue to do his job at his radio station. In many cases a music director or program director must almost be a behavioral psychologist in determin- ing how to motivate people to listen to his station. This then takes us to motivational research, ‘semantic differential,’ which is a way of speaking to an audience to entice a specific demographic to listen to you, e.g., if your morning show is low in men, perhaps injecting some sports talk may attract them. Another manner of speaking to the audience is called the ‘child-parent syn- drome,’ which is where the announcer assumes the role of a parent in speaking to his audience (‘the child’) —- many people react to this. There are many areas that a good PD or MD may touch on to make his station more effective in his market, which is just part of good research.” Revamp Themselves It almost goes without saying that many stations across the country could do much to revamp their research methods to make them more accurate and more effective. At best, this sharing of ideas from people in the same or related fields has given us food for thought in order that we may expand our views and seek to improve wherever im- provement is needed. ash Box/December 25, 1976 175
